Designation is `settings.toolTypes` (the listTabs posture), toggled from the type's edit page ("Offer as a tool," PATCH `/api/types/[key]/tool`; built-in tool types refuse — the card would double). `custom-tools.ts` joins settings to the type registry for real labels; the record fan-out dresses the def (a deleted/hidden type retires the card, restoring restores it). The card renders the generic preview rows + a typed `AddContainedItemButton`; Add a Tool (record) and the Build sections editor both offer designated types; the collection full page carries the typed add. Drill-down, count gear, and bulk actions all ride existing machinery unchanged.
- **Task grouping, opt-in.** The Tasks widget gains `options.groupBy` (none | milestone | priority; default none) edited from the card's hover gear (SectionCountGear grew a "Group by" radio block writing through the same composition PATCH). Pure `task-grouping.ts` groups rows one way for the card (client) and the full list (server, which reads the record's tasks-instance option so the two agree). Milestone sections suppress the per-row flag chip (it would repeat the header).
- **Favorite highlights, visual only.** `ProjectCard.favorited` (from settings.favorites) renders a small accent star on the title and a subtle accent border/glow on the card frame (`projectCardFrameClass`), on the grid, list-view cards, and boards. Deliberately NO reordering ("nothing crazy") — noted for later, since lens pagination would need a query-side boost to float favorites honestly.
- **The passive check-in.** Viewing a widget-home record IS the review: `RecordViewBeacon` POSTs `/api/items/[id]/viewed`, which writes the PJ1 `checkin_reviewed` event throttled to one per 12h — the half-built loop (derived last_reviewed_at, digest staleness reset) finally has a writer, with no button. `DEFAULT_DIGEST.stalenessDays` 7 → 14. Per-project control: a muted "Check-ins" line beside Add a Tool (DigestControl popover: enabled + quiet window, writing `behaviors.digest`). Surfacing: `digest/stale.ts` (the runDigestNotify selection minus milestones — done/archived projects exempt, no-activity-ever exempt) renders quiet projects atop Tasks → Today as P1-styled "Check on <project>" rows — VIRTUAL rows, not created tasks, so there is nothing to dedup or clean up and opening the project dissolves the row. `checkin_reviewed` is filtered from the Recent Activity card display (plumbing, not narrative; the log keeps it).
**Rejected:** *a manual Check-in button* (Tyler's explicit call — reading the page is the gesture); *real auto-created P1 tasks* (data spam, dedup burden, trash on completion — a deterministic virtual row does the same job and self-heals); *a types-table column for tool designation* (settings jsonb models it without a core schema change).
**Verification:** `tsc`, `eslint`, `next build` clean; all 59 pure suites pass; user guide updated (ADR-189). NOT browser-verified this session — the preview click-through is the test.
**Affects:** `src/lib/widgets.ts`, `src/lib/custom-tools.ts` (new), `src/lib/settings.ts`, `src/app/api/types/[key]/tool/route.ts` (new), `src/components/build/ToolTypeToggle.tsx` (new), `src/app/build/types/[key]/edit/page.tsx`, `src/components/canvas/{WidgetCanvas,SectionGrid,SectionCountGear,DigestControl}.tsx`, `src/lib/task-grouping.ts` (new), `src/components/canvas/widgets/TasksWidget.tsx`, `src/app/items/[id]/collection/[key]/page.tsx`, `src/lib/project-cards.ts`, `src/components/projects/ProjectCardGrid.tsx`, `src/components/views/ViewRenderer.tsx`, `src/app/list/[type]/page.tsx`, `src/lib/composition.ts`, `src/app/api/items/[id]/viewed/route.ts` (new), `src/components/records/RecordViewBeacon.tsx` (new), `src/lib/digest/stale.ts` (new), `src/lib/record-widgets.ts`, `src/app/tasks/page.tsx`, `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`.

## ADR-201: MCP write tools reject unknown arguments instead of silently dropping them
**Date:** 2026-08-18
**Status:** accepted (Tyler, 2026-08-18) — CORE per ADR-183 (tightening validation on an existing MCP call); Brandon gets the heads-up via this entry. The mitigating frame: the tool schemas have declared `additionalProperties: false` all along; this makes the server enforce what the contract already promised, so any caller it breaks was already broken (its field was being thrown away).
**Context:** Observed failure 2026-08-18: a `create_item` call passed the note body as `body` instead of `bodyMarkdown`. The call "succeeded" and returned the created item — with an empty body. A follow-up `update_item` with the same wrong key errored `no fields to update`, which pointed away from the real cause. Root cause: nothing validates incoming tool args against the schema; `buildWriteRaw()` (`src/lib/mcp/tools/args.ts`) cherry-picks known keys and ignores the rest.
**Decision:** `buildWriteRaw()` builds the full allowed-key set (WRITE_FIELDS + the call's `extra` keys + `bodyMarkdown` + a new `handlerKeys` param for args the handler reads itself: `relateTo` on create, `id` on update) and throws `ItemError("bad_request", …)` naming any leftover key, with a did-you-mean hint for the likely body mis-names (`body`/`content`/`text`/`markdown` → `bodyMarkdown`) and the accepted-field list. `update_item` also pre-empts the shared lib's bare `no fields to update` with a message that names the tool's own fields (the shared `item-mutations.ts` message can't say `bodyMarkdown`, and it used to fire exactly when a caller mis-named it — that shared message is unchanged). Accepted parameter names are untouched: validation only. One retired name goes with it: `kind` is dropped from WRITE_FIELDS — ADR-055 retired the column, `parseItemPayload` never parses it, and neither tool schema advertises it, so it was a dead pass-through that the new error message would have listed as accepted.
**Rejected:** *full JSON-Schema validation at the transport* (a validator dependency for one failure mode, rule 5); *silently accepting `body` as an alias* (two names for one field forever, and the schema says otherwise); *changing the shared `item-mutations.ts` message to mention `bodyMarkdown`* (that layer serves REST, where the field really is `body`).
**Verification:** new pure suite `scripts/verify-mcp-write-args.mts` (11 checks: rejection + hints + legit calls pass-through), auto-discovered by verify-ci; `tsc` and `eslint` clean; grep confirms no verify script or internal caller passes a now-rejected key.
**Affects:** `src/lib/mcp/tools/args.ts`, `src/lib/mcp/tools/items.ts`, `scripts/verify-mcp-write-args.mts` (new).

## ADR-202: The stacked task row — description line, connections strip, project chip, click-to-edit date — and the capped excerpt carve-out
**Date:** 2026-08-18
**Status:** accepted (Tyler, 2026-08-18) — mostly NOT core (row UI + batched reads), with ONE core-adjacent piece flagged for Brandon: the excerpt read bends the "list queries never select body" invariant, see below.
**Context:** Tyler's tasks-screen cleanup (2026-08-18, with a mock). The flat single-line row hid everything: the body (often the actual instruction, e.g. an imported Todoist description), the connections (tags rode at the leading edge but people/records didn't show at all), the project, and recurrence. The date was read-only, so a quick reschedule meant the row menu or the canvas. Subtask folding already existed (ADR-199's n/m pill), but sat at the row's trailing edge.
**Decision:**
- **The row stacks (TaskListRow.tsx):** title line (title, milestone flag, P-badge, status chip, then the date at the far right — kept where it was, per Tyler), a one-line body excerpt under it when the task has one, then a meta line: the n/m subtask pill (still closed by default), the connections strip, and the project chip on the far right.
- **The excerpt (the flagged piece):** `taskRowMeta` (new, `src/lib/task-row-meta.ts`) selects `left(body->>'text', 240)` — a fixed DB-side head, never the body column — and the pure `excerptLine` (`src/lib/excerpt.ts`, verify-covered) reduces it to one markdown-stripped line. This is a deliberate, capped carve-out of the "no `body` in list queries" invariant: the rule's intent (small list payloads) holds at ≤240 chars/row, but the letter is bent, so it rides in this ADR for Brandon's eyes rather than shipping silently. The cap is a constant; don't widen it or copy the pattern elsewhere without re-arguing this.
- **Connections:** all outgoing edges (mention edges excluded — body links are the body's affordance) batched per page in the same helper, tags first. The first project-role edge (home preferred) becomes the right-edge chip with a "Parent / Project" breadcrumb (one more batched read over the projects' own home edges); the rest render in a horizontally scrollable strip (`ConnectionStrip.tsx`, `[data-scroll-x]` so SwipeRow yields, ADR-142) with a "›" pill when chips are hiding. Project-scoped surfaces (the Projects tab's cards, a record's task list) pass `showProject={false}` — the chip would repeat their header.
- **Click-to-edit date (`TaskDateEdit.tsx`):** the date text is a button opening the shared draft-commit `DateInput` (ADR-169). It edits **what's shown** — scheduled if set, else due (Tyler's explicit pick over always-scheduled) — plus Clear; an undated row gets a hover-ghost "＋ date" that sets scheduled. A repeating task shows a loop glyph beside the date (read-only; the rule lives on the canvas).
- **Pill placement by context slot:** `SubtaskExpandableRow` gains `pillPlacement="slot"` + `<SubtaskPillSlot />` (a function child can't cross the server→client boundary), so the redesigned row puts the pill on its meta line while the generic list / views / widgets keep the trailing-edge default untouched.
**Rejected:** *a stored `excerpt` column* (schema change + backfill for a glance line jsonb the DB can substring); *selecting the full body in list queries* (the invariant exists for exactly this temptation); *a gradient overflow fade on the strip* (rows sit on varying backgrounds — page, hover wash, project cards — so a hardcoded fade color always mismatches somewhere; the "›" pill doesn't).
**Verification:** `tsc`, `eslint`, `next build` clean; all 61 pure suites pass including the new `scripts/verify-task-excerpt.mts` (19 checks on the line extractor). Browser check: the Vercel preview click-through is the review gate before merge.
**Affects:** `src/lib/excerpt.ts` (new), `src/lib/task-row-meta.ts` (new), `src/components/tasks/{TaskListRow,TaskDateEdit,ConnectionStrip}.tsx` (row rebuilt, two new), `src/components/subtasks/SubtaskExpandableRow.tsx`, `src/app/tasks/page.tsx`, `src/app/items/[id]/collection/[key]/page.tsx`, `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`, `scripts/verify-task-excerpt.mts` (new).

**Addendum (same branch, 2026-08-18):** two follow-ons from Tyler's preview review. (1) The row's date popup moved onto the shared `Popover` (body portal — the first cut's in-flow absolute panel clipped under the row) and both it and the canvas Schedule/Due popovers now render a Todoist-shaped picker: `DayPickerPanel` (quick-pick rows with resolved weekdays + `MonthCalendar` month grid + the free-text box) with Time/Repeat expanders on the row popup reusing `ScheduledTimeControl`/`RecurrenceControl` bare. (2) The task canvas rail became a visually separate tinted panel (`CanvasTwoPane` gains opt-in `railPanel`; tasks pass it, events unchanged), narrower (248), with Todoist-style stacked sections: label line over an icon+value line (`RowFace` restyled; Schedule/Due/Priority get glyphs), Project hoisted to the top, the "Properties" umbrella heading removed (each field self-labels), and relation/People fields drawing their own label line with a right-aligned "+" (`RelationField` gains `heading`/`readOnlyChips`; `RelationProperties`/`PeopleRow` gain `rail`). Classic canvas layouts are byte-identical (all new modes opt-in).

**Addendum 2 (same branch, 2026-08-18, Tyler's second preview round):** the Tags/People rail sections open their picker on a click anywhere in the section (like Priority; chips/✕/input keep their own jobs via a closest() guard); Priority's value sits inline-right of its label (`RowFace inline`); list rows color the project name with the accent; the whole list row is clickable through a stretched title-link overlay (interactive bits `z-[1]`-raised; the excerpt became plain text, no hover shift); the task canvas drops its right padding at the split so the rail panel reaches the container edge; completing from a list optimistically fades the row out (`SubtaskCheckbox vanishRow` — deliberate closest("li") DOM styling, restored on failure, since the server-rendered li is out of React state's reach) instead of lingering until the coalesced refresh; the tasks page's serial reads went parallel (getType+tz; rollups+meta+staleProjects); the tab row gained **Overdue** (before Projects — every past-due task, reschedulable in place) and the **Inbox tab became All** (every active task; untriaged capture keeps /inbox); and the add card treats a word-boundary "/" in the title as "jump to description" (dates like 9/13 and URLs don't trigger). Guide updated.

**Addendum 3 (same branch, 2026-08-18, Tyler's third round):** (1) **Person gets a built-in Image** — migration `0053` (+ seed mirror) appends a url-kind `image` property to the person type's property_schema, guarded so an owner-added `image` field is left byte-identical (types-row data change, ADR-199's 0052 posture — flagged in COLLAB.md). `personImage()` (pure) reads it; the new `PersonAvatar` (client, onError fallback) renders the face as a circle — on project cards' people row (initials fallback, the pre-avatar look) and on task rows' person chips (glyph fallback), via an `image` field on `taskRowMeta` connections. Plain `<img>`, not next/image (owner-supplied hosts). (2) **The add card grows Tag and Person chips + a working kebab.** Tag chip picks from the loaded tag list or creates by name (merged + name-deduped with "#" tokens at save); Person chip is a small person typeahead feeding the same `linked` list "@" uses (related edges); both are Quick-Add-hideable (`tags`/`person` keys, Settings list updated). The dead ⋯ button became a real chip-height kebab: it lists the task type's OTHER custom scalar properties (relation + multi_select excluded) and opens a compact per-kind editor (text/number/url/phone/email/date/checkbox/select) whose values ride the POST's properties. `pendingTags` is computed before `persist()` so verify-optimistic-tasks' parse-before-branch check stands.

**Addendum 4 (same branch, 2026-08-18, Tyler's fourth round):** the person page gets a real picture box (`PersonImageBox`, rendered by MarkdownCanvas for person only, replacing the raw url row in both the classic and grid layouts): a square that opens upload-or-URL — uploads are center-cropped SQUARE on a canvas (deterministic v1 of "force square"; a drag-to-position cropper is the follow-up) and capped at 512px, then ride the standard presigned-R2 attachment path, with the stable public URL landing in `properties.image`. Add-card fixes from live use: the kebab hides entirely when the task type has no custom scalar properties (schema now loads on mount), its icon line is h-5 so the chip height matches its siblings, all four chip popovers (date/tag/person/kebab) dismiss on outside click via a shared `[data-chip-pop]` guard, clicking anywhere outside the card cancels it (Cancel still works), and the Date chip now opens the shared DayPickerPanel instead of a bare date input — one date UI everywhere.

**Addendum 5 (same branch, 2026-08-18, Tyler's fifth round):** (1) **Faces on the project page's header People chips** — `WidgetItemRow` gains `image` (populated by the shared `row()` mapper for person rows; null elsewhere), `WidgetCanvas` passes it through, and `ProjectPeople` renders `PersonAvatar` (initials fallback) in place of its hand-rolled initials circle. (2) **A created task can no longer lose its project** (Tyler hit it live on a record's full task list): REST `POST /api/items` gains an optional, additive `relateTo: [{targetId, role?}]` (the ADR-183 carve-out) written server-side in the same request; failures come back as `relateErrors` instead of vanishing. `AddTaskCard` now sends the destination project, "@"-linked items, and existing tags through it — only brand-new tags keep the post-create flow (the tag must exist first) — and toasts when the server reports a relate failure. This also fixes the offline outbox's orphan hole: the replayed create body carries `relateTo`, so a task captured offline comes back WITH its project. `verify-optimistic-tasks` updated to pin the new shape (+3 checks).

## ADR-203: One owner resolution per request — the vanished-chrome incident
**Date:** 2026-08-19
**Status:** accepted (Tyler, 2026-08-19) — NOT core: `resolveOwner`/`resolveOwnerState` signatures and the `AuthProvider` interface are unchanged; this hardens internals (the ADR-184 posture). Auth-adjacent, so COLLAB carries the heads-up.
**Context:** Tyler, on prod after a cold Safari start: the Today page rendered his real tasks while the nav, user menu, and his accent color were gone (default blue) — "as if it doesn't have my account yet." One more navigation rendered everything. So within a single request, the PAGE resolved the owner while the LAYOUT and NAV did not. Three structural findings: (1) the root layout, `Nav.tsx`, and every page each call `resolveOwner()` independently — three resolutions per request that are allowed to disagree; (2) the layout swallows any failure into default chrome with a bare `catch { /* defaults */ }`; (3) `clerkAuthProvider.getCurrentUser()` makes a NETWORK call to Clerk's Backend API (`currentUser()`) on every invocation just for the email, which `resolveOwnerState` only needs on its clerk_id-miss fallback — so a transient Clerk flake read as "signed out." A cold-start correlation (first request of the day = cold Neon compute + a burst of parallel Clerk calls) explains why it recurs after browser restarts.
**Decision:**
- **`resolveOwnerState` wrapped in React `cache()`** — the layout, Nav, and page now await the SAME resolution, so the chrome and the content can never tell two stories. A failure is now consistent-and-loud (the request errors) rather than split-and-silent. In route handlers cache() is a passthrough; both functions keep their exact signatures for the ~80 callers.
- **One retry (~300ms) on the resolution's first DB read** — the cold-compute flake becomes latency, not a signed-out morning.
- **The Clerk email fetch can no longer fake a sign-out** — `currentUser()` failures fall back to a null email; `auth()`'s local JWT verification alone decides signed-in/out, and the clerk_id lookup doesn't need the email.
- **The layout's defaults fallback logs** (`layout.settings` warn, rule 9), rethrowing Next's `DYNAMIC_SERVER_USAGE` marker so builds keep their dynamic detection.
**Rejected:** *caching `getSettings`* (updateSettings re-reads after writes in the same request — a stale-after-write footgun for a cosmetic dedupe); *a Suspense/error boundary around Nav* (would make disagreement prettier instead of impossible); *redirect-to-sign-in on a null owner* (still loops, per ADR-184).
**Verification:** `tsc`, `eslint`, `next build`, all 60 pure suites pass. The incident itself is timing-dependent — the proof is the next cold morning rendering normally, and the drain staying quiet (or showing the new `layout.settings` warn if something still slips).
**Affects:** `src/lib/owner.ts`, `src/lib/auth/clerk.ts`, `src/app/layout.tsx`, `runbook.md` §7.

## ADR-204: Widget-home is an explicit opt-in for custom types, and the tool-card add works for custom types
**Date:** 2026-08-19
**Status:** accepted (Tyler, 2026-08-19, from live use) — adjusts one ADR-200-era default, so it rides in COLLAB.md for Brandon's eyes; the capability model, schema, and canvas resolution are untouched (no migration, no new column — `types.capability = 'widget-home'` already models per-type opt-in, which is exactly why this is a default flip and not a build).
**Context:** Tyler created a "Project Purchases" custom type and hit two things. (1) The type silently got the full widget homepage (Tools grid, Add a Tool, progress-flavored chrome) because TypeBuilder wrote `capability: "widget-home"` on every custom type since 2026-07-01 — a simple record type read as "treated as a Project" without ever asking for it. (2) He flipped **Offer as a tool** on the type (ADR-200), the card appeared on a project, and the card's "+ Add" did nothing: `/api/records/[id]/contain` carried a hardcoded built-in allowlist (`task/note/milestone/event/link/mindmap`), so the custom type got a 400 — which `AddContainedItemButton` swallowed with a bare `return`, the exact silent failure rule 9 exists to forbid.
**Decision:**
- **"Project-style page" is a checkbox on the type editor, off by default for new types.** TypeBuilder no longer defaults custom types to `widget-home`; the checkbox writes it. One capability slot, three explicit claimants (tabs, project-style, a borrowed bespoke canvas) — checking one unchecks the other, and the checkbox hides where it can't apply (system types, types borrowing a real bespoke canvas). Unchecking it on a type that has it clears the capability back to null (the plain document canvas).
- **Existing types are grandfathered ON, no migration.** Every type created under the old default already carries `capability = 'widget-home'` in its row, so it keeps the page it has; its checkbox simply starts checked, and unchecking it is the one-click off. Nothing changes on either instance until an owner touches a type.
- **The contain route accepts any live type.** The built-in set stays as a fast path (it includes `milestone`/`mindmap`, which are hidden types); anything else is checked against `listTypes()` (live, non-hidden). Downstream was already generic — `createItem` + a home edge with role `contains`.
- **The add button toasts on failure** (`showToast` from ActionToast) instead of returning silently.
- **MCP is already right and unchanged:** `create_type` treats `capability` as omit-for-default, so the MCP surface was opt-in all along; this brings Build to the same posture.
**Rejected:** *a tools-picker at flip-time* ("pick which tools the page starts with") — the page already starts from the standard composition and Add a Tool shapes it from there; a second picker at the checkbox is a nice-to-have, queued, not blocking the default fix. *Folding the built-in allowlist into the registry check* — `milestone` and `mindmap` are hidden types that `listTypes()` excludes, so the set stays as the fast path with a comment saying why. *Project-like types as tools on projects* (a hub type as a card on another record) — deliberately NOT decided here; it's the open recursion/containment question in next_steps.md, wanted as a real discussion with Brandon first.
**Verification:** `tsc`, `eslint`, `next build`, all pure suites incl. `verify-user-guide`. Live check: new custom type → plain canvas; check the box → widget home; offer as tool → a project card's "+ Add" creates and opens the item.
**Affects:** `src/components/build/TypeBuilder.tsx`, `src/app/api/records/[id]/contain/route.ts`, `src/components/canvas/widgets/AddContainedItemButton.tsx`, `src/lib/modules.ts` (comment), `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`.

**Addendum (same branch, 2026-08-19, Tyler):** the tool cards' hover gear grows **Rename** — a per-record display title for any card ("Docs" → "Sermon research" on one project, untouched everywhere else), stored as `options.title` on the widget instance in the record's composition (the same PATCH mechanism as `options.limit`/`groupBy`; the parser already passes options through, so no shape change). The pure reader is `widgetTitle()` in `composition.ts` (trim + 60-char cap, null = no override); the card header AND the card's full drill-down page (`/items/[id]/collection/[key]`) both honor it, so the two never disagree — which is also why the drill-down's composition resolution was hoisted out of its task-only block (one extra `types` row read on non-task collections, picker-sized). The gear now renders on EVERY card, not just collection/timeline ones — the count presets stay conditional on a preview cap, but Rename applies universally (`SectionCountGear` kept its name; the count is still its founding job). Empty save removes the key and restores the default. Guide updated.

## ADR-205: The Today subtask fold — one place per task, pre-expanded, overdue never hides
**Date:** 2026-08-19
**Status:** accepted (Tyler, 2026-08-19, from live use) — NOT core: list-surface rendering + additive props on shared components (`SubtaskExpandableRow.defaultOpen`, `SubtaskCheckbox.openSubtasks`, both default-off/0 so every other caller is byte-identical). COLLAB carries a heads-up because the parent-completion toast is visible on Brandon's instance.
**Context:** Tyler, using Today daily: a dated subtask rendered as a flat top-level row next to its own parent, and the pair read wrong two ways — it wasn't obvious which was the parent, and the adjacency implied the parent couldn't be checked until the child was. Meanwhile strict folding (top level = parentless only) would make a dated subtask vanish whenever its parent wasn't on the list, and blocking parent completion until children finish was rejected outright: finishing a parent can genuinely moot its children, and the hierarchy should inform, never gate.
**Decision:** on the two today surfaces (the Today home page's Tasks section and `/tasks` → Today), **a task renders in exactly one place**, decided by the pure `foldTodayTasks` in `src/lib/subtask-fold.ts` (shared by both surfaces so they can't disagree; `verify-subtask-fold` pins it, 22 checks):
- A **due-today** task whose parent is anywhere on the page folds under the parent — no top-level row of its own — and the parent's subtask tree **starts expanded** (`expandIds` → `SubtaskExpandableRow defaultOpen`, which fetches the subtree on mount), so the folded work is visible without a click. The pill still collapses it.
- An **overdue** task folds only when its parent is also overdue. Overdue is where the owner acts (the roll-forward), so an overdue child never hides behind a merely due-today parent — it stays flat in the Overdue group with its breadcrumb chip for context. The Today home roll count is computed PRE-fold, matching what the endpoint actually moves.
- A task whose parent is **not on the page** stays flat, always: dating a subtask means "on my plate today" regardless of its parent. The helper also restores any fold whose ancestor-climb finds no rendered row (only reachable with a corrupt parent cycle) — flat beats hidden, always.
- When folds chain, the climb pre-expands the topmost rendered ancestor; the tree renders recursively so the whole chain is visible.
- **Parent completion stays a plain checkbox.** Completing a parent with open children fires an informational toast ("Completed. N subtasks still open") via `SubtaskCheckbox`'s new `openSubtasks` prop — informed, never blocked. A "complete them too" toast action was considered and deliberately deferred until real use asks for it.
- The Today home page's lightweight rows adopt the shared expandable row (n/m pill + inline tree, `childRollups` batched); Focus-zone rows get the pill but never fold anything — focus is an explicit, curated set. All, Upcoming, and Overdue tabs stay flat on purpose (All is the inventory; Upcoming is day-paged, where a dated subtask must appear under its own day).
**Rejected:** *blocking parent completion until children are done* (gates instead of informs; Tyler: "annoying"); *strict folding* (dated work disappears); *flat with duplication* (the child both flat and inside the parent's tree — the confusion that started this).
**Verification:** `tsc`, `eslint`, `next build`, all pure suites incl. the new `scripts/verify-subtask-fold.mts` (22 checks: fold, carve-out, off-page parent, chains, mixed chains, cycle safety, order preservation).
**Affects:** `src/lib/subtask-fold.ts` (new), `scripts/verify-subtask-fold.mts` (new), `src/components/subtasks/{SubtaskExpandableRow,SubtaskCheckbox}.tsx`, `src/components/tasks/TaskListRow.tsx`, `src/app/tasks/page.tsx`, `src/app/_today-home.tsx`, `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`.

**Addendum (same day, 2026-08-19, Tyler):** subtask creation graduates to the full add card. "+ Add subtask" on a task's canvas used to be a bare title input (Enter to add, nothing else); it now opens the same `AddTaskCard` used everywhere a task is created — date/priority/tag/person chips, "/" to description, "@" links, NL dates in the title, the custom-property kebab — via a new `parentId` mode: the card posts `body.parentId`, the destination picker hides (a subtask's place IS its parent — no inbox flag, no project destination, though a typed "+project" still becomes a plain project relation rather than a silent no-op), and the button reads "Add subtask." `AddSubtask` is now a thin wrapper over `InlineAddTask` (which gained `parentId` + `buttonClassName` pass-throughs and `w-full` on its card/provisional rows so flex-wrap hosts give them their own line), keeping the optimistic provisional-row + settle flow for free and the deliberately bright button (Tyler, 2026-08-14). Create-time subtask dates are stored absolute — the parent-offset mechanic stays where it lives, in the canvas `SubtaskSchedule` edit control. Guide updated.

**Addendum 2 (2026-08-20, Tyler's live-use round, screenshots):** three follow-ons. (1) **The fold now covers all the task lists**, because Upcoming showed the exact duplication the fold exists to kill (a dated subtask flat in its day AND inside its parent's expanded tree): Upcoming folds **per day** (a subtask under its same-day parent, pre-expanded; a subtask whose parent sits on another day keeps its own flat row under ITS day), Overdue folds overdue-under-overdue pre-expanded (the header count stays pre-fold — it names how many tasks are overdue, not how many rows render), and **All folds collapsed** — the inventory reads as a tree, click the arrow (Tyler's original ask verbatim). Same pure `foldTodayTasks`, no new rule shapes. (2) **Dates in the subtask tree are click-to-edit**: `MiniRow` renders each of a task node's dates through `TaskDateEdit`, which gained a `minimal` mode (date-only popover, no Time/Repeat expanders — the subtree payload doesn't carry recurrence/time, and a "no rule" RecurrenceControl on a task that HAS a rule could overwrite it). `SubtaskExpandableRow` gains an optional `today` (app-timezone) threaded from the task-tab and Today-home hosts, local-day fallback elsewhere. (3) **`SubtaskSchedule` (the canvas subtask date control) opens the standard Popover + DayPickerPanel** instead of a bare date input — same offset-from-parent commit logic, just the normal picker. Also in the batch: `v1-goals.ts` Tyler statuses re-called from live use (tasks/notes/projects done, Papers pulled back to in_progress, Songs in_progress, Sermons partially complete via Brandon's module version). Guide updated.

**Addendum 3 (2026-08-20, Tyler's second live round):** three fixes. (1) **The tree's date popup looked dead on the task tabs — the write always landed; the DISPLAY was stale.** The expanded subtask tree renders from client state (`nodes`, fetched once per expansion), which `router.refresh()` can't reach — so picking "Today" committed the PATCH, closed the popover, and changed nothing visible. `TaskDateEdit` gains `onCommitted`, and the tree refetches its subtree through it (`load(force)`); the canvas control never had the problem because it keeps its own local state. (2) **An undated subtask in the tree now has a "＋ date" ghost trigger** (scheduled — the planning field; hover-revealed like the row ghost) instead of nothing to click. (3) **The Tools (default sections) editor on a type's edit page now renders only for types that resolve to the widget canvas** (`canvasIdForType(...) === "widgets"`: project, pursuit, opted-in custom types) — it rendered unconditionally, so a plain document type still showed a Tools panel and read as "still treated as a Project" after ADR-204. Also: `v1-goals.ts` Tyler's list gains the parked item-windows round (peek + full screen + arrange + their bugs) as a 1.0 goal, per Tyler.

**Addendum 4 (same day, Tyler's screenshot of a long checklist):** completed subtasks in the expanded tree hide by default behind a **"Show N completed"** line at the tree's bottom ("Hide completed" flips back). Pruning is recursive — a done node's subtree rides out with it, and N counts everything tucked away, so an open child under a done parent is hidden but honestly counted. Checking a subtask off in the tree refetches it (`SubtaskCheckbox` gains `onToggled`, same posture as `TaskDateEdit.onCommitted`), so the row tucks away instead of lingering struck-out on stale client state.

**Addendum 5 (same day, Tyler):** two small ones. (1) `file:///…` URLs on link items looked broken — a browser refuses to navigate to a local file from a web page (a security rule no app can override), so the click silently did nothing. New shared `SmartHref` (`src/components/ui/SmartHref.tsx`): normal URLs open in a new tab exactly as before; a `file:` URL renders as a copy-on-click button with a toast ("paste it into the address bar"). Wired on the two link surfaces (LinkList rows + the longform byline URL chip); use it anywhere else an item URL renders as an anchor. Guide notes the behavior and why. (2) The "Offer as a tool" description now quotes the type label ("Put "Project Purchases" in the …") — Tyler read the label as merging into the following word.

## ADR-206: Local hub/spoke alongside cloud: sync spine, local runtime, cutover plan
**Date:** 2026-08-22
**Status:** accepted (Tyler, verbal, 2026-08-22). CORE: touches the provider interfaces (auth, scheduler, DB driver), the cross-cutting invariants (a sync engine reads and writes every synced table), and the machine/MCP API contract (a new `/api/machine/sync` endpoint and a new peer-auth mechanism). This ADR activates `explorations/local-pc-hub.md` from exploration into a scheduled build; the full phase-by-phase plan lives in `plans/local-hub-idea-to-cutover.html` (gitignored local artifact, the working source of truth for the build).
**Context:** The local-pc-hub exploration (consolidated 2026-08-15) landed the shape: same app, same schema, same repo on every device, each with its own local Postgres, synced over a Tailscale mesh, with Brandon's always-on PC as the hub peer hosting the MCP, phone PWA, email-in, and crons through a Tailscale Funnel. What was missing was a build strategy that didn't put a week of production data at risk. The exploration's "localhost test week" probe implied a fork: live on a local copy for a week, then somehow reconcile. The plan replaces that probe with **alongside operation**: the existing Vercel + Neon deployment becomes **peer #1, the first hub**. The sync engine ships in shared code and lands on prod as an additive migration; Brandon's PC runs the full stack locally as a spoke syncing continuously against the cloud hub, and both copies stay live and identical for as long as he wants. **Cutover is a role swap**, not a migration: flip the MCP connector and phone URL to the PC's Funnel, reorder the hub list so the cloud becomes the backup peer. There is never a fork, so there is no data-loss window and nothing to reconcile by hand.
**Decision:** build the hub/spoke model alongside the cloud deployment, per the fifteen decisions landed 2026-08-22 (each weighed against the code as it actually is):
1. **Real embedded Postgres, not PGlite.** Ledgr leans on pg_trgm, FTS, jsonb, and (new here) triggers, and a hub serves many concurrent surfaces; PGlite is single-connection with partial extension coverage. The `embedded-postgres` npm package downloads per-platform binaries (Windows and Linux), and the supervisor runs it as a child process: no system install for the user.
2. **Oplog capture via Postgres row-level triggers, not app hooks.** Research found 14 write sites that bypass the `item-mutations.ts`/`relations.ts` funnels (todoist sync, calendar sync, recurrence advance, notify stamps, mentions, and more) plus 14 independent `types` setters. App hooks would drift the day someone adds the next write site; a trigger on the synced tables logs every write forever, including future ones. Plain SQL, so the same migration runs on Neon.
3. **Conflict clock: per-field last-writer-wins on the op's timestamp, device-id tiebreak; HLC deferred.** Single user, so concurrent cross-device edits of the same field inside a clock-skew window are rare, and a losing body lands in `revisions` anyway. Cursoring uses a per-device monotonic sequence, never time, so skew can't lose ops. If observed skew ever bites, upgrading the timestamp to an HLC is additive; this is the calibration knob, left in on purpose.
4. **Vercel + Neon stays as the secondary/backup hub after cutover.** It is the already-built answer to the backup-hub requirement and keeps the "PC died mid-trip" fallback (flip the MCP URL back, work against day-old data, merge on return). Dropping Neon entirely is a separate later decision, made from experience.
5. **No local username/password in v1.** Spokes get a no-login `localAuthProvider` (env `LEDGR_LOCAL_OWNER_EMAIL`, server bound to localhost/tailnet only, so the machine login is the boundary); the hub's public Funnel surface keeps Clerk exactly as today. `devAuthProvider` already proves the fixed-identity shape; a password system would be standing code (hashing, sessions, reset) protecting a machine the owner already unlocks. Revisit only if a shared-family-machine case appears.
6. **Updates: prompted everywhere via the existing ADR-194 `/build/updates` card.** The whole surface (report, schema axis, gate, button, changed-commits list) is reused; only the apply strategy is new. On a local peer, "Update now" signals a **sidecar supervisor** (git pull, `npm ci` if the lockfile changed, fresh-directory build, migrate, keep-last-good swap; any failure keeps serving the last good build). Hub auto-update is a supervisor config flag, deferred until keep-last-good is proven.
7. **Dev/preview workflow unchanged.** Dev stays the dev Neon branch + Vercel previews; local peers are runtime installs of released code, not dev environments. Nothing about how Brandon and Tyler build changes.
8. **Blobs stay on R2 for all peers through cutover.** Every peer reads and writes the same bucket, so there is zero blob sync to build now. The local blob store + OneDrive tiering (the "Netflix model") is a post-cutover phase behind the existing `StorageProvider` interface.
9. **Probes 1-2 retired; probe 3 folded into phase 5; probe 4 promoted.** Alongside operation replaces the pain-measurement and localhost-week probes. Probe 3 (Funnel the PC, point a claude.ai MCP connector and a Clerk phone sign-in at it) is the first checkpoint of phase 5 rather than a step-0 spike (Brandon's call, same day): nothing in phases 1-4 depends on the Funnel, the walkthrough needs Brandon's PC and accounts anyway, and Cloudflare Tunnel is the drop-in fallback if Funnel disappoints. Probe 4 (the oplog spike) becomes phase 1 proper.
10. **Installer = one downloaded bootstrap script** (`install.ps1` now, `install.sh` later), not an MSI or Electron bundle. The script installs Node and clones the repo, then hands off to a cross-platform Node wizard (`npm run local:setup`) that fetches the Postgres binaries, restores-or-joins, asks hub-or-spoke, and registers the supervisor as a service (Task Scheduler / systemd). Everything after the download is shared Node code, which is also the Linux story.
11. **The sync loop runs inside the app process** via an instrumentation hook, armed only when `LEDGR_SYNC_HUBS` is set. `next start` on a local peer is one long-lived Node process with direct DB access, so no second process is needed; hubs (passive) and Tyler's instance never run the loop. The supervisor stays focused on lifecycle: Postgres, build, swap, restart.
12. **Tyler's instance receives the migration (tables + triggers) but zero sync behavior.** Shared schema means the sync tables land everywhere; with no `LEDGR_SYNC_HUBS` and no peer pulling, his oplog just accrues and is pruned by retention. He can opt into the whole model later by running the same installer.
13. **Cadence: fast, per Brandon.** Push debounced ~2s after a write, pull every ~10s, both supervisor-config knobs. Honest caveat, noted not blocking: during the alongside phase a 10s pull keeps Neon awake around the clock, so the CPU-hours line rises until cutover; the knob exists if the bill annoys, and after cutover the polling is all local and free.
14. **v1 synced tables: `items`, `relations`, `types`, `revisions`, `dashboards`, `views`, `templates`, `users` (settings only).** Everything the owner authors or configures. Deliberately excluded: `error_log`, job/cron state, push subscriptions, oauth tokens and codes, cached calendar feeds (per-instance by nature, some secret-bearing). The trigger migration names the list explicitly; adding a table later is one additive migration.
15. **Peer auth = DB-backed per-device tokens.** Generate on the hub, copy, paste once into the spoke wizard; the sha256 hash lives on the peer's `sync_peers` row (reusing `machine.ts`'s hash + timingSafeEqual), no expiry, no rotation ceremony. Chosen over env machine tokens precisely so the hub UI can revoke a device without a redeploy: `/build/updates` grows a "Synced devices" section (name, last seen, cursor lag, Revoke), and Revoke makes the hub refuse that device's next sync.

**The hard-to-reverse bets, locked here on purpose:**
- **The op wire format:** `sync_ops(device_id uuid, seq bigserial, at timestamptz, tbl text, row_id uuid, kind insert|update|delete, changed jsonb, schema_ver text)`, with `changed` holding only the fields that changed (old/new diffed in the trigger) and `schema_ver` carrying the drizzle journal tag from day one. Peers exchange these rows verbatim over `/api/machine/sync`, and the endpoint refuses mismatched versions. Once two peers have exchanged ops the format is load-bearing; it gets the most design care and its own verify script before anything syncs for real.
- **The merge semantics:** field-level LWW for properties and columns; bodies LWW with the losing version snapshotted to `revisions` (the existing table, forced) plus a "merged offline, check revisions" flag; relations and deletes as set operations (soft-delete only, so tombstones are just updates). Deterministic, no model in the loop (Principle 3 holds). Changing merge rules after peers hold diverged data is painful, so they are fixed here.
- **Cloud = participating peer via additive migration.** The sync migration (tables + triggers) runs on prod Neon. Reversible in the ordinary sense (drop triggers, drop tables), but it makes prod a participant, which is the point: it is what removes the fork risk. Additive only; no existing column or behavior changes.

**Phases** (each ships and is useful on its own; full detail in the plan HTML): **0** record + de-risk (this ADR, the COLLAB heads-up, the Funnel/MCP/Clerk spike); **1** sync spine (migration + pure merge engine + `/api/machine/sync` + `verify-sync.mts`, no UI); **2** local runtime on the PC (`pg` driver branch, embedded Postgres, `localAuthProvider`, supervisor v1); **3** alongside (the sync client armed on the PC against the cloud hub, SyncPill, Synced devices, weeks of soak); **4** installer + updates (bootstrap script + wizard + the local apply path); **5** hub duties on the PC (Funnel as a service, local crons, ordered-hub failover); **6** cutover (URL flips + runbook, reversible, Brandon's call). **Phase 1 starts immediately on branch `local-hub-sync-spine`.**
**Rejected:** *the localhost test week* (a fork with a reconciliation problem; alongside gives the same answer with zero data at risk); *PGlite* (single-connection, partial extensions); *app-hook oplog capture* (14 known bypassing write sites today, more tomorrow); *HLC now* (complexity ahead of an observed need); *local username/password* (standing auth code guarding an already-locked machine); *an MSI/Electron installer* (packaging ceremony the script can grow into later); *env machine tokens for peer auth* (revoking a device shouldn't take a redeploy).
**Verification:** per-phase exit criteria in the plan HTML; the standing bar is `tsc`, `eslint`, `verify:ci` green every phase, `verify-sync.mts` (new, phase 1) converging two DBs after concurrent offline edits with the losing body in revisions, version-mismatch refusal, and owner-scope held on every op. The user guide gains the sync/updates entries in the same PRs (ADR-189).
**Affects (this ADR, docs only):** `decisions.md` (this entry), `COLLAB.md` (the heads-up), `explorations/local-pc-hub.md` (status flipped to decided/scheduled). Code lands per phase, phase 1 first.

**Addendum (LH2 implementation notes, 2026-08-22, branch `local-hub-runtime`).** Five choices made inside the ADR's allowed space while building the local runtime: (1) **live-build selection is a pointer file** (`<dataDir>/live.json` holding `{dir, sha, flippedAt}`, read by the supervisor at spawn), not a symlink or Windows junction: identical on all three platforms and needs no privileges. (2) **Each build is a self-contained git worktree with its own real `node_modules`** (Turbopack rejects symlinked node_modules); "npm ci only if the lockfile changed" is realized as copy-node_modules-from-the-live-build when unchanged. Nothing ever mutates the serving directory, which is what makes keep-last-good airtight; the cost is two builds' worth of disk (prune keeps 2). (3) **The updates card's local apply path is an explicit `ApplyStrategy` (`"github-merge" | "supervisor-signal"`)**, and the signal path requires BOTH a non-Vercel env AND `LEDGR_SUPERVISOR_DIR`, same fail-closed `LEDGR_SELF_UPDATE` gate: a Vercel deploy with a stray supervisor var can never take the signal path. Additive API change, solo-shippable under ADR-183; the `localAuthProvider` slot-in is the auth-seam change decision 5 already covers. (4) **`local:restore` also resets the `job_state` sync cursors** (`sync:cursor:%` rows) in addition to the planned truncate of `sync_ops` / re-seed of `sync_device` / truncate of `sync_peers`: the cursors are the hub's, and cloning them would make a restored spoke skip ops. (5) **`pg_restore` is an external prerequisite for restore** (the embedded-postgres binaries ship the server, not the client tools); documented in `supervisor/README.md` alongside the Windows bring-up checklist.

**Addendum 2 (LH4 field revisions from Brandon's first hub install, 2026-08-22).** Two gaps the real install surfaced, both fixed on branch `local-hub-restore-sources`: (1) **initial data has three sources now, not one.** The wizard asked only for a backup dump file, which meant hunting in OneDrive for a file up to six days stale. Brandon's call: offer the **live database pull** as a peer option (`--from-url <direct connection string>`), since a fresh dump also leaves less for the first sync to reconcile, plus start-empty as before. The live pull dumps to a temp file and reuses the existing restore path unchanged. Credential rules, which are the load-bearing part: the connection string is never printed (only the hostname, per `migrate.mjs`'s convention), never written to `config.json`, redacted out of `pg_dump` stderr, and the temp dump is unlinked in a `finally` on success or failure. A `-pooler` hostname is **refused before any network call**, because `pg_dump` needs a direct connection: this is the deliberate inverse of `src/db/index.ts`'s `assertPooledUrl` (which requires the pooler for the app), and both sites carry comments saying so, so nobody "fixes" one to match the other. (2) **`install.cmd` is the file you download.** Windows Explorer opens a `.ps1` in an editor instead of running it, which stopped the first install attempt cold. The `.cmd` runs `install.ps1` when it sits alongside, fetches it from the pinned repo raw URL otherwise (same trust boundary as the `git clone` moments later), passes arguments through, and **pauses at the end** so a double-click user can read the outcome instead of watching the window vanish. The Postgres client tools joined the installer's winget prerequisites, non-fatally, since both restore sources need them but start-empty does not.

**Addendum 3 (the live pull needs no external tools, 2026-08-22).** The first real install failed at the live pull: it shelled out to `pg_dump`, and PostgreSQL's Windows installer does not register its `bin` directory on PATH (unlike Git and Node, which do), so a successful install still left the binary unresolvable. Our bundled `embedded-postgres` ships only `initdb`/`pg_ctl`/`postgres`, so no client tools were available either. **The fix removes the dependency rather than patching PATH detection:** a live pull does not need `pg_dump` at all, because the local database gets its schema from running our own migrations, so only ROWS need copying. `scripts/lib/pg-copy.mjs` copies them natively with the `pg` driver we already ship. Three mechanisms make it correct: `SET session_replication_role = replica` on the destination for the duration (which both removes any need to sort tables by foreign key AND stops migration 0054's sync triggers from logging an op per copied row, so a fresh spoke does not try to push the whole database back at its hub on first sync); generated columns and sequence-owning columns discovered from the catalog rather than hardcoded (so `items.search` is recomputed locally instead of copied, and future columns come along free); and keyset pagination on the primary key with batch size derived from the parameter cap. **Two bugs the integration test caught, both silent-corruption class:** a plain INSERT collides with migration-seeded rows (the system `types`, the `sync_schema_ver` singleton), so every insert is `ON CONFLICT (pk) DO UPDATE`, which also makes a re-pull idempotent; and the `pg` driver serializes a JS array as a Postgres array literal rather than JSON, which would have quietly mangled every jsonb column holding a top-level array (`types.property_schema` above all), so parameters are explicitly JSON-stringified. **A UX consequence worth noting:** the `-pooler` refusal is gone with `pg_dump`, since plain row reads work fine through the pooler, so the wizard no longer sends the owner to the Neon dashboard for a direct string. `pg_restore` remains required for the backup-FILE path, which is inherent to that format; `install.ps1` now discovers an installed-but-off-PATH `C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\*\bin` and says those tools are only needed for that path.

**Addendum 4 (three sync guardrails before arming production, 2026-08-22).** Brandon asked what else should exist before the first push from a spoke touches live data, which is the riskiest moment in this build. Three guards, migration `0055_sync_pull_only` (additive `sync_peers.pull_only boolean not null default false`). **(1) Pull-only mode.** A device may pull and never push: `syncMode: "full" | "pull-only"` in supervisor config, and, crucially, a hub-side `pull_only` flag whose enforcement is a 403 in `/api/machine/sync` before any op is applied, so the guarantee never depends on the spoke behaving. Flippable per device from the hub UI, and Add-device defaults to pull-only, because that is the safe posture for a brand-new peer. **(2) First-push size guard.** The failure it prevents is a spoke whose oplog is unexpectedly full (a bad restore, a re-pull that logged ops, a bug) shoving the whole database at the hub as if every row were an edit. Above `maxFirstPush` (default 500) the client holds instead of pushing, surfaces the count and the release path in its own status message, and gates only the FIRST push of a process lifetime so a legitimately busy spoke is never throttled. **(3) Clock-skew detection.** Merge is last-writer-wins on op timestamps, so a wrong clock silently lets stale writes beat newer ones and nothing noticed before. The sync response now carries `serverTime` (additive), and the client warns above `skewWarnMs` (5s) and withholds push above `skewHoldMs` (60s). **The shared safety property, verified rather than assumed: all three withhold only the PUSH side.** The pull half of an exchange runs unconditionally, so a held, skewed, or pull-only device still receives hub data and cannot get stranded. Amber on the SyncPill and detail in the Sync section for every state, because a silent guardrail is not a guardrail. The README documents the arming sequence: add the device pull-only, confirm data flows down, then flip to full.

**Addendum 5 (the sync status was reading a second copy of its own module, 2026-08-22).** The first real spoke pulled correctly for hours while `/api/sync/status`, the SyncPill and `/build/updates` all reported "Offline, never synced": `job_state` proved three pull cycles had landed, and the UI said nothing had ever happened. A silent misreport, which is exactly what Principle 9 exists to prevent, and worse than an error message because it argues the guardrails are dead when they are working. **Cause, confirmed from the build artifacts rather than reasoned about:** Turbopack emits the instrumentation hook and each route handler as separate server entries, and `src/lib/sync/client.ts` lands in a chunk on each side (`chunks/_1-xuuuz._.js` for `instrumentation.js`, `chunks/src_lib_sync_1h8tah_._.js` for `app/api/sync/status/route.js`, per their `.nft.json` traces, both carrying the module). One process, two module instances: the loop mutated one instance's module-level `status` object, every reader read the other's, and that one sits at its constructed defaults forever. Decision 11 ("the loop runs inside the app process") is unaffected and still right; what was wrong was the inference in the code comment that one process therefore means one module instance. **Fix:** `status`, the `firstPushDone` one-shot flag, and the loop-arming guard all move onto a single `globalThis.__ledgrSync` holder. The loop guard was ALREADY on globalThis for this exact reason, which is the tell: the guard worked and the state it guarded did not, so the state had to join it. Both chunks now reference the same holder (verified the same way, post-fix). **The named ceiling:** this fixes duplication within a process, which is the observed cause. It cannot fix separate processes, so if the app is ever served by more than one, status has to move into `job_state` alongside the cursors. **Guard:** `verify-sync-ui.mts` asserts the holder exists, that a mutation through it is visible to `getSyncStatus()` (which is what a reader in the other chunk calls), and that `getSyncStatus()` still hands out a copy so a reader cannot write the loop's state by accident; confirmed to exit 1 against the pre-fix module. Not core: no schema, no wire format, no response shape changes, and the `/api/sync/status` contract is byte-identical, it just stops lying.

**Addendum 6 (synced bodies now rebuild their own passage edges, 2026-08-23).** Found while listing what still had to be tested before arming bidirectional sync, which is exactly the right time to find it. `passage_refs` is deliberately NOT in decision 14's v1 synced set (it is derived, so syncing it would put the same fact on the wire twice), and it has no database trigger: it is maintained solely by `syncPassageRefs` inside `item-mutations.ts`. The sync apply path writes item rows **directly** — that is the whole point of the trigger-based design, and it is why decision 2 preferred triggers over app hooks — so a body arriving over sync never went through `item-mutations.ts` and never rebuilt its edges. **Every synced body edit left the receiving peer's passage index frozen at whatever its fill copied, silently.** Measured on Brandon's laptop peer: 189,320 edges from the fill, and nothing would have updated one of them again. Already true on the pull side, and bidirectional would have made it symmetric with no authoritative copy to rebuild from. **Fix:** `replacePassageRefs(exec, itemId, body)`, added *beside* `syncPassageRefs` in `src/lib/passages/refs.ts` so the rule for what refs a body implies (`collectPassageRefsFromMarkdown`) keeps exactly one home; the apply path calls it for each merged action that wrote an items body, passing its **transaction**, so the row and its derived edges commit together and no crash window can strand one without the other. Reconcile is replace-not-diff (the caller already knows the body changed, and a passage_refs id is never persisted anywhere). The action filter is the pure `passageBodyFromAction`: an insert carrying a body, or an update whose merged `fields` include one — so a 500-op batch derives only for the bodies actually in it, and a soft-delete stamp, a title edit, a `types` write and a hard delete (whose edges go by cascade) all correctly derive nothing. **Rejected:** *adding `passage_refs` to the synced set* (a derived table on the wire, and two writers for one fact); *a post-transaction pass* (leaves a crash window, and needs a re-read to find the winning body when the merged action already carries it); *accepting the drift with a documented rebuild command* (silent wrongness in scripture search, which is a core use of this system, is not an acceptable steady state). **Verification:** `verify-sync.mts` gains 8 pure cases for the filter plus a tier (b) end-to-end against two real clusters — a body carrying two distinct passage links (one cited twice) replicates as exactly 2 deduped edges on the receiving peer, and clearing the links clears them. Confirmed to FAIL (0 edges) with the derivation removed. `scripts/rebuild-passage-refs.mts` repairs a peer that already ran a pre-fix build. Not core: no schema change, no migration, no wire-format change, no merge-semantics change — the ops on the wire are byte-identical, the receiver just stops leaving derived data behind.

**Addendum 7 (a one-statement family delete wedged every peer that replayed it, 2026-08-23, branch `fix/sync-apply-fk-order`).** Found by the first two-spoke dev rig within minutes of arming: both spokes locked in a permanent retry loop at cursor 0, failing on `delete from items where id = $1`. **Cause, read from the dev hub's oplog rather than reasoned about:** a verify run had created a parent and child and hard-deleted both in ONE statement; the statement passed the hub's `items_parent_id_items_id_fk` because Postgres checks FKs at end-of-statement, but the row-level triggers logged one op per row in arbitrary physical order — parent (seq 25) BEFORE child (seq 26), same `at`. The apply layer replayed them as separate statements with immediate FK checks: the parent's delete failed, the whole batch transaction rolled back (taking the batch's re-inserts with it, which is why the spoke showed no trace), the cursor never advanced, and every tick retried the same batch forever. A hard wedge, and a general one — prod's trash purge hard-deletes families routinely, so the first purged parent-with-children would have wedged the real spoke the same way. **Fix, two halves.** (1) `applySyncOps` now runs a batch's `items` delete actions as ONE `delete … where id = any(…)` per origin at the end of the batch (`planActions`, pure), restoring the end-of-statement FK semantics the hub had; grouped per origin so GUC echo-stamping stays per-writer. items.parent_id is the only restricting FK among the synced tables (everything else cascades from items), so items-only grouping is the whole fix, not a special case of a bigger one. Accepted reordering ceiling, in the comment: a hard-delete-then-re-insert of the SAME uuid inside one batch would now execute insert-then-delete; no app path re-inserts a purged uuid. (2) Both batch caps — the hub's pull (`PULL_BATCH`) and the client's push (`PUSH_BATCH`) — now extend past 500 to the end of the last op's same-`at` run (`at` is `now()`, so a run = one transaction), because a family split across batches cannot be grouped by (1). Bounded by `RUN_EXTEND_CAP` (500); a >500-op same-transaction delete family could still split, named ceiling. **Not core:** no wire-format change (a batch was always allowed to be any size), no schema change, no merge-semantics change — the same actions produce the same final state, only their statement grouping changed. **Verification:** `verify-sync.mts` +5 — pure `planActions` grouping/order checks, a structural guard that apply wires the plan, and a tier (b) end-to-end that replicates an FK-linked family to peer B and applies a hand-crafted parent-before-child delete pair (the rig's exact wedge): applies clean, both rows gone. Confirmed to fail with `apply.ts` reverted.

## ADR-207: MCP write tools accept `body` as an alias for `bodyMarkdown` (reversing ADR-201's rejected alternative)
**Date:** 2026-08-22
**Status:** accepted (Brandon, solo). Purely additive per the ADR-183 carve-out (an optional argument on existing tools; every existing caller keeps working byte-for-byte), so it does not need the both-agree gate. It IS, however, a deliberate reversal of an alternative ADR-201 named and rejected, so it is logged here rather than merged quietly, and flagged for Tyler in `COLLAB.md`. **Do not re-reject the alias without reading the Context below** — the rejection was tried, and it did not stop the failure it was aimed at.
**Context:** ADR-201 (2026-08-18) made `buildWriteRaw` reject unknown args and rejected the alias with "two names for one field forever, and the schema says otherwise." The empty-body saves kept happening anyway: 2026-08-22, a `remember` call carrying a substantial body saved an empty memory, and so did a second one. Two reasons the rejection missed. (1) **Coverage:** `buildWriteRaw` guards only `create_item` and `update_item`. Three other write tools hand-parse their own body — `remember` (`memory.ts`), `add_to_record` (`records.ts`), `add_subtasks` (`tasks.ts`) — and all three still dropped `body` in silence, which is where both August 22 losses landed. (2) **Direction:** rejecting is the right answer for a typo (`duedate`), but `body` is not a typo. It is the field name every other system in the caller's world uses, including Ledgr's own REST API and the `items.body` column, so a model caller reaches for it by correct analogy and an error just costs a round trip. The cost of the alias is one extra accepted name; the cost of the rejection was measured in lost writing.
**Decision:** One shared helper, `optBodyMarkdown(args, at?)` in `src/lib/mcp/tools/args.ts`, is now the single place every MCP write path takes a body from. It accepts `bodyMarkdown` or `body` (`bodyMarkdown` wins if both are passed) and throws `ItemError("bad_request", …)` naming `bodyMarkdown` on a non-string, including the REST `{format,text}` shape, which is NOT aliased. All five write paths route through it: `create_item` / `update_item` via `buildWriteRaw`, plus `remember`, `add_to_record`, `add_subtasks`. `body` joins the allowed-key set in `buildWriteRaw` and leaves `KEY_HINTS`; `content` / `text` / `markdown` keep ADR-201's did-you-mean rejection, because those genuinely are wrong names rather than a competing convention. The tool schemas still declare `bodyMarkdown` as the only property with `additionalProperties: false` — the alias is a safety net for callers that guess, not a second public field — and the `bodyMarkdown` property descriptions say it is also accepted as `body` so the schema is not lying by omission.
**Rejected:** *declaring `body` in the schemas alongside `bodyMarkdown`* (that really would be two public names forever, ADR-201's objection, and it invites new callers to pick the alias); *renaming the field to `body` outright* (that breaks every existing caller, the one thing the carve-out does not permit); *leaving ADR-201's rejection in place and only extending it to the three unguarded tools* (consistent, and it would have converted the silent drops into errors, but it still spends a failed call on a caller who guessed by correct analogy — the whole point is that the write should land).
**Verification:** `scripts/verify-mcp-write-args.mts` extended from 11 to 17 checks — the alias lands as the body on create and update, `bodyMarkdown` wins when both are passed, the non-string `{format,text}` shape errors clearly, nested entries carry their path (`subtasks[2].`), and ADR-201's unknown-key rejections and pass-throughs all still hold. Pure suite, no DB, auto-discovered by verify-ci. `tsc` and `eslint` clean.
**Affects:** `src/lib/mcp/tools/args.ts`, `memory.ts`, `records.ts`, `tasks.ts`, `items.ts` (descriptions only), `scripts/verify-mcp-write-args.mts`.

## ADR-208: The staleness refusal — /api/machine/sync refuses a cursor that predates the oldest retained op
**Date:** 2026-08-23
**Status:** accepted (Brandon via the 2026-08-23 session queue; Tyler agreed 2026-08-23, relayed by Brandon — core per ADR-183's carve-out: a new refusal on an existing machine call is tightening validation, both-agree + ADR). Branch `sync-staleness-refusal`, PR #302.
**Context:** A spoke that sleeps past the oplog's retention window could not rejoin safely, and nothing told it so. `/api/machine/sync` served `seq > sinceSeq` with **no comparison against the oldest retained op anywhere in the sync code**, so a peer whose cursor pointed into pruned territory received whatever remained, advanced its cursor, and reported **synced** — a permanently partial database, silently (the same class as the start-empty trap, and the same Principle 9 violation). Today the gap opens only through the revoke-then-return path (a live registered peer pins the prune via `min(last_pulled_seq)`), but the coming **paused** device state exists precisely to drop that retention hold, so the refusal must land first.
**Decision:** three pieces, one slice.
1. **The prune records what it deleted.** `pruneSyncOps` upserts the highest seq it actually deleted into `job_state` under `sync:prunedThrough` (monotonic — a smaller later run can never move it backwards; instance-local on purpose, like the cursors). Exact by construction: "min(seq) − 1" would over-refuse across bigserial gaps that were never ops; this never does. A hub that has never pruned (or pruned only before this landed) reads 0 and refuses nobody — the status quo, so the change is safe to deploy with no backfill.
2. **The refusal.** After the version and pull-only gates, the route reads `prunedThrough` and refuses with **HTTP 410 Gone** (`{error, sinceSeq, prunedThrough, pushApplied: true, applied, rejected}`) when `cursorTooStale(sinceSeq, prunedThrough)` — i.e. `sinceSeq > 0 && sinceSeq < prunedThrough`. `sinceSeq = 0` is deliberately exempt: a freshly filled peer legitimately starts at cursor 0 with current data and replays the retained oplog as a LWW no-op. **The refusal lands AFTER the push half on purpose:** a waking peer's local edits are ordinary new ops and still drain to the hub, because the staleness remedy is a re-fill and a re-fill destroys anything local that never pushed. Only the pull half refuses.
3. **Push dedupe.** The route now drops incoming ops with `seq <= sync_peers.last_pushed_seq` before applying. Without it, ANY re-delivered batch — a response lost after the hub applied it, or an old client looping on the new 410 — was re-applied, and each re-apply's row writes had their triggers log fresh hub ops: unbounded oplog growth. This closes a pre-existing re-delivery bug, and it is what makes the 410 safe for a client that predates it. Named ceiling (comment in `peers.ts`): a spoke restored from its own old local backup rewinds its seq and would see its first pushes dropped — that spoke needs a re-fill anyway, which resets its device identity.
The client (`src/lib/sync/client.ts`) handles the 410: it advances its **push** cursor when the body says `pushApplied` (otherwise it would re-send the same batch every tick forever), **never** advances the pull cursor (staying put keeps the refusal firing until the owner acts, instead of quietly resuming past a hole), and surfaces "too far behind this hub … re-fill required: `npm run local:restore -- --from-url <hub db url>`" as `lastError`, which the SyncPill (offline/red) and the /build/updates Sync section already display.
**The return path this sets up — the three-mode model (design, not yet built):** replay the oplog (short absence, built), **reconcile only what differs** (long absence, the missing middle), full fill (no shared history, built; ~4 min measured). The middle is ordinary anti-entropy: the waking peer sends a compact digest — `(tbl, id, updated_at)` per row, ~1MB at 23k items, later bucketed hashes when little changed — the hub diffs it, and only genuinely-differing rows travel. Two traps recorded 2026-08-23 that the design must respect: **(a) "differs" must not become "the hub wins"** — a differing row still resolves by the SAME per-field LWW rules as sync (reconciliation that overwrites with hub state is a different, wrong semantic); which means the reconcile payload for a differing row must carry per-field stamps (or the full rows travel and merge through `mergeOps` exactly as ops do), never a bare row replace. **(b) Any row digest must exclude generated and derived columns** — `items.search` is generated and `passage_refs` is derived (`pg-copy.mjs` already discovers generated columns from the catalog for exactly this reason), so a whole-row hash would mismatch on every row forever; `updated_at` alone is the v1 digest for this reason, upgraded to a column-aware hash only if timestamp-equal-but-differing rows are ever observed. Reconcile is a distinct machine endpoint (or a mode flag on sync) gated behind the 410: the client sees the refusal, the owner picks "reconcile" or "re-fill", and the paused device state (which drops the retention hold, item 2/3 of the sleeping-spoke entry) becomes safe to add only once this path exists.
**Rejected:** *refusing before the push half* (strands a waking peer's unpushed local edits, which the re-fill then destroys — data loss by advice); *a 200 response carrying a `stale` flag* (an old client ignores unknown fields, advances its cursor, and keeps the silent lie — the 410 makes even pre-refusal clients fail loudly); *`min(seq) − 1` as the boundary* (over-refuses across bigserial gaps; recording what the prune actually deleted is exact); *refusing `sinceSeq = 0`* (would break every legitimate fresh fill against a hub that has ever pruned).
**Verification:** `scripts/verify-sync.mts` +13 checks — pure `cursorTooStale` truth table (5), `dedupePushedOps` (3), structural wiring guards that fail if the route or client unwires the refusal/dedupe/410 handling (5), and tier (b) asserts the prune records `prunedThrough` exactly at the highest deleted seq and advances it monotonically across deeper prunes (2 more). **Confirmed to FAIL with the bug reintroduced:** reverting `route.ts` to main flips the three structural route checks red. `tsc`, `eslint` clean; full suite green including both ephemeral-cluster tiers.
**Affects:** `src/app/api/machine/sync/route.ts`, `src/lib/sync/peers.ts` (`cursorTooStale`, `dedupePushedOps`, `readPrunedThrough`, prune recording), `src/lib/sync/auth.ts` (identity carries `lastPushedSeq`), `src/lib/sync/client.ts`, `scripts/verify-sync.mts`, `supervisor/README.md` (parking section), `next_steps.md`, `COLLAB.md`.

## ADR-209: Build → Network — the sync topology on one page, a GUI-editable hub list with a token per hub, and per-hub status
**Date:** 2026-08-23
**Status:** accepted (Brandon's design 2026-08-23; Tyler agreed to the direction, relayed via Brandon's session queue the same day). CORE-adjacent: the `/api/sync/status` response gains an additive `hubs` array (existing fields byte-identical), the sync client's hub configuration changes shape (env pair → per-hub entries), and two new owner routes land — all additive, no wire-format or schema change, no migration.
**Context:** The sync surfaces were two sections buried in `/build/updates`: "Sync" (this instance's own uplink) and "Synced devices" (what syncs into it). With a third node that stopped being legible. Worse, the hub list lived in `LEDGR_SYNC_HUBS` with ONE `LEDGR_SYNC_TOKEN` for every hub — a shape that cannot express "a token per hub", which adding a second hub requires (each hub mints its own device tokens). And an instance's first GUI-added hub needs the loop already ticking, which the env-only arming could not provide.
**Decision:**
1. **The hub list is a per-instance `job_state` store (`sync:hubs`, `[{url, token}]`), env is only the initial value** — the exact ADR-121/PR #297 override pattern the mode toggle proved. `effectiveHubs` (pure): a stored list wins even when EMPTY (removing every hub means "stop syncing", never "fall back to config"); absent falls back to the env pair, the single env token applied to each env hub. The loop re-reads the list every tick, so add/remove needs no restart. The stored token sits plaintext in the local database — the same trust boundary as the plaintext `deviceToken` in `supervisor/config.json` on the same disk.
2. **Arming widens to supervisor-managed peers.** The instrumentation hook (and `startSyncLoop`) now arms when the env pair is set OR `LEDGR_SUPERVISOR_DIR` is set, so a peer whose first hub arrives via the GUI already has the loop ticking; an empty effective list makes a tick a single cheap local read. Cloud deploys set neither, so hubs stay passive (decision 11 intact).
3. **Per-hub status.** `SyncStatus` gains `hubs: [{url, lastSyncAt, lastError}]`, rebuilt to the current list each exchange walk and updated per attempt, so the Network page shows which uplink is healthy rather than one blended state. Additive on `/api/sync/status`.
4. **Build → Network (`/build/network`, MAINTAIN)** shows the whole topology: hubs this instance syncs TO (url, primary/backup by order, per-hub last sync + last error, Remove, **+ Add hub** asking for a URL + a token minted on that hub — the deliberate mirror image of Add device), this instance's own link state (the mode toggle and held/skew detail, moved from Updates), and the devices that sync FROM it (the existing SyncedDevices table, moved). `/build/updates` keeps a pointer; the SyncPill now opens Network. The page states the one thing that is deliberately NOT a button: repointing at a different primary is a re-fill (`npm run local:restore -- --from-url`), because changing the URL alone would merge two diverged databases field by field.
5. **Routes:** `GET/POST/DELETE /api/sync/hubs`, owner-authed like `/api/sync/mode`. Tokens are write-only — GET never returns them; replacing one is remove + add. The first write copies the env-derived effective list into the store, so env and GUI never fight. `/api/sync/mode`'s gate now reads the effective list, so a GUI-only-hubs instance can set its mode.
**Deliberately deferred:** reorder (order = insertion; remove + re-add to promote), per-hub cadence/role (the multi-hub replication slice — the client still walks first-success-wins), per-hub pending counts (global pending shown), and a GUI release for the held first push (its own queued item).
**Rejected:** *keeping the env vars authoritative with the GUI writing config files* (the app cannot reach supervisor/config.json on every platform, and a restart per edit is the friction PR #297 just removed); *a `sync_hubs` table* (job_state IS the per-instance key-value store, and a table would invite syncing it — the one thing this data must never do); *returning tokens on GET* (a bearer credential for a remote system has no read-back use).
**Verification:** `verify-sync-ui.mts` +5 (`effectiveHubs` precedence truth table: stored wins, empty-stored means none, env fallback with the shared token, missing token arms nothing, malformed entries dropped); `verify-user-guide.mts` green with the new `/build/network` route; `tsc`, `eslint`, `next build` clean; exercised live on the dev rig (two spokes against devledgr).
**Affects:** `src/lib/sync/client.ts`, `src/instrumentation.ts`, `src/app/api/sync/hubs/route.ts` (new), `src/app/api/sync/mode/route.ts`, `src/app/build/network/page.tsx` (new), `src/app/build/updates/page.tsx`, `src/components/network/HubActions.tsx` (new), `src/components/nav/SyncPill.tsx`, `src/lib/build-nav.ts`, `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`, `scripts/verify-sync-ui.mts`.


## ADR-210: Per-hub cadence and fallback trust — pushing to every hub, gating only the pulls, and asking before leaning on a backup
**Date:** 2026-08-23
**Status:** accepted (Brandon's design, refined 2026-08-23 in the same session; the three open questions answered by him directly). CORE-adjacent, the same shape as ADR-209: `HubConfig` gains two optional fields on a store that already exists, `/api/sync/status` gains additive fields, `/api/machine/sync` gains ONE optional request field (`pull`), and no schema change or migration. Every caller written before this keeps working byte-for-byte, so the ADR-183 carve-out covers the API surface.
**Context:** ADR-209 shipped the GUI half of adding a hub, but nothing expressed *how each hub behaves*. Two consequences. First, `exchange()` walked the ordered list and returned at the first hub that succeeded — that is failover, not replication, so an archive hub received **nothing** for as long as the primary was up. A backup that stops receiving is not a backup. Second, there was no way to say "this hub is a fast peer machine, that one is a cloud archive I check daily," which is exactly Brandon's post-cutover topology (the PC as primary, Vercel+Neon demoted to a daily archive peer).
**Decision:**
1. **Two independent axes, not one role enum.** An earlier draft of the queue item proposed a single `role: mirror | archive`. Brandon's refinement splits it, and the split is real rather than pedantic. **Cadence** (`continuous | daily`) is how often we exchange. **Fallback trust** (`automatic | prompt`) is whether this instance may start *relying* on a hub silently. A fast hub you would happily fall back to and a daily hub you want to be asked about are the common pair, but the axes are genuinely independent — a daily *automatic* archive and a continuous *ask-first* peer are both legal — so nothing derives one from the other. Both are optional fields on `HubConfig` in `job_state` `sync:hubs`, parse-tolerant: an entry written before this reads as continuous + automatic, which is precisely what it was already doing.
2. **The rule that makes "prompt first" coherent, because using a hub is two different things.** **Pushing is always safe and never prompts** — depositing a copy of your changes somewhere cannot corrupt you — so *every* configured hub is pushed to on its own cadence, automatic or emergency. **Pulling is where trust lives.** Not because stale rows are dangerous in the merge (per-field LWW means an older row loses to your newer one), but because your sense of freshness degrades silently: you would be reading a system that has not heard from your other machines in a day while the UI says "synced." That is the same Principle 9 failure ADR-208's staleness refusal fixed from the other direction. So `exchange()` now visits every hub due on its own schedule, and an emergency hub is **push-only** until the owner approves reading from it.
3. **Push-only is explicit on the wire.** `/api/machine/sync` accepts an optional `pull: false`, which skips the pull half entirely: no ops served, no `lastPulledSeq` advance (the retention hold has to keep reflecting what the peer has actually *read*), and no staleness refusal (nothing was pulled to be stale).
