(The same hazard argues for keeping automated writes out of that blob generally, which is why the ADR-218 run stamp is throttled to once an hour.)
3. **The announce rides `purge`**, the one job ADR-214 says every instance runs itself, daily. No new scheduler, no new schedule to forget, and a cloud deploy enters the roster exactly like a local peer. Day granularity is all any surface reads.
4. **`last_seen_at` is written by the copy itself**, so it means "this copy was RUNNING then" rather than "it reached me then" — the stronger fact, and the same reasoning that made ADR-218's liveness a run stamp rather than a sync timestamp.
5. **The periodic announce NEVER writes `label`.** The owner names a machine once and can rename it from any device; a heartbeat that also wrote the label would silently revert that on the next run. The config-supplied name SEEDS the row and never re-seeds it, for the same reason. `verify-installs.mts` asserts the upsert's `set` clause contains no label.
6. **The wizard ASKS for the machine name** rather than taking the hostname (Brandon's collision answer), because two machines answering to one word is what makes "which copy runs the backup?" unanswerable — and it stays editable in the GUI afterwards, which he asked for explicitly. Collisions cannot be *prevented* across copies that have never met, so they are detected and named on the page.
7. **A re-fill keeps this machine's identity.** `npm run local:restore` deliberately assigns a fresh `sync_device` id, and both ownership and the roster are keyed by it — so without help, a documented, expected operation turns the machine into a stranger: its claimed jobs point at nothing and the roster shows a ghost beside a newcomer. Both fill paths now read the prior identity BEFORE the wipe and, after it, rewrite the roster row's id and re-point any job that named the old one. This flaw existed in ADR-218 as shipped; it is fixed here.
8. **"Different build", never "behind".** A copy cannot tell which build is newer without a commit graph it does not have, so the surface says what it actually knows.
**Rollout, and it is not free:** `0058` moves the bundled journal tag, and ADR-206's version gate only exchanges ops between peers on identical tags — so **sync pauses between peers until each one takes this update** (the same shape as ADR-213 and ADR-215). The migration itself is additive: one table, one index, one FK, two triggers, and a one-row stamp update.
**Rejected:** the three alternatives above, each recorded with what it would have cost. Also: *linking `sync_peers` to `installs`* — the hub could learn the association (it authenticates a peer and receives ops stamped with that peer's own id), but it buys only the merging of two UI lists that mean genuinely different things (who may connect to me vs. what copies exist), so it stays unbuilt. *Removing your own roster row* — refused, because it would make the list lie about the machine you are looking at and the next announce would recreate it anyway.
**Verification:** `scripts/verify-installs.mts`, 16 pure checks in CI: the copy you are looking at is always present whatever its timestamp; quiet, gone and never are distinguished because the fix differs; the threshold is a boundary; no health line uses engineering vocabulary; collisions are detected case- and space-insensitively but REPORTED as the owner typed them (a live render caught this saying "cloud" for a machine named "Cloud"); the wizard refuses an empty name rather than falling back to the hostname; the GUI and the wizard judge a name by the same rule; a differing build is never called "behind"; and four wiring assertions — `installs` is in `SYNCED_TABLES`, the migration carries both triggers and moves the wire stamp, the announce rides `purge`, both fill paths carry the identity forward, and the announce's upsert does not touch the label. **Proven live against the dev Neon branch:** the migration applied (seven columns, both triggers present, stamp moved to `0058_installs_roster`); an announce created the row with `isSelf` true; the oplog trigger fired (`installs`/`update` rows in `sync_ops`); **a rename survived a re-announce**, which is decision 5's load-bearing rule; the picker rendered four copies with health lines and build shas plus the duplicate-label warning; a job was assigned from this machine to another copy ("Runs on Old Laptop"); and `jobRunVerdict` then returned `{run: false, reason: "not-owner", ownerLabel: "Old Laptop"}` here while an unclaimed job still ran — the exactly-one guarantee, end to end. **One real bug found by that testing and fixed:** `announceOwnInstall` resolved the owner as the earliest `users` row, but a database can hold several (a dev branch accumulates throwaway owners from the verify suites), so the row was attributed to a test owner and the page showed an empty list while the row sat there. It now resolves the owner the way every other scheduled job does, with the earliest row only as a fallback — and both roster reads log rather than swallow, because an empty list and a broken read looked identical on the page.
**Affects:** `drizzle/0058_installs_roster.sql` (new), `drizzle/meta/*`, `src/db/schema.ts`, `src/lib/sync/engine.ts`, `src/lib/installs-plan.ts` (new), `src/lib/installs.ts` (new), `src/app/api/installs/route.ts` (new), `src/components/network/CopiesList.tsx` (new), `src/components/updates/JobOwnerControl.tsx`, `src/lib/job-owners-store.ts`, `src/app/api/jobs/owner/route.ts`, `src/app/api/machine/purge/route.ts`, `src/app/build/updates/page.tsx`, `src/app/build/network/page.tsx`, `scripts/local-setup.mjs`, `scripts/local-setup-lib.mjs`, `scripts/local-restore.mjs`, `scripts/verify-installs.mts` (new).

## ADR-221: Two more jobs move, cadence becomes an interval, and "hub" stops being a word the owner reads
**Date:** 2026-08-25
**Status:** accepted in full. The job half and the vocabulary half were solo (a continuation of ADR-218's stated plan, and UI copy); **the cadence half is CORE-adjacent (the sync engine, ADR-206/ADR-210) and is ACKED by Tyler (relayed via Brandon, 2026-08-25)**. Nothing here moves a migration or the wire, so a peer on an older build is unaffected either way.
**Context:** three of the four things `explorations/sync-node-maturity.md` still had open, taken in the order Brandon ranked them. ADR-218 shipped the job picker with only `export` claimable and wrote the next slice down verbatim: prove one handoff at a time and flip `movable: true` per job. ADR-210 shipped a two-value cadence enum that §4 called "too coarse" the moment it met a real archive peer. ADR-219 did the plain-language pass on the Network page's *status* half and left the *controls* still saying hub.

### 1. `email-import` and `calendar-sync` become claimable

**What the blocked reasons said, and what turned out to be true.** Both were held back on the same worry: the record of what has already been done lives in per-instance `job_state`, which does not sync, so a new owner starts blind. That is true of the record. It is not true of the *answer*, and the answer is what matters.

- **Email capture.** "Reading the mailbox consumes it" was correct; the conclusion drawn from it was not. What consumes a message is `markImported` MOVING it out of the `Ledgr Import` folder, and that move happens in the mailbox, which every copy can see. A new owner opens a fresh delta and gets the folder's current contents, which is exactly the messages nobody has filed. The stored token is an optimization on top of that, not the record. The second guard is `items.properties.email.internetMessageId`, and `items` syncs, so even a message created but not yet moved (the crash window) is recognized on a different machine and skipped.
- **Calendar sync.** The worry was a duplicate meeting, and it cannot happen: dedup keys on `items.ms_event_id`, which syncs. There is no place in the queue to lose either, because each run pulls the whole window fresh. `calendar_events` is a per-copy cache of what is on offer, and a new owner refills and re-links it on its first run.

**So the honest control is a consequence, not a block.** Each row states its own trade instead of refusing: email capture waits for that machine to be on but misses nothing, and calendar sync keeps every meeting already brought in correct everywhere while the *waiting to be added* list only refreshes where the job runs. That last one is a real cost, and it is said out loud rather than discovered.

**`todoist-sync`, `transcription-poll` and `health-check` stay blocked**, each with its own reason, because none has been proven and two of them (writing to Todoist, notifications registered per machine) look like genuinely different problems rather than the same one again.

### 2. Cadence becomes an interval, with the retention trap closed

`HubCadence` was `"continuous" | "daily"`, and `cadenceIntervalMs` existed purely to turn it into a number. It is the number now: minutes, 0 meaning "every normal round". The presets are the ordinary ladder (continuous, 1, 5, 15, 60, daily, weekly) and stay presets rather than free entry, for the reason the supervisor's job config already gives.

**Reads are tolerant, so nothing migrates:** a hub stored as `"daily"` reads as 1440, `"continuous"` as 0, garbage as 0. Unreadable resolves toward *more* syncing on purpose, because the cost of syncing too often is a few wasted round trips and the cost of syncing too rarely is a peer falling out of the retention window without noticing. `HubConfig.cadence` is typed to admit the two legacy strings, which is honest about the stored shape and forces every reader through `hubCadence`.

**The guardrail is the point, and the rule is: you must be able to miss one sync and still be inside the window.** A hub prunes its change log; a peer's cursor holds it only while the hub has heard from that peer inside `grace_days`. Fall outside and the next exchange is a 410 and a full re-fill (ADR-208), the safety working exactly as designed, which is no comfort to someone a dropdown walked into it. Two intervals rather than one, because a machine switched off over a long weekend has missed exactly one, and that is the ordinary case. Against the default 14-day window the rule lands on weekly, which is why the ladder stops there and why anything longer is refused with the reason.

**Two things this deliberately does NOT build, and the trigger for each:**

- **`grace_days` defaulted from cadence** (the doc asked for it). The window lives on the HUB, per remote device; the cadence lives on the peer. Opposite machines, so deriving one from the other is a wire change. It is also unnecessary today: every cadence the picker can produce already fits inside the default window, by construction of the cap above. **Build it the day a preset longer than weekly is wanted**, and expect to pay for the wire then.
- **Anchored `{at: "HH:MM"}` alongside the interval** (the doc asked us to decide). Decided: interval only. The supervisor's jobs are anchored because a backup at 04:10 is about when the work is cheap; sync is about how stale you are willing to be, and the interval form self-heals across a sleeping laptop where an anchored one silently skips a day. Supporting both doubles the scheduling grammar for no owner-visible gain. **The real use case that would justify revisiting is "only sync overnight" for bandwidth**, and that wants a window, not an instant.

**The local check is safe by construction, which is why no wire field was needed at all.** Both peers run the same build (the version gate refuses an exchange otherwise), so the default window is a shared constant rather than a fact to fetch, and a hub-side override can only widen the window. A local check can therefore only be wrong in the direction of refusing something that would have been fine.

### 3. "Hub" stops being a word the owner reads

The exploration's own resolution, taken as written: **do not rename code.** `hub`, `spoke` and `role` stay as identifiers, config fields and doc vocabulary, because they name a real bundle (published, always-on, others point at it) and a name for that bundle is worth keeping. What changed is only what is rendered:

- The controls ADR-219 left behind now speak in copies: **Add a copy**, "Web address of that copy", "One-time code from that copy", "Stop syncing to this copy?", "What your usual copies said", "Reading from a backup copy". The residual "instance" leaks in the same files went with them.
- **The setup wizard asks the question behind the word**: "Will other devices sync from this machine? (y/n)" instead of "Role (hub or spoke)". `validateRole` accepts y/yes/n/no alongside the two role names, so `--role hub|spoke` keeps working verbatim for unattended runs and for anyone who already knows which they want. The explainer above the prompt still names the flags, once, in a parenthesis.

**Rejected:** renaming the code identifiers (expensive in docs, buys nothing the copy pass does not); a `--hub`/`--spoke` flag pair (a second grammar for a flag that already works).

**Verification.** `verify-job-owners.mts` grew six checks and lost a hardcoded list: the movable set is asserted as an invariant (a movable row must state its trade, a blocked row must state its reason) plus one deliberate guard on the SIZE of the claimable set, so flipping a fourth job on has to touch that line and carry a reason. Three of the new checks are structural tripwires under the handoff proofs, and they exist because the behavioral suites run against ONE database while a handoff is by definition two: the email guard must read the synced `items` table and key on the stable id, `markImported` must still follow `createItem` (reversed, a crash loses the message for every copy at once), and calendar dedup must stay on `items.msEventId` rather than the per-copy cache. `verify-sync-ui.mts` grew the cadence ladder: every preset the picker offers is one the guardrail accepts, weekly passes and a fortnight is refused, the refusal moves with the window it protects, and the tolerant read is pinned in both directions (legacy strings, fractions floored, over-cap clamped, negatives read as continuous). Behaviorally: **`verify-email-in.mts` now hands the job over mid-flight** against a source that models the real folder, with two messages filed and moved, one created-but-never-moved, one genuinely new, and the stored place-in-the-queue deleted; it proves the new owner imports exactly the new one, recognizes and clears the stuck one, and leaves no message with two items. **`verify-calendar-sync.mts` empties `calendar_events`** (exactly what a machine taking over has) and proves the next run creates nothing, duplicates nothing, and re-links the cache to the meetings that already exist.
**Not yet proven on hardware:** the two acceptance tests Brandon still owes both need PR #327 merged and deployed first, and neither is affected by this ADR: turning local snapshots on for one hourly run, and claiming `export` on the PC to watch the OneDrive backlog drain.
**Affects:** `src/lib/job-owners.ts`, `src/lib/sync/client.ts`, `src/app/api/sync/hubs/route.ts`, `src/components/network/HubActions.tsx`, `src/components/network/FallbackPrompt.tsx`, `src/components/network/ReleasePushButton.tsx`, `scripts/local-setup.mjs`, `scripts/local-setup-lib.mjs`, `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`, `scripts/verify-job-owners.mts`, `scripts/verify-sync-ui.mts`, `scripts/verify-sync-summary.mts`, `scripts/verify-setup.mts`, `scripts/verify-email-in.mts`, `scripts/verify-calendar-sync.mts`.

## ADR-222: The GUI owns every setting the owner has; three surfaces stopped lying about it
**Date:** 2026-08-25
**Status:** accepted. Three fixes to shipped work (ADR-217, ADR-220, ADR-219/210), none of them core: no migration, no wire change, no change to the provider seams. Behavior is unchanged for anyone who does not touch the new switch.
**Context:** Brandon opened the surfaces ADR-217 through ADR-221 shipped and found three things that were not so. The three have one root and one new rule.

**The rule, stated by Brandon and now a working convention in `CLAUDE.md`: the config file is never the end user's lever.** Every setting a person is expected to change lives in the GUI. `supervisor/config.json` is for standing an install up and for testing, not for switching a feature on. A checkbox that is really "edit this JSON and restart a Windows service" is not a feature that shipped, it is a feature with a builder attached.

### 1. Restore points are a checkbox, not a config edit

ADR-217 put the *keep* number in the app and left the *switch* in `crons.snapshot`, so turning the safety net on meant editing a file and restarting the local service. The Snapshots section even said so in monospace.

**The fix inverts which layer decides.** The supervisor now schedules `snapshot` hourly on **every** peer (`LOCAL_JOBS.snapshot.on: true`) and the endpoint asks `job_state` whether to do anything: absent or false, `GET /api/machine/snapshot` returns `{ok: true, skipped}` without dumping, which the cron state records as a clean run rather than a failure. The owner's switch is `snapshots:enabled`, beside the keep number, read fresh on every run so flipping it needs no restart and applies on the hour.

**Off is still the default**, for ADR-217's reason (snapshots cost real disk) — the default just moved from the config file to the database. `"crons": {"snapshot": false}` still un-schedules the job entirely; that stays as a testing lever, not as the owner's control. **Switching off never deletes what is on disk**: a safety net you turn off should not also empty. Turning it on where the local service predates this change is the one case that needs a restart, and the section says exactly that instead of naming a file.

### 2. The roster filled a day late, which read as broken

ADR-220 decision 3 rides the announce on `purge`, daily at 03:10 — right for hearing about the *other* copies, and it was the only writer. So a copy that had not yet run its first purge was **missing from its own roster**, and the "Runs on" picker on that machine offered nothing but "Wherever it is switched on" and "Nowhere, pause it". Both of ADR-220's headline payoffs looked unbuilt on the day they shipped.

A roster READ now also refreshes this copy's own row when it is absent or older than twelve hours, best-effort so a failed write can never turn a readable roster into an empty page. Twelve hours holds it to at most two extra synced ops a day, which is the constraint that kept announce off the request path in the first place. The daily heartbeat is unchanged and still the mechanism; this is a floor under it.

### 3. A copy that only receives was told it syncs with nothing

`summarizeSync`'s first branch keyed on `sync.enabled`, which means "does this copy have somewhere to send changes". A main copy has nowhere: everything pushes **into** it. So the cloud install opened with *"This device is not syncing with anything. Everything you write stays here."* while a local peer pushed into it every ten seconds — the busiest node on the network calling itself an island, which is the Principle 9 failure this page keeps re-committing in new places.

Sync has two directions and the headline reads both now. With no outbound copies and live inbound devices it says how many send changes here and points at the list; with both, the normal sentence carries the inbound clause too. "Where your changes go" says the same thing in its empty state instead of "everything you write stays on this device only". A revoked or pull-only peer is not counted: neither can push.

**Rejected:** *making `keep: 0` mean off* — one knob fewer, but the number's job is how much history to hold and switching off would then destroy it, which is the opposite of what a safety net does on the way out. *Announcing on every request* — the reason ADR-220 rejected it stands; the twelve-hour floor buys the same correctness for two ops a day. *Joining `sync_peers` to `installs` so the headline could name the inbound machines* — ADR-220 already weighed and rejected that link; a count answers the question the sentence asks.

**Verification:** `verify-snapshots.mts` (29 checks) asserts the catalog now schedules the job for a peer that asked for nothing, that an explicit `false` still un-schedules it, that the endpoint reads the switch **before** the dump rather than after, that the app can write it, and that the Snapshots section contains no config-file path — the last one is the rule from the top of this ADR as a tripwire. `verify-sync-summary.mts` (15 checks) adds three: a receive-only copy is never called an island and is offered its device list, one inbound device is singular while zero still reads as alone, and a copy in the middle reports both directions in one sentence.
**Not yet proven on hardware:** the hourly snapshot actually taking a dump after the switch is turned on (it needs the local service restarted to pick up the new schedule).
**Affects:** `supervisor/lib.mjs`, `supervisor/config.example.json`, `supervisor/README.md`, `src/lib/snapshot-settings.ts`, `src/app/api/machine/snapshot/route.ts`, `src/app/api/snapshots/route.ts`, `src/components/updates/SnapshotKeep.tsx`, `src/app/build/updates/page.tsx`, `src/lib/installs.ts`, `src/lib/sync/summary.ts`, `src/app/build/network/page.tsx`, `scripts/verify-snapshots.mts`, `scripts/verify-sync-summary.mts`, `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`, `CLAUDE.md`.
## ADR-223: Finishing a project — a checkbox that completes what's inside, the board as the project's front door, and two order bugs behind it
**Date:** 2026-08-25
**Renumbered 2026-08-26:** written as ADR-217 and committed under that number (the commit messages on `feat/projects-done-and-kanban` still read ADR-217), moved to 223 when the merge with `main` found ADR-217 already taken by Local snapshots. Same story for the API-credentials ADR below: written as 218, moved to 224, and its migration generated as `0058` then regenerated as `0059` behind `0058_installs_roster`. `main` was authoritative in all three cases.
**Status:** accepted (Tyler, 2026-08-25) — NOT core: UI/UX plus a purely additive API route (ADR-183's carve-out) and two additive lens kinds. No schema change, no migration, nothing touched in the data model. `list-lenses` gains two parse-tolerant kinds, so an instance that never sees them behaves identically.
**Context:** Tyler put a project in Done and it stayed on his kanban, which opened up four separate problems at once. (1) There was no one-gesture way to *finish* a project: the status pill could set Done, but the project's twenty-odd open tasks stayed open, so its progress bar sat at 29% and its tasks kept surfacing in every task list. (2) His hand-built "Projects Board" rendered a column headed `STATUS_7` with Done on the FAR LEFT. (3) Project descriptions had silently vanished from every project but one. (4) There was nowhere to review finished work.
**Decision, in four parts.**
*The completion sweep.* A **Mark this project done** checkbox in the record header (`ProjectDoneCheckbox`) over a new `POST /api/items/[id]/complete-project`, split deliberately into **plan** (GET, read-only) and **apply** (POST). Opening the confirm fetches the plan and names real counts — "completes this project and 18 tasks, 3 milestones" — because a bulk write the owner can't preview is a bulk write they can't trust; applying raises the standard undo toast holding every item's PRIOR status, and reverts verbatim. Scope is **containment, not association**: a home edge or a `project`/`contains` role. The record-widget collections are deliberately association-wide (a Tasks card shows anything linked), but completing things through "was linked here once" would be silent damage. **The sweep is generic over types, with no allowlist** (Tyler's actual point, 2026-08-25): completability is decided by looking each contained item's type up *at plan time* and asking two questions — does this type track completion, and what status key does it call done — so a type that gains a Done checkbox later (a Receipt, a Purchase, a type that doesn't exist yet) is swept from that moment on, completing to **its own** done key rather than a literal `"done"`, with no code change and nothing to register. That rule is now the exported pure `sweepDecision`, asserted directly (a future type with a checkbox; a custom `delivered` status; completion-off, unknown-type and no-done-key skips), specifically so nobody narrows it to a hardcoded task/milestone list — which would silently drop every type invented after today, and nobody would notice until a finished project quietly kept a tail of open work. Two classes are skipped and *reported rather than dropped*: **repeating tasks** (completing one advances it to its next date — ADR-073's model — so sweeping it would quietly reschedule a chore) and types with `statusMode: "none"` (writing "done" to a note or event is a no-op no surface can show or reverse). The project is written LAST, so a sweep that dies partway never leaves the record reading Done over a pile of open work. **Unchecking reopens the PROJECT only** (Tyler's call): the undo toast is how you take back a sweep; unchecking weeks later shouldn't resurrect twenty tasks you genuinely finished since.
*The board as the project's front door.* Two new **synthetic** lens kinds, `board` and `completed`, which build a `ViewDefinition` on the fly from the type instead of pointing at a saved view — which is what lets a type ship a kanban as its DEFAULT tab (a `view` lens needs a stored view id, which a fresh instance hasn't got). Both ride the existing ViewRenderer pipeline, so status columns, project cards, drag-to-change and the collapsed Done column come for free with nothing stored and nothing to migrate. Their ids are stable strings (`board:project`), deliberately not valid view ids, so `hostable: false` keeps the Desk's "Open beside" from advertising a dead `/views/<id>`. Terminal columns (done + archived) **collapse to a rail by default** (`board-prefs.ts`, `useSyncExternalStore` per `related-prefs.ts` so SSR and first paint agree) — still counted, still expandable, and **still a drop target**, so dragging onto collapsed Done completes a project without expanding it. Mobile is snap-scrolled full-width columns, and snapping is DROPPED mid-drag because the touch-drag hook auto-scrolls imperatively and mandatory snap yanks it back.
*The two order bugs, which were not the same bug.* (a) The list-page lens path (`view-render.ts`) computed a board's `groupOrder` only for *property* groupings, never status ones, and never passed `statuses` at all — so `orderedGroups` had no known order and every column fell through to its ALPHABETICAL tail (`done, ongoing, status_7`: Done first, raw keys as headers). Fixed in all three resolvers plus `related-views.ts`. (b) Then, **found only by rendering a real board**, every one of the four call sites built the order as `statuses.map(s => s.key)` — but `resolveStatusSchema` preserves the order statuses were AUTHORED in; `orderedStatuses` is the function that sorts by category. On Tyler's schema that put Done FIFTH of seven, mid-strip, with Blocked and Background to its right. All four now use `orderedStatuses`. The first draft of the verify script passed straight through (b) because it fed itself `orderedStatuses(...)` by hand — it tested the helper, not the pipeline — so the trap is now asserted directly. Statuses also gained **↑/↓ reordering within a category** in Build: category order is fixed, so a status added later was pinned to the end of its group forever with no fix short of deleting and recreating it.
*The vanished descriptions.* Not lost — verified by reading the body straight out of production. The 2026-07-01 redesign dropped `overview` from the default project layout, and the canvas rendered the description ONLY when the composition carried that section, so every project whose layout was stored without it hid real text indefinitely. The rule is now: render the Overview when the layout asks for it **OR** whenever the body has content and the owner hasn't explicitly hidden the section. The `hidden` check keeps defer-by-hiding intact; the OR makes it self-healing, so no migration touches a single record. `overview` is back in the project default too (free when empty — it collapses to a glyph).
**Rejected:** *a checkbox that only sets status* — the whole complaint was the open tail left behind. *Sweeping everything `relatedTo` the project* — completes a neighbour's linked task. *Completing `statusMode: "none"` items anyway* — an invisible, unreversible write; the honest answer is to report them and point at the Build toggle that would include them. *Reopening the swept tasks on uncheck* — Tyler's call, above. *A migration to backfill `overview` into stored layouts* — the render-time OR fixes every existing record with no write. *Hiding done projects from the board entirely* — collapsed-but-droppable keeps the column useful as the completion gesture.
**Verification:** `tsc`, `eslint`, `next build` clean; `verify-project-done.mts` 30/30 (new, pure, in CI) including both order traps and the generic-over-types contract; `verify-user-guide` and the other 67 pure suites pass. Rendered against the real dev database: board columns now read Waiting → Paused → Future → Ongoing → **Done** (collapsed rail, rightmost), the Completed tab renders its search box, and the plan endpoint returns honest counts on live data (`{"count":7,"summary":"5 milestones, 2 tasks","skipped":{"noCompletion":13,...,"recurring":1}}`). **Not exercised against a database: the apply + undo write path** — deliberately, since ADR-206 sync could propagate a local write; Tyler runs that one on a test project.
**Affects:** `src/lib/project-completion.ts`, `src/lib/board-prefs.ts`, `src/components/views/BoardColumn.tsx`, `src/components/lists/SearchableList.tsx`, `src/components/lists/CompletedLensBody.tsx`, `src/components/canvas/widgets/ProjectDoneCheckbox.tsx`, `src/app/api/items/[id]/complete-project/route.ts`, `scripts/verify-project-done.mts` (all new); `src/lib/view-render.ts`, `src/lib/related-views.ts`, `src/lib/dashboard-resolve.ts`, `src/app/views/[id]/page.tsx`, `src/lib/status.ts`, `src/lib/list-lenses.ts`, `src/lib/composition.ts`, `src/components/views/{ViewRenderer,BoardDnd}.tsx`, `src/components/lists/ViewLensBody.tsx`, `src/components/canvas/WidgetCanvas.tsx`, `src/components/build/{StatusSchemaEditor,ListTabsEditor}.tsx`, `src/components/ui/ConfirmButton.tsx`, `src/app/list/[type]/page.tsx`, `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`.

## ADR-224: API credentials — a key ID and a secret you create in the app, revocable by a row flip
**Date:** 2026-08-26
**Status:** accepted (Tyler + Brandon, 2026-08-26; Brandon agreed before merge, relayed by Tyler). **CORE, and treated as such:** it adds a table to `schema.md` (`api_credentials`) with migration `0059_api_credentials`, and it adds a credential path to the machine-auth contract. The *additive* half is covered by ADR-183's carve-out (a new way to authenticate, no existing caller changed); the new table is not, which is why it went to Brandon first; he agreed, and this merged on that agreement. Nothing existing changes shape: `verifyMachineToken` and `verifyApiToken` keep their signatures and their behavior, `LEDGR_API_TOKENS` is still read first on every request, and `scripts/make-token.mjs` is untouched.
**Context:** getting an `api`-scoped token meant `node scripts/make-token.mjs <name> api`, pasting the hash into `LEDGR_API_TOKENS` on Vercel, and redeploying. Revoking meant deleting the entry and redeploying again. So every credential and every revocation cost a production deploy, which is a real disincentive to issuing one per caller and a worse one to revoking promptly. The ADR-160/ADR-179 minters removed the deploy from *issuing* by going stateless (signed blobs, no row), but they bought that by giving up per-credential revocation entirely: rotating `LEDGR_APP_SECRET` kills every app token at once, so the page had to tell the owner "there is no list of active tokens and no way to revoke one individually." Meanwhile `sync_peers` already stored token hashes on rows, and `machine.ts`'s own header comment pointed at it (plan decision 15: revocation is a row flip, not a redeploy). The general API credential was the odd one out, and it was the one an owner most wants to hand out and take back.
**Decision.** A two-part credential stored on a row, in the shape Planning Center, Stripe and AWS use.
1. **Key ID + secret, not one opaque token.** `lgrk_<24 hex>` is public, stored in plaintext, and is the lookup handle; `lgrs_<48 hex>` is hashed with `hashToken()` and shown exactly once. Three reasons for the split, in order of weight: **lookup** becomes one indexed row fetch plus one `timingSafeEqual` compare, where the env scheme must walk and compare every entry; **identification** becomes possible at all, so the UI can show which credential is which and a key ID found in a log or a client config names its credential without exposing the secret; and **leak handling** improves, because the half that shows up in logs and screenshots is the half that grants nothing.
2. **HTTP Basic is the documented path.** `Authorization: Basic base64(keyId:secret)`, so `curl -u` and every HTTP client work with no custom header. `Bearer <keyId>:<secret>` is also accepted for clients that only do bearer. The key-id prefix plus the colon is what keeps this from ever colliding with an existing opaque Bearer token, which has neither.
3. **Both credential sources resolve, env first.** Two async resolvers, `verifyMachineRequest()` and `verifyApiRequest()` (`src/lib/auth/credentials.ts`), try the unchanged env/stateless check and only then the DB lookup. So an existing caller's request resolves exactly as it did before, `CRON_SECRET` and every current entry keep working, and the DB is not touched at all on the hot path for those callers.
4. **The module sits beside `machine.ts`, not inside it.** The prompt asked for the resolution to live in `machine.ts`; it lives in a new `credentials.ts` instead, because `machine.ts` is imported by `oauth.ts`, whose header comment commits it to being pure `node:crypto` with no DB. Putting `getDb()` in `machine.ts` would have made every OAuth code path transitively import the database. `src/lib/sync/auth.ts` already set this layering precedent for device tokens.
5. **Revocation is `revoked_at`, not a delete.** The row survives so the list still shows what the credential was, what it could do, and when it last worked. Verification reads the row on every request and nothing is cached, so revoking takes effect on the very next call.
6. **Least privilege by default.** Permissions are checkboxes over the real scopes (`api`, `mcp`, `cron`, `diag`), nothing pre-ticked, each labelled in plain language with the scope string shown small underneath. Scopes are re-validated server-side against the same list, so a credential cannot name a permission the form never offered, and cannot widen its own.
7. **`last_used_at` is advanced off the request path**, via `after()` (falling back to a detached promise outside a request scope) and throttled to one write a minute. A failure there is swallowed: a missing usage stamp must never turn a valid credential into a 401.
8. **Caps instead of a rate limiter**: 25 active credentials and 10 created per hour, both counted in the DB rather than in process memory, because a serverless instance's memory resets on every cold start.
**Rejected:** *one opaque token, hashed* — keeps the linear walk, and gives the UI nothing to display, which is most of what makes a credential list useful. *Storing the secret encrypted so it can be re-shown* — a recoverable secret is a worse secret, and "shown once" is the behavior every comparable product has trained people to expect. *Deleting the row on revoke* — throws away the record of what had access. *Retiring the env path* — an entry in `LEDGR_API_TOKENS` is the credential a job needs *before* the app can serve a page and the one that still works when the database does not (`CRON_SECRET`, a bootstrap script, a restore), so it stays documented as the deliberate fallback. *Deleting the ADR-179 app-token minter* — folded behind a disclosure on `/build/api` instead (defer by hiding, not deleting), so an app already holding one can be handed a replacement. *An in-memory rate limiter* — resets per cold start, so it limits nothing.
**Verification:** `tsc`, `eslint` and `verify-provider-seams` clean (the seam guard learned the two new helper names, and its Clerk check went from FAIL to PASS, see below). New `scripts/verify-api-credentials.mts`, 28 checks against the live dev DB: shape, hash-only storage, Basic and Bearer both authenticating, and every failure closed (wrong secret, unknown key ID, unheld scope, api-only refused on an `mcp` check, an opaque Bearer not misread as a pair, no header), plus `last_used_at` advancing, owner-scoped revoke, double-revoke as a no-op, another owner's id refused, and the caps refusing. Then the end-to-end HTTP test against a running server: a minted `api` credential returned 200 on `GET /api/machine/items` over both `-u` and `Bearer key:secret`, 401 on `/api/machine/purge` (holding `api`, not `cron`); revoking it from a separate process, with the server never restarted, turned the same call into 401 — the no-redeploy claim, observed rather than argued. Regression-checked the paths that had to keep working: a freshly issued CLI env token authenticated a `cron` route and echoed its own identity from `/api/machine/ping`, and a static env `mcp` token completed an `initialize` against `/api/mcp`, as did a minted `mcp` credential, while an `api`-only credential was refused there. **Not exercised locally:** the OAuth and clipper token paths, since `LEDGR_OAUTH_SECRET` and `LEDGR_CLIPPER_SECRET` are unset on this dev instance; their code is untouched and still runs before the DB lookup.
**Drive-by, unrelated to this feature:** `verify-provider-seams` was already failing on `main` before any of this work (confirmed by stashing), because ADR-216's `NavAuthHeal.tsx` imports `@clerk/nextjs` directly and the auth-seam check caught it. Fixed at the seam rather than by widening the allowlist: a new `src/lib/auth/client.ts` (`"use client"`) exports `useClientSession()`, the one hook reporting whether the *browser* thinks a session exists, and `NavAuthHeal` reads that. Clerk stays confined to seam files, and the allowlist grows by a seam file rather than by an app component. `npm run ci` was red on `main` for this; it is green now.
**Affects:** `src/lib/auth/credentials.ts`, `src/lib/auth/credential-actions.ts`, `src/lib/auth/client.ts`, `src/components/settings/ApiCredentials.tsx`, `drizzle/0059_api_credentials.sql`, `scripts/verify-api-credentials.mts` (all new); `src/db/schema.ts`, `src/app/settings/page.tsx`, `src/app/build/api/page.tsx`, `src/lib/build-nav.ts` ("API Tokens" to "API"), `src/lib/health.ts`, `src/components/nav/NavAuthHeal.tsx`, `scripts/verify-provider-seams.mts`, `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`, `runbook.md` §3, and the eighteen `/api/machine/*` routes plus `/api/mcp` (each swapping its sync verify call for the async resolver).


## ADR-225: Ownership is the only switch, and the picker stops promising a speed the network does not have
**Date:** 2026-08-26
**Renumbered 2026-08-26:** written as ADR-225 and committed under that number, moved to 225 when the merge with `main` found 223 and 224 already taken by Tyler's project-completion and API-credential ADRs. Its migration was generated as `0059` and regenerated as `0060` behind `0059_api_credentials`, for the same reason. `main` is authoritative.
**Status:** accepted (core: the scheduler seam's default set, and what an unset ownership slot means; Tyler acked 2026-08-26).
**Context:** Brandon opened Scheduled work on the cloud copy, moved the offline backup, calendar sync and email capture to his always-on PC, and got three green indicators. Then he opened the same page on the PC, which said all three still ran *"wherever it is switched on"*. He asked the right question: is that how it is supposed to work?

It was not. Two separate faults were wearing one symptom.

### 1. Ownership was two switches, so a job could be assigned to nobody

ADR-219's slot granted **permission**; `crons` in `supervisor/config.json` granted the **trigger**, and for every exclusive job that config default was `off`. So naming a peer moved the permission to a machine with no trigger. The cloud re-read the slot, correctly saw it was no longer the owner, and stood down. The peer was never called. Measured on the live rig: the cloud held claims for all three jobs, the peer's `ledgr-ctl status` listed only `purge`, `relatedness` and `snapshot`, and the backup, calendar sync and email capture were running on **neither machine**. Nothing said so, and the liveness warning would not have said so for a day.

**The fix is ADR-222's pattern applied to the jobs the picker can move.** The supervisor schedules `export`, `calendar-sync` and `email-import` unconditionally (`on: true`) and the endpoint's existing gate decides. One lever, and it is the GUI.

That changes what an **absent** slot means, which is the part worth stating precisely. It used to mean "as before this feature existed", survivable only because of the config default. It now resolves per install kind: the **cloud runs it** (as it always did) and a **supervised peer stands down** (as it always did, by way of that default). Same behavior for anyone who never opens the picker, Tyler's cloud-only instance included. The difference is that naming a machine is now sufficient, with no file edited and no service restarted. `LEDGR_SUPERVISOR_DIR` is the signal, because it answers exactly the question that matters: is something out there about to call these endpoints on a timer?

A stood-down run is **recorded as a stand-down**, not as work done: the supervisor reads the endpoint's `{skipped, detail}` and the surfaces print "this job runs on Cloud, not here". A job scheduled everywhere that reported a clean run everywhere would be the same silent lie in a new place. The three jobs the picker refuses to move (`todoist-sync`, `transcription-poll`, `health-check`) stay unscheduled on peers, and CI now refuses the combination that made this bug possible: a default-on exclusive job that either the picker cannot move or whose route does not call the gate.

### 2. The confirm dialog promised "within seconds", which is a cadence away from true

The move said *"That takes effect everywhere within seconds."* True between copies syncing continuously. Brandon's PC syncs hourly, and the per-hub cadence gates the whole exchange in both directions, so the claim written at 12:30:35 was 59 minutes from a peer whose last exchange was 12:29:31. The GUI has to match what the network can actually do, so:

- The confirm says what happens instead: this copy stops when you confirm, and the machine you chose picks the job up **at its next check-in**. It names the handover gap out loud, which the per-job consequence lines were already written to make survivable ("the next run catches up"), and it warns when the target is a copy nothing has heard from, because assigning a job to a quiet machine is how it ends up running nowhere.
- **"Check in now"** on Build → Network exchanges with every copy immediately, cadence ignored. This is what makes a slow cadence a choice rather than a trap: before it, nothing anywhere could ask a peer to sync sooner, in either direction. It sets a flag the loop reads on its next tick (~2s) rather than running an exchange of its own, so it cannot race the cursors.
- The default option is **"Leave it to the cloud"**, not "Wherever it is switched on": there is no longer a per-machine switch for that phrase to refer to. Both `/build/updates` sentences pointing the owner at `crons` in `supervisor/config.json` are gone (the ADR-222 rule).

**Rejected:** *a push channel from cloud to peer*, because the hub is passive by design (ADR-206 decision 11) and a peer is behind NAT, so this would be a second sync path to maintain for one message. *Having the browser ping the peer after an assignment*: cross-origin, works only when the owner happens to be on the same network, and lies differently. *Holding the old owner until the new one acknowledges*: an ack protocol for a gap the three movable jobs are already documented to survive. *A capability check in the picker* ("refuse to assign to a machine that has not scheduled it") was the obvious fix and the wrong one: it makes the two-switch design permanent and puts the config file back in the owner's path.
**Verification:** `verify-job-owners.mts` (27 checks) adds four: an unnamed job runs in the cloud and stands down on a peer with exactly one of the two running, naming a peer moves it there and only there, the flag resolves absence and nothing else, and a stand-down reads as "the cloud has this" while pointing at the one lever. `verify-supervisor.mts` proves the new default set, and for **every** default-on exclusive job that the picker can move it and that its route calls `standDownIfNotOwner`, plus that a stand-down reaches the cron record.
**Not yet proven on hardware:** the peer actually running an assigned job after its next check-in. It needs this build on both copies and the local service restarted.
**Affects:** `src/lib/job-owners.ts`, `src/lib/job-owners-store.ts`, `src/lib/job-owner-guard.ts`, `src/lib/sync/client.ts`, `src/app/api/sync/check-in/route.ts`, `src/components/network/CheckInButton.tsx`, `src/components/updates/JobOwnerControl.tsx`, `src/app/build/updates/page.tsx`, `src/app/build/network/page.tsx`, `supervisor/lib.mjs`, `supervisor/ledgr-supervisor.mjs`, `supervisor/README.md`, `scripts/verify-job-owners.mts`, `scripts/verify-supervisor.mts`, `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`.

## ADR-226: `users.settings` merges per key, because one blob made every preference a race
**Date:** 2026-08-26
**Status:** accepted (core: the oplog trigger and a merge rule; Tyler acked 2026-08-26). Migration `0060_users_settings_perkey`, function body only: no table, column or wire change.
**Context:** Found while proving ADR-225 propagates. `users.settings` is a single jsonb column holding every per-owner preference, and the sync merge is per **field**, so the whole blob was one last-writer-wins unit. `updateSettings` writes the complete normalized blob, so any settings write on any copy carried that copy's entire view of settings and, on arrival, replaced the other side's, silently reverting every key the writer had not yet pulled.

Job ownership turned that from a theoretical hazard into a scheduled one. The slot lives in `settings.jobOwners`, and the assigned machine stamps `lastRunAt` into it after a run. So the machine holding a job writes settings from an up-to-an-hour-old copy of every *other* key, on a timer. The owner moves a job in the cloud, changes an unrelated preference on the peer, and the assignment undoes itself with nothing in any log, indistinguishable from the bug ADR-225 just fixed.

**The trigger now logs only the top-level settings keys that changed**, and the engine stamps and merges them independently (`settings.<key>`), writing the merged blob back. Two copies editing different preferences both survive; a copy that rewrites a key with the value it already had logs nothing for it, which is what makes a stale base harmless. A whole-blob op, meaning anything already sitting in an oplog written before this migration, still merges correctly, just with every key stamped at once, so nothing needs migrating.

The one case the diff cannot express is a **removed** top-level key, because the diff walks the new blob's keys. Nothing removes one (`parseSettings` always writes a complete blob), and if anything ever does, the trigger falls back to sending the whole blob: coarser merge, never a lost change.

**Rejected:** *fixing it in the merge alone*, since without the trigger sending the changed keys there is nothing to stamp and every arriving op would still claim every key. *A jsonb patch write action*: the merge base is the row apply just read, exactly as it is for every other field, so writing the merged column needs no new executor path. *Splitting settings into columns or a table*: a schema change of real size to solve what a diff solves, and the blob-per-owner shape is deliberate (a new preference is not a migration).
**Verification:** `verify-sync.mts` adds eight checks. Pure: a settings op stamps its keys rather than the column, both keys survive when two copies edit different ones in either arrival order, a contested key is still LWW in both directions, a legacy whole-blob op still merges, applying twice is a no-op, and the migration really does diff against `OLD`. On two real Postgres clusters: a settings write logs **only** the key that moved, and then the live failure itself, where the cloud names a machine, the peer writes an unrelated preference later from a stale copy, and after exchanging both ways both copies hold both the assignment and the preference.
**Affects:** `drizzle/0060_users_settings_perkey.sql`, `drizzle/meta/_journal.json`, `drizzle/meta/0060_snapshot.json`, `src/lib/sync/engine.ts`, `src/lib/sync/apply.ts`, `scripts/verify-sync.mts`.

## ADR-227: A Restart button, because the app cannot restart its own parent
**Date:** 2026-08-26
**Status:** accepted. Not core: no schema, no wire change, no seam change. New request file, new state file, two owner-authed routes, and a supervisor that can hand off to its successor.
**Context:** Shipping ADR-225 ended in "now go restart the local service", and Brandon named the rule it broke: he wants the GUI to handle 99% of the tasks on a Ledgr install, and if a restart is ever needed there should be a button he can press and be confident it stops, starts and reaches healthy again — whatever the reason, including an update that required it. Then the manual path proved his point twice in one evening: the `restart` verb he typed did not exist, and the two commands that replaced it left his peer down.

**Why this is not simply "add a button".** The supervisor owns the app process, so the app cannot restart the supervisor: stopping your own parent leaves nobody to start you again. The mechanism is therefore the one already proven twice here — the app writes a REQUEST FILE, a process that can actually do the thing carries it out, and the outcome is written back (ADR-211's `stop-requested` and `startup-requested`) — with one twist. The process carrying out a restart is the one going away, so before it exits it **spawns its successor** and hands over its own pid to wait for.

### What makes it reliable rather than merely wired

1. **The successor waits for the outgoing pid to exit** before claiming the lock, so two supervisors never contend for the cluster or the port. Bounded: if the old one never leaves, the new one stands aside and records why rather than seizing a live lock.
2. **Postgres start retries** (four attempts, 0/2/5/10s). This is the fix for the failure that took the peer down for ten minutes on 2026-08-26: a supervisor that dies without a clean shutdown can leave an orphaned backend holding the cluster's shared memory, Windows keeps that segment attached until the last one exits, and a start into that window fails instantly with *pre-existing shared memory block is still in use*. Every restart attempt died on it, including the owner's. The window is seconds long, so waiting through it is the whole fix.
3. **"Healthy" means the port answered.** The first version wrote healthy whenever a build pointer existed, which would have recorded a clean restart for a peer whose app never came up. The successor now probes its own port and writes `healthy` or `failed` with the reason.
4. **The button proves a restart by a CHANGED pid**, not by its own request succeeding. It records which process is serving, asks, then polls `/api/local/service` until a different one answers — every failed fetch in between is expected, and only the two-minute deadline is a failure, with the CLI named as the next step.
5. **Every phase is on disk** (`supervisor-state.json`): requested, stopping, handing-off, healthy, failed. `handing-off` is deliberately the outgoing process's last word, so a state stuck there is the only possible evidence that a successor never started — the process that would report it is the one that went away.

### The thing nobody was telling the owner

A running supervisor holds the code it started with, so an update that changes the supervisor's own files (the job catalog, the schedule, its update logic) is installed but not in effect, silently. It now fingerprints its own source at startup and re-reads it from disk on every state write, so **This machine's Ledgr service** says *"An update has arrived that this service predates"* and offers the button. Proven live: the fingerprint went stale under the running process, the restart applied it, and the new process reported the installed fingerprint.

**Two bugs found in passing, both fixed here.** The boot task's caveat was printed from `startup-state.json` — a string recorded at registration time and never re-checked — so a task later upgraded to run with nobody signed in was still reported as if it could not, with advice for a password Ledgr no longer uses; `status` now computes it from what Windows holds. And Task Scheduler registers no working directory, so a boot-started supervisor inherited `System32`; it now `chdir`s to its own repo, which removes the class rather than the symptom.

**Rejected:** *the app killing the supervisor and relying on Task Scheduler to restart it* — the task is registered "at system start", so nothing would have brought it back until a reboot. *A watchdog process to supervise the supervisor* — a third process to keep alive, to solve a restart that takes five seconds. *Auto-restarting after any update that changed the supervisor* — the right end state and one line away now, but a restart loop on a bad update is worse than a button, so the mechanism proves itself on hardware first (queued in next_steps).
**Verification:** `scripts/verify-restart.mts`, 23 checks. The highest-value ones are the agreements a refactor would silently break: the app writes exactly the basename the supervisor watches (a one-character drift is a dead button), the .mjs writer and the .ts reader agree field-for-field about the state file, the successor is spawned only AFTER Postgres is confirmed down, the port probe gates `healthy`, and the route says "requested" where it cannot say "restarted". Plus the wording: stale code is the only state that asks the owner to act, an unknown state never renders as health, and a missing fingerprint reads as "no answer" rather than "act now".
**Proven on hardware (2026-08-26):** the button's exact request path, twice. First run 4.6s from request to a new pid reporting healthy; second run 5.1s, and that one carried a stale-code case end to end — running `58225c1b` against installed `5a356654`, then the same fingerprint on both sides afterwards, with `GET / → 200` and the 23,543-item database up. `npm run local:restart` was exercised in both directions: as a handoff, and as a cold start when nothing was running.
**Affects:** `supervisor/lib.mjs`, `supervisor/ledgr-supervisor.mjs`, `supervisor/ledgr-ctl.mjs`, `supervisor/README.md`, `package.json`, `src/lib/supervisor-state.ts`, `src/lib/local-service.ts`, `src/app/api/local/restart/route.ts`, `src/app/api/local/service/route.ts`, `src/components/updates/RestartServiceButton.tsx`, `src/app/build/updates/page.tsx`, `scripts/verify-restart.mts`, `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`.

## ADR-228: item bodies store a stable attachment address, not the storage provider's URL
**Date:** 2026-08-26
**Status:** accepted — CORE, **agreed by Tyler 2026-08-27** (relayed by Brandon), merged the same day
**Context:** Brandon asked whether to drop Cloudflare R2 and store files on the local install instead, since staying inside the 10GB free tier had him shrinking images and avoiding attachments. Measured first: 7,371 attachments total **0.20 GB**, 2% of the tier, and past it R2 charges ~1.5¢/GB/month with no egress fee. The discipline was guarding about a dollar a year, so the decision was to stay on R2 (2026-08-26).

But the investigation surfaced the real lock-in, which is not the bytes. Moving 100GB between providers is one `rclone` run. What was expensive is that **every attachment's full provider URL was written into the item body** (`imageToMarkdown` on the presign response's `publicUrl`), so the stored content was a copy of the storage decision. Changing providers, or even just the public base URL, meant rewriting URLs inside thousands of bodies — with revisions, sync, and a full re-export behind each one. That bill grows every day in either direction, which is what made "go local and maybe come back" feel like a one-way door. The same tax was already due for a change we want anyway: the bucket serves through Cloudflare's `r2.dev` development URL, which Cloudflare rate-limits and recommends for testing only.

**Decision:** bodies (and a person's `image` property) store `/files/<attachmentId>`. A new route redirects that to wherever the bytes currently live. Switching the public base URL or the storage provider is now an env change with **no body rewrite**.

1. **`/files/[id]` is a 302 redirect, never a proxy.** Bytes must not pass through the app server (principle 8). The browser follows the redirect to the CDN and reads exactly as before. `cache-control: max-age=3600` — an hour, not a year, because the redirect *target* changes on a base-URL switch.
2. **The address is relative, on purpose.** An absolute URL would pin a body to one install, and bodies sync between the local and cloud installs.
3. **The route is public,** matching `/share` and `/api/ics`: the attachment UUID is unguessable and is the credential. It *must* be — a public share page renders a body whose images are these addresses, and that viewer has no Clerk session. Not a privacy change: the provider URLs this replaces were world-readable too. Short-lived presigned GETs are the upgrade path if a privacy tier ever lands (ADR-075 declined one for v1.0), and it would be a change in this one file.
4. **The export rewrites these addresses to relative `_attachments/…` paths.** Required, not optional: `/files/<id>` resolves against the app, which is meaningless in a markdown file sitting on OneDrive. This makes the exported tree fully self-contained, so images render offline in Obsidian with the app down and no internet — **strictly better than the provider URLs it replaces**, which always needed the network. Principle 4 gets stronger here, not weaker. The indirection is also what makes the rewrite easy: the attachment id is right there in the URL, where before it would have meant matching storage keys.
5. **`publicUrl` is unchanged and still returned** everywhere; `fileUrl` is added beside it. Purely additive to the machine API and MCP, so per the ADR-183 carve-out no existing caller changes. `embed_attachment` normalizes whichever it is handed, so an AI passing the old field still stores the stable form.

**Two silent-degradation bugs this change would have caused, both fixed at the shared helper rather than per caller.** `personImage()` accepted only `http(s)` URLs, so the moment uploads stored a relative address **every uploaded avatar would have quietly fallen back to initials** — no error, just a wrong picture. `task-row-meta.ts` had the same test copied inline and would have dropped avatars from the connection strip. The URL helpers therefore live in `src/lib/attachment-url.ts`, pure and client-safe with no DB import, so the one place that decides what an avatar renders is shared instead of duplicated. A stable address also carries no filename and no extension, so `embed_attachment` now resolves "is this an image, what do I call it" from the attachment row; without that, every stable address embedded as a file link labelled with a UUID.

**Why / alternatives:** *Absolute app URLs in bodies* — same lock-in, one host swapped for another, and it breaks sync between installs. *Proxying bytes through the route* — violates principle 8 and puts every image on the app's compute budget. *Owner-scoped auth on the route* — breaks public share pages, and buys no privacy the provider URLs offered. *Leaving it alone and rewriting bodies at each provider change* — that is the cost being removed, and it only grows. *Moving to local file storage* — the question that started this; declined on the measured numbers, and R2 also gives durability, CDN reach from a phone on cellular, and one bucket shared by both installs.

**Migration:** `scripts/migrate-attachment-urls.mts`, dry-run by default. Local install: **1,412 items, 9,854 URLs**. It writes no revision snapshots (a mechanical address change, not a content edit; a backup is the undo) and bumps `updated_at` so the export re-writes those files with the new relative paths.
**Verification:** `scripts/verify-attachment-urls.mts`, 27 checks — base-agnostic normalization (a URL under the OLD base must still normalize after the domain move, or the migration silently misses half the corpus), an unknown id left alone rather than rewritten into a 404, idempotence, export depth for live vs `_archive` items, and the `personImage` acceptance that guards the avatar bug. Proven live: `/files/<id>` → 302 → 200, 152,722 bytes of PNG, rendered in a real browser; bad ids 404; no session needed. Full suite green (75 verify scripts, typecheck, lint, build).
**Affects:** `src/lib/attachment-url.ts` (new), `src/app/files/[id]/route.ts` (new), `scripts/migrate-attachment-urls.mts` (new), `scripts/verify-attachment-urls.mts` (new), `src/lib/attachments.ts`, `src/lib/person-image.ts`, `src/lib/task-row-meta.ts`, `src/lib/export/engine.ts`, `src/lib/mcp/tools/attachments.ts`, `src/proxy.ts`, `src/components/markdown-editor/ItemEditor.tsx`, `src/components/people/PersonImageBox.tsx`, `runbook.md`.

## ADR-229: a pid is not an identity — the peer comes back from an unclean reboot on its own, and says so from the notification area
**Date:** 2026-08-27
**Status:** accepted — not core (the local supervisor's own lifecycle; no schema, body format, provider interface or API contract moves)
**Context:** Brandon restarted the PC and Ledgr did not come back. Windows *did* start the service at 8:05:27 PM, so ADR-211's boot registration worked. Everything after it failed, in three separate ways that each hid the next.

**Postgres refused to start, four times in seventeen seconds, and the peer gave up.** The restart had not shut the cluster down cleanly ("database system was not properly shut down", in its own log), which leaves `postmaster.pid` behind naming the pid Postgres last ran as — 3144. Postgres refuses to start when that pid belongs to a live process. Right after a boot, Windows is handing low pids straight back out, so 3144 belonged to a stranger. By 8:13 PM that stranger had exited and the identical start command worked on the first attempt, which is the whole proof: nothing was wrong with the database, only with a number in a file.

**None of that was written down.** A Task Scheduler action has no stdout. The supervisor attached `supervisor.log` and `supervisor.err.log` only when restarting *itself*, so a supervisor Windows launched wrote its startup into nowhere. The single surviving sentence was `Postgres would not start: undefined` — "undefined" because embedded-postgres rejects with no value at all when the server exits early, so even the shape of the failure was lost.

**And the peer could not be restarted, by anyone.** The dead supervisor's lock still named pid 4080; Windows had reissued 4080 too. The old check asked only whether that pid existed, so `local:status` reported "supervisor running (pid 4080)" the entire time Ledgr was down, and starting one was refused outright: *"A supervisor is already running."* Recovery required a person who knew which file to delete. The `ponytail:` comment on `lockVerdict` had named this exact window and judged it too narrow to close; it took eleven days.

Brandon's framing set the bar past "log it better": unclean shutdowns will keep happening, so the peer has to come back **confidently**, on its own.

**Decision:**

1. **A pid is only evidence; identity comes from the process.** `lockVerdict` now takes `identified` — read from the running process's command line — and aliveness alone never decides. Provably a supervisor, refuse. Provably something else, steal the lock and start. Unreadable, fall back to whether Postgres is actually listening, because guessing wrong there would put two supervisors on one data directory. `supervisor/proc.mjs` (new) holds the asking; the deciding stays pure in `lib.mjs`, where the verify suite can reach it. The cheap pid check remains for wait loops, which ask a different question: has the process I already identified gone away yet?
2. **A provably stale `postmaster.pid` is deleted automatically.** Postgres's own documented recovery, with two guards that make it safe to automate: nothing may be listening on the port, and the process behind the pid must be provably not a postmaster. It buys one fresh round of start attempts, once — Postgres writes that file itself before deciding it cannot run, so an unbounded retry would loop forever on a cluster broken for some other reason.
3. **An orphaned Postgres is shut down cleanly rather than fought over.** The mirror case: a supervisor that dies without stopping its database leaves it *listening*. Nothing may be deleted there, but the port is taken and no fresh peer can have it. Narrow on purpose — our port, our data directory's lock file, and really a postmaster — then `pg_ctl stop -m fast`, the path that already existed for ordinary shutdown.
4. **Windows starts `ledgr-ctl boot`, not the supervisor.** One indirection buys both missing things: the supervisor is spawned with the peer's two log files already attached, so a boot failure leaves a reason; and a stale lock is cleared on the way past, so a peer that died badly still comes back. `boot` is idempotent — run it on a healthy peer and it says "Already running" and stops — which makes it safe from a schedule, a shortcut, or a double-click.
5. **The control script sets `process.exitCode` instead of calling `process.exit()`.** Exiting while the sockets from a health check are still closing trips a libuv assertion on Windows and kills the process with status 127 *after the work succeeded*. Cosmetic from a terminal; not cosmetic from Task Scheduler, which would have recorded every successful boot as a failure. Winding down naturally is also faster here (~160ms versus ~430ms).
6. **A notification-area icon, because the local service had no face.** It ran as a console window nobody could interpret, and hiding that window left no way to know it was running at all — while the one surface that could have answered, Ledgr itself, is exactly what is missing when the answer is "it isn't". So: a dot near the clock. **Green** serving, **amber** the database is up but the app is not answering, **red** nothing. Right-click gives Open, Check status (both ports and the build), Start, Restart, Stop. It supervises nothing itself — every action shells out to the same `ledgr-ctl` verb a terminal would run, so the icon can never disagree with the CLI — and it watches two TCP ports rather than spawning anything, so the poll costs nothing.

**Why / alternatives:** *Log the failure and stop there* — what Brandon explicitly ruled out; a legible outage is still an outage. *Compare process start times instead of command lines* — the alternative the old `ponytail:` note weighed; it needs per-platform plumbing to answer a question the command line answers directly. *Delete `postmaster.pid` unconditionally before every start* — two postmasters on one data directory corrupts it; the guards are the point. *A tray icon from an npm dependency* — Windows ships PowerShell and WinForms, so the icon costs no new package (principle 5). *Put the tray in the boot task* — different lifetimes: the service runs with nobody signed in, and an icon means nothing without a desktop. It gets its own Startup shortcut, so it can be switched off without touching whether Ledgr runs.

**Verification:** the outage was reproduced on the live rig rather than argued about — Ledgr killed, the lock overwritten with a live non-supervisor pid, `postmaster.pid` left stale. `boot` recovered it unattended in **4.4 seconds**, and again in 3.3 from a crashed-supervisor state. The Windows path proved end to end with a throwaway scheduled task: task result 0, and the service still serving after the launcher exited. 22 new pure checks in `scripts/verify-supervisor.mts` cover both verdict functions, the `postmaster.pid` format, the task command and the tray's posture; `verify-setup.mts` updated for the new task action. Typecheck, lint and the suite green.

**Three bugs in this work's own code, all found by testing rather than reading.** The tray's "is one already running?" query ran inside a PowerShell whose *own* command line therefore contained the pattern it was searching for, so it matched itself, reported a different "tray pid" on every call, and hid the fact that no icon was running at all; the pattern is now built from two halves so the contiguous string never appears. Spawning `powershell.exe` detached with no stdio does not survive — it is a console host with no console — so the icon is launched through `Start-Process`, and its pid is looked up afterwards rather than taken from the spawn.

**And `formatSchtasks` had been printing a command that cannot work in the shell its own message names.** Every "schtasks failed" path tells the owner to run the printed line in an Administrator *PowerShell*, but the line carried cmd.exe backslash-quote escaping; Brandon pasted it and got `Invalid argument/option`. The trap is what came next: the two natural repairs — wrapping the `/TR` value in single quotes, or holding it in a variable — both report **SUCCESS** while registering a task whose command has lost every quote, because PowerShell re-quotes native arguments on the way to the executable. Verified by registering all three forms and reading back what Windows stored. That task would run on these machines and break the day a path contains a space, which is the same shape as the avatar bug in ADR-228: not an error, just quietly wrong. `formatSchtasks` now takes the shell (`cmd` for the elevation path's batch file, `powershell` for anything pasted) and the PowerShell form carries `--%`, which hands the line over verbatim. The messages also now offer `npm run local:startup -- --always` from an elevated prompt first, since that path passes an argument vector straight to `schtasks` and has nothing to mistype.

**Affects:** `supervisor/proc.mjs` (new), `supervisor/ledgr-tray.ps1` (new), `supervisor/lib.mjs`, `supervisor/ledgr-supervisor.mjs`, `supervisor/ledgr-ctl.mjs`, `scripts/verify-supervisor.mts`, `scripts/verify-setup.mts`, `package.json`, `runbook.md`, `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`.

## ADR-230: `horizon` says what stays true, `pinned` says what loads — the always-on set is pinned and nothing else

**Date:** 2026-08-27 · **Status:** accepted, CORE — **acked by Tyler 2026-08-28**, relayed by Brandon · **Supersedes the loading half of ADR-137**

**The bug was one word doing two jobs.** AI Memory (ADR-137) gave a memory two properties that mean different things. `horizon` is a **truth** property: does this claim stay true as time passes? `pinned` is a **load** property: does the agent need this in front of it on every run. They are orthogonal — a fact can be permanently true and almost never needed, or temporary and needed constantly. But the always-on query was `evergreen + pinned + recently-touched`, which put a truth property inside a loading decision. Once `evergreen` decided what loaded, it silently came to mean "important", and the agents writing memories set it for that reason instead of the intended one. The tool descriptions taught the confusion directly: `horizon` was introduced as a truth property and then defined by its effect on loading ("Seasonal/episodic age out of the always-on set"), and `pinned` was framed as an escalation of horizon ("regardless of horizon/age") rather than a separate axis.

**Measured on Brandon's live store, 2026-08-28, before the change.** 127 memories, 123 of them returned by the "always-on" filter. The filter excluded **four**. It collapsed because 85 of 127 were marked evergreen (which never ages out by definition) and the store is only eight weeks old (so "recently touched" caught nearly all the rest). Cross-tabulated against `kind`, `horizon` was almost a perfect restatement of it — 40 of 44 `project` memories seasonal, 43 of 43 `reference` evergreen — meaning nobody was making a per-memory judgment about truth decay; the field was being set by type reflex and carried no independent signal. Twelve of the 85 evergreen memories had explicitly time-bound titles ("NOT live until the next prod deploy", "BUILT (2026-08-19)"), filed as permanently true.

**It had already broken a real run.** A plain `get_memory_stumps()` call exceeded the MCP tool-result ceiling: 75,539 characters, ~19,000 tokens, 1,956 lines of pretty-printed JSON. The harness spilled it to a file and told the agent to summarize it in a subagent — and a subagent's only channel home is its final message, so the ids were destroyed and `get_item` became impossible for that entire run. Nothing warned anyone. Of that payload only 16,500 characters were titles, the actual signal; 23,282 were `linked` arrays (40 stumps had none) and ~36,000 were structural JSON, indentation, and raw UUID text.

**The fix, in four parts.**

1. **The always-on set is `pinned` only.** `horizon` no longer appears in the query. Everything unpinned is Tier 2, pulled on demand by `search_items(<name>, type: "memory")` anchored on whatever entity the task names. The per-horizon aging windows (45 days seasonal, 10 episodic) are deleted. Tier 1 is the CLAUDE.md equivalent: standing behavioural rules with no entity to search on, so search can never reach them. Brandon's seven current pinned items are exactly that shape, and they are the calibration reference; the documented ceiling is 15.
2. **`horizon` is consumed at read time, not query time.** A `seasonal` or `episodic` memory untouched for 90 days renders a `STALE` marker. It is never hidden and never deleted: "this was true once" is a memory Brandon explicitly wants to keep.
3. **Every stump renders its date and relative age**, in the index and on `search_items` memory hits. This is the highest-value single change: the store already held `updatedAt` and simply never showed it, so humans and agents compensated by typing dates into titles by hand. A stale claim is now self-evident with no maintenance.
4. **Compact serialization.** One line per stump (`<id> [kind/horizon] (date, age) title`) with a header giving the counts and the recall instruction, replacing pretty JSON. `linked` is dropped from the wire (a third of the payload, absent on a third of stumps); `get_item` pulls relations along with the body. Ids stay full: the default set is a handful of lines, and truncating them would only pay off on the rare `includeAll` browse while forcing `get_item` to resolve ambiguous prefixes.

**Rejected: an always-loaded catalog of every stump title.** The case for it was unknown-unknowns, since search only finds what you know to look for. It lost because any real task names an entity, and entity-anchored search retrieves reliably once the type filter is passed (measured: `search_items("James")` returned 15 hits and zero memories, buried under Douglas Moo commentaries on the Epistle of James; `search_items("James", type: "memory")` returned the four correct memories, well ranked). The genuine gap is entity-less standing rules, and that gap is precisely what `pinned` covers. A catalog would reintroduce the payload problem to solve a case already handled.

**Rejected: a `supersedes` relation.** Date-based fade won instead. Agents write these memories, not Brandon, and a supersedes link needs the writing agent to locate a prior contradicting memory it may never have loaded — that fails often and fails silently. Fade is self-maintaining, with zero write-time burden. The failure costs are lopsided: fade's worst case is an agent reading two dated claims and reasoning about them, which is the intended behaviour, while supersedes' worst case is a wrong link hiding a true memory or a missing link preserving a false one, both invisible.

**Rejected: fixing this in the harness prompts.** An earlier draft proposed telling Brandon's scheduled tasks not to delegate memory retrieval to a subagent. That treated a symptom in the wrong codebase. Fixed in the server it fixes desktop, mobile, CLI, and every scheduled run at once; fixed in one client's prompt it drifts from the rest. Same principle as Brandon's own pinned memory: never route durable behaviour to local files.

**Why CORE.** ADR-183's carve-out makes *additive* MCP surface a solo change, but this changes a response's shape (`get_memory_stumps` now returns text, not JSON) and an existing tool's default result set. Existing callers do not keep working byte-for-byte, so it needs Tyler's ack before it merges. Nothing about the schema changes: `kind`, `horizon`, and `pinned` keep their columns, their meanings, and their data. This is a read-path and description change, and no stored memory is mutated or deleted by it.

**Affects:** `src/lib/memory.ts`, `src/lib/mcp/tools/memory.ts`, `src/lib/mcp/tools/items.ts`, `src/lib/mcp/tools/index.ts`, `src/lib/mcp/guide.ts`, `src/lib/mcp/server.ts`, `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`, `src/components/memory/AiMemoryGuide.tsx`, `src/app/build/memory/page.tsx`, `scripts/verify-memory.mts`, `scripts/verify-mcp.mts`.

## ADR-231: the bucket is private — a share token, not an unguessable id, is what lets an anonymous reader see a file

**Date:** 2026-08-28 · **Status:** accepted, CORE — agreed by Tyler 2026-08-28, discussed with Brandon the same day · **Extends ADR-228, replaces its access model**

**ADR-228 got the addressing right and had to leave the access model where it found it.** Bodies stopped storing the provider's URL and started storing `/files/<id>`, which is the durable fix. But that route had to be public, and the ADR said so plainly: a public share page renders an item body whose images are now `/files/<id>`, and an anonymous viewer has no session. It was not a privacy regression — the provider URLs it replaced were world-readable too — but it did carry the old posture forward: **the attachment's UUID was the credential, and the bytes were readable by anyone who ever saw the URL.** ADR-228 named short-lived presigned GETs as the upgrade path if a privacy tier ever landed, and pointed at ADR-075, which declined one for v1.0.

**What forced it.** Tyler wants to keep documents like a scan of a social security card in Ledgr. Under the old model those bytes sit behind an unguessable-but-permanent URL with no expiry and no revocation, in a system whose bodies get exported, printed, synced between installs, and shared. An address that leaks once leaks forever. Brandon's case is equally real and does not go away: a shared item's images must render for someone with no account. **Both have to be true at the same time**, and the earlier design could only express one of them.
