**The fix is that "public route" and "public bucket" are separable, and only the first is needed.** The R2 bucket is private: `publicUrl()` is gone from `StorageProvider`, replaced by `presignDownload()`, and there is no unsigned URL to any object. `/files/<id>` stays exactly where ADR-228 put it and stays in the public matcher, because the share path takes no session — but "public route" now means Clerk does not *require* a session, not that the handler skips its own check. It grants a read two ways and no others:

1. **the owner**, by Clerk session — the app's entire normal path; or
2. **an anonymous viewer holding `?s=<share token>`**, but only if that token is live and belongs to **this attachment's parent item**.

Then it 302s to a freshly signed GET. It is still a redirect and never a proxy, so bytes still never touch the app server (principle 8). Both failures are a flat **404, never a 403**: a revoked or wrong token must not confirm that an id exists.

**The share render carries the token, so nothing stored changes.** `/share/[token]` rewrites each `/files/<id>` in the body to `/files/<id>?s=<token>` on the way out. The database keeps the plain, token-free address, so this is a render concern and not a second thing that can drift from what is stored. Two properties fall out for free: **revoking a link revokes its images in the same act**, and a token for item A is not a skeleton key for every attachment the owner has.

**Dropping `R2_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` strengthens ADR-228 rather than undoing it.** That ADR's stated win was that changing the public base — r2.dev to a custom domain, or R2 to another provider — becomes an env change with no body rewrite. There is now no public base at all: one less storage detail that can end up copied into stored content. The env drops from five vars to four.

**Rejected: a per-attachment `visibility` column.** The obvious shape, and it loses on its defaults. Defaulting to public keeps Brandon's behaviour untouched but **fails open** — forgetting to mark the SSN scan is exactly the leak being designed against, and the cost of forgetting is unbounded and silent. Defaulting to private fails safe but silently breaks images on already-shared items until each file is marked, which is a per-file chore nobody will remember to do. Deriving access from the share the reader actually holds needs no column, no migration, no default to get wrong, and no UI to maintain.

**Rejected: a public bucket for a "public tier" alongside a private one.** R2 has no useful per-object ACL, so this means two buckets, two key spaces, and a file that must move between them when its sharing changes. Every stored address would then depend on which bucket a file happens to live in, which is precisely the coupling ADR-228 removed.

**Rejected: proxying bytes through the app for private files.** It would have made the owner path a single hop instead of a redirect, but principle 8 exists for a reason and a 2GB meeting recording is the case that proves it. Signing costs one HMAC and no I/O.

**Why CORE.** `publicUrl()` is removed from the provider interface and `/files/<id>` changes who may read it, so this is not additive and does not fit ADR-183's carve-out. **No schema change and no migration**: no column is added and no stored body is rewritten — ADR-228's addresses are already exactly what this needs. The `publicUrl` *field* survives on the API and MCP responses for back-compat and now carries the same stable address as `fileUrl`, so no existing caller breaks. `scripts/verify-storage-r2.mts` gains a standing canary: an **unsigned** GET must be refused, which fails loudly the day someone makes the bucket public again.

## ADR-232: a resource may be relevant to several records; a thing that completes lives in exactly one

**Date:** 2026-08-28 · **Status:** accepted — Brandon proposed the per-type split, agreed by Tyler 2026-08-28 (relayed) · **Refines ADR-138/PJ1's containment model without changing it**

**The complaint.** A note or a meeting can genuinely serve two projects, and Ledgr had no way to say so. Attaching an item to a second project took it out of the first, because the only write path the record cards had was `setHome`, which clears any prior home edge.

**What the investigation found** (`explorations/item-in-two-projects.md`). Most of this already worked. The typed collection cards have been role- and home-agnostic since 2026-07-01 (`record-widgets.ts`, Tyler: "the box should pull anything of that type that is associated with the project"), and the contain route already writes exactly this dual edge in production, for a note jotted on a meeting bubbling up to the meeting's project. PJ1 asserts one home per item and never argues for it, while carving out `home=false` as "surfaced-elsewhere" in the same sentence. So *home is singular by definition* was deliberate; *an item can only be in one project* was a consequence of which write path the UI happened to call.

**The decision: it is a per-type rule, and the rule is derived, not configured.** A type with no completion concept (`statusMode: "none"` — note, event, link) is a RESOURCE: attaching it to a record adds a plain `related` edge and leaves its home alone. A type that completes (task, milestone) rolls up into one record's progress bar and one record's completion sweep, so it lives in exactly one and attaching MOVES it. `mayLiveInManyRecords()` in `src/lib/types.ts` is the whole policy.

Deriving it reproduces the wanted split exactly with nothing to configure: `milestone` moved off `statusMode: "none"` in migration 0051, so it lands on the containment side by itself. The tradeoff is stated where the helper lives: giving a type a Done checkbox in Build narrows it to one record from then on.

**Why the second edge is `related` and not `contains`.** The project-completion sweep scopes on `r.home or r.role in ('project','contains')`. A `contains` edge would therefore put a note that merely VISITS a project inside that project's completion net, and the only thing making that safe today is the sweep's separate rule that types with no completion concept are skipped. Using `related` makes it structurally safe instead of incidentally safe: association is never swept, now or after someone gives the type a Done checkbox. It also matches the model's own language — home is what makes a thing live somewhere, association is what makes it show up.

**The ✕ is the delineation, not just an action.** A row on a card that carries a detach ✕ is a resource visiting this record; a row without one lives here. That is the only visible difference, on purpose (Brandon). It is an always-rendered per-row control, which departs from ADR-142's "row actions live in the RowMenu" standard: the affordance is carrying information, and a menu you have to open cannot tell you anything at a glance. Detaching removes one `related` edge, scoped by role so it cannot touch a home or `contains` edge, and fires the standard undo toast.

**Why NOT core, and what did not change.** `home` stays singular for every type, the partial unique index is untouched, and there is no schema change and no migration. `homeParentOf`, breadcrumbs, Next Action advancement, progress rollups and the completion sweep all keep their current guarantees, because the types that would have forced new answers for them are exactly the types that stay contained. What changed is which edge one write path writes.

**Language: filed under, not inside.** The attach toast deliberately does not say "moved here" (Brandon caught this the day it shipped). "Here" reads as *inside this record*, which implies deleting the record takes its contents with it — and it does not: `softDeleteItem` cascades through `parent_id` only, so a deleted project leaves every task, note and meeting it held untouched. The honest difference between the two cases is how many records a thing can be filed under, so that is what the toast says, and the guide states the non-cascade outright.

**Two things the browser check caught, both now part of the decision.**

*The first record to take an unfiled resource adopts it.* Attaching a note that is filed nowhere writes a home edge rather than a `related` one; only a later attach makes it a visitor. Without this a note attached to two projects was a visitor in both and a resident of nowhere, so the ✕ marked every row and distinguished nothing.

*Re-filing clears the old edge.* `setHome` only DEMOTES a previous home edge (`clearHomeEdges` sets `home = false`), and the typed collection cards are home-agnostic — so re-filing a task under a second project left it rendered on BOTH projects' Tasks cards, and a completing type has no ✕ to get it off the old one. This is a pre-existing consequence of PJ1's demote meeting the 2026-07-01 home-agnostic cards, not new here, but "belongs to one record" is false while it stands. The attach path now deletes the old `project`/`contains` edges (role-scoped, so a deliberate `related` or `tags` edge to the old record survives) before calling `setHome`. `filedUnderRecords()` in `src/lib/relations.ts` is what tells it which. **`setHome` itself is unchanged**, so any other caller that re-files an item still leaves the demoted edge behind; flagged to Tyler as a probable general bug rather than fixed unilaterally.

**Cost.** Collection rows gain a `contained` boolean, resolved by one query per record page (`containedIds`) using the same predicate as the completion sweep — so "no ✕" and "the sweep may touch this" can never drift apart. `scripts/verify-containment.mts` covers the derived policy, that a second attach leaves the home alone, that the second edge is outside the sweep's scope, and that both records' cards still show the item.
## ADR-233: Postgres is started through `pg_ctl`, because the at-boot task runs elevated and Postgres refuses to run as an administrator

**Date:** 2026-08-29
**Status:** accepted — not core (the local supervisor's own lifecycle; no schema, body format, provider interface or API contract moves)

**Context.** Brandon rebooted the PC and Ledgr did not come back, again. The notification-area icon from ADR-229 was present and reported "not running", which is exactly the honesty that ADR built, so this time the outage announced itself. What it announced was new.

Windows started the boot task correctly. Postgres then refused to start, four times, and the peer gave up. Its own words, captured because ADR-229 attached the log files: "Execution of PostgreSQL by a user with administrative permissions is not permitted." This is a deliberate refusal in Postgres, not a crash and not a permissions accident.

**The asymmetry is the whole bug.** Clicking "Start" in the tray worked every time; the boot task failed every time, with the same command. Windows strips administrator rights from *interactive* sign-ins through User Account Control, so anything launched from a signed-in desktop runs with a filtered token. A Task Scheduler action registered with the `--always` scope (ADR-211) runs at system start with nobody signed in, and gets the **unfiltered** token. So the one launch path that has to work unattended was the one path Postgres would always reject. Every reboot ended with Ledgr down until a person clicked Start, and the tray, being accurate, could only report it.

ADR-229 diagnosed the previous reboot failure as a stale `postmaster.pid` and fixed that. The stale pid was real, but it was not the only thing wrong: underneath it sat a start command that could never succeed from a boot.

**Decision.**

1. **`pg_ctl start` replaces spawning `postgres.exe` directly.** `pg_ctl` exists for this: on Windows it builds a restricted token (dropping the administrator privileges Postgres objects to) and launches the server under it. The same command then works elevated and unelevated, so the boot task and the tray button stop disagreeing. Postgres's own output goes to `postgres.log` in the data directory via `-l`, which is also where a failure now explains itself.
2. **`pg_ctl` is spawned, never waited on.** On Windows it does not exit once the server is up: it stays alive as the restricted-token parent holding the job object. Waiting for it to return is waiting forever.
3. **Readiness is a real connection, not a process exit and not a listening port.** The supervisor polls with a `pg` client until the server accepts a connection, against the built-in `postgres` database (`ledgr` is created after). A listening port is not readiness, since Postgres opens it before crash recovery finishes.
4. **The forced-stop fallback goes by `postmaster.pid`.** Starting through `pg_ctl` means there is no child handle to kill, so `pg.stop()` (which kills the process *it* spawned) no longer has anything to act on. The fallback reads the pid file and keeps ADR-229's guards: alive, and provably a postmaster, so a reissued pid cannot get an unrelated process killed. `pg_ctl stop -m fast` remains the ordinary path and is untouched.

**Why / alternatives.** *Register the boot task at sign-in instead* (drop `--always`): one line, and it genuinely avoids the elevation, but the hub then stays down after every reboot until Brandon logs in, which defeats the reason it is a hub. *Run the task as a dedicated unprivileged account*: correct in principle, but it needs a second Windows account created and kept in step for a single-user machine. *Keep spawning `postgres.exe` and drop privileges ourselves*: reimplementing `CreateRestrictedToken` in Node to do what a shipped binary already does, and the exact shape principle 5 exists to refuse.

**Two bugs in this work's own code, both found by running it rather than reading it.** The first version waited on `pg_ctl` with `spawnSync`, which hung the supervisor indefinitely with a perfectly healthy database underneath it: Postgres ready at 12:21:11, supervisor still waiting twenty minutes later, no log line either way. That is what decision 2 above is. The second version then polled `pg_isready` for readiness, which can never succeed here, because the embedded-postgres packages ship the server only (`postgres`, `initdb`, `pg_ctl`) and `pg_isready` is not among them. It reported a healthy cluster as dead until the start timed out. `supervisor/README.md` had already written down which three binaries ship; the fix was to read it. That is decision 3.

**Verification.** Proved on the live rig against the real failure path, not a simulation: the peer was stopped and started with `schtasks /Run /TN "Ledgr Supervisor"`, which is the actual elevated boot task. It shut down an orphaned Postgres left by the previous run, started the cluster, and answered HTTP 200 on :3000 one second later. Postgres's log shows a clean start with no privilege error and no crash recovery. The graceful `pg_ctl stop` path was confirmed separately ("database system is shut down", `clean: true`). Five new checks in `scripts/verify-supervisor.mts` pin each decision, including a negative one that fails if the probe ever depends on a binary again; two existing checks were updated from the mechanism they used to describe. Suite green.

**Affects:** `supervisor/ledgr-supervisor.mjs`, `supervisor/lib.mjs`, `scripts/verify-supervisor.mts`, `runbook.md`.

## ADR-234: a push batch is bounded by bytes as well as by count, because a count cannot bound a payload that carries bodies

**Date:** 2026-08-29
**Status:** accepted — not core (batch sizing inside the existing sync client; the wire shape, the schema, and the guardrail model are all unchanged)

**Context.** Brandon's hub reported 3,332 changes waiting to reach the cloud copy and would not send them. The first-push guardrail (ADR-206) was holding, correctly: the attachment-address migration of ADR-228 had rewritten 1,413 item bodies in one minute on 2026-08-27, and the OneDrive export re-stamped 1,491 items the next morning in response. Both are legitimate work, and 3,332 is well past the 500-change limit that asks the owner first.

Releasing the hold from Build → Network did not fix it. Every exchange then failed with **HTTP 413**, and the queue could not drain at all.

**The bug.** `unpushedOps` capped a push batch at 500 ops and at no size whatsoever. Ordinary edits are a few hundred bytes each, so 500 of them are trivial and this held for the life of the feature. These 500 were whole rewritten item bodies: 4.2 MB measured, against the 4.5 MB request body a Vercel function will accept. The batch was refused, the cursor did not move, and the next round assembled the identical batch and was refused again. Nothing about it was self-correcting, and no amount of owner action could clear it.

This is not specific to one install or one migration. Any change that touches many bodies at once puts any peer into the same permanent stall, Tyler's included.

**Decision.**

1. **Batches are capped by serialized size (3 MB) as well as by count (500).** The budget sits under Vercel's limit with headroom for the request envelope, and is overridable with `LEDGR_SYNC_MAX_PUSH_BYTES` for a hub with a different ceiling.
2. **The size cut never splits a same-`at` run.** One local transaction's ops must travel together, because the hub applies a batch's items deletes as a single statement (ADR-206 addendum 7) — the same invariant the count cap already respected via `RUN_EXTEND_CAP`. `trimBatchToBytes` therefore measures forward and cuts only at a run boundary, rather than popping ops off the end.
3. **A batch is never empty.** A first run over the whole budget still ships alone. Returning nothing would stall the queue permanently, which is the exact failure this ADR exists to end. A single op larger than the hub's limit would still be refused; that needs a wire change to split one row across requests, and is marked in the code as the upgrade path if a body ever exceeds 4.5 MB.
4. **"Drained" now means the push side sent everything pending,** not `ops.length < PUSH_BATCH`. A size-trimmed batch is under the count cap and still has more behind it, so the old test would have reported a backlog as caught up — the silent misreport principle 9 forbids. `ops.length === 0` keeps a pull-only or held peer finishing in one round, unchanged.

**Why / alternatives.** *Raise the hub's body limit*: not ours to raise on Vercel's serverless functions, and a fixed limit of any size is still a limit a body-heavy batch will find. *Lower `PUSH_BATCH` to a smaller count*: trades a stall for a slower drain and still cannot bound a payload, since one op's size is unbounded. *Compress the request*: real, and orthogonal; it moves the ceiling without ever removing the need for one.

**Verification.** Five checks in `scripts/verify-sync-ui.mts` pin each decision: an under-budget batch goes whole, an over-budget batch is cut, a same-`at` run is never split, an over-budget first run still ships, an empty batch stays empty. Typecheck and lint clean.

**Addendum (2026-08-29, same day): the gate is spent by an ACCEPTED push, never an attempted one.** Shipping the byte cap exposed a second bug immediately. Brandon's "Send anyway" had already been consumed: `pushSelectionForHub` commits `firstPushDone` optimistically, before the request goes out, and the stored one-shot is cleared as soon as any hub runtime reports the gate done. So four refused 413 rounds burned the owner's permission without a single op landing, and the hold returned on the next restart with nothing left to release. `exchangeWith` now rolls that commit back and re-applies it only after the hub answers OK. Two checks in `scripts/verify-sync-ui.mts` pin the ordering; the decision itself is pure and already tested, so what needed pinning was where the impure call site commits it.

**Affects:** `src/lib/sync/client.ts`, `scripts/verify-sync-ui.mts`, `runbook.md`.

## ADR-235: an expired delta token is a resync instruction, not a failure to retry

**Date:** 2026-08-29
**Status:** accepted — not core (one provider adapter's recovery behavior; the mail provider interface, the import engine and the stored job state are all unchanged)

**Context.** Email import failed every ten minutes from 2026-08-24 to 2026-08-29 and nothing said so anywhere Brandon looks. It was found only while investigating an unrelated sync stall. Five days of mail addressed to Ledgr simply never arrived.

Microsoft Graph's `messages/delta` hands back a token meaning "tell me what changed since here". Graph expires those, after roughly 30 days or whenever the mailbox's own sync state rolls over, and then answers **HTTP 410** with a body naming the generation it no longer has. A 410 here is not an error in the ordinary sense: it is Graph's documented instruction to start over.

Ledgr treated it as an ordinary failure. `listNewMessages` let the 410 propagate, `runEmailImport` kept the stored token because the run had errored, and the next run ten minutes later asked the identical rejected question. Nothing in that loop could ever converge, and no owner-facing control existed to clear it.

**Decision.** `GraphMailSource.listNewMessages` catches a 410 on the stored token, discards the token, and reads the import folder whole. Exactly one retry: a 410 on the full read is a real failure and is thrown, because retrying that is the endless loop this ADR exists to remove. Any other status (403, 404, 429) still surfaces unchanged, so a permissions problem can never be laundered into a silent, expensive re-read.

**Why a full re-read is safe, and why it always was.** An imported message is *moved* into the Imported subfolder (slice 26). A full read of the import folder therefore returns only what has not been imported yet, and the `internetMessageId` dedup sits behind that as a second line. The recovery this ADR adds was available from the day the feature shipped; nothing but the 410 handler was missing.

**The walk is extracted so the retry starts clean.** A 410 can arrive several pages into a delta stream, with messages already accumulated and their attachments already fetched. `walkDelta` owns one walk and its own accumulator, so the retry cannot inherit a half-finished one and double-report.

**What this does not fix.** A cron that fails every ten minutes for five days is still invisible until somebody reads a log. That is a monitoring gap, not this bug, and it is the more valuable of the two — principle 9 asks for surfaced failures, and a job dying silently for five days is the case it exists to prevent. Left open deliberately rather than bundled in here.

**Verification.** `scripts/verify-email-delta-resync.mts`, ten checks, pure — it drives the real `GraphMailSource` with its two network seams stubbed, so it runs in CI with no mailbox, no credentials and no database. It pins each decision including the two negatives: exactly one retry, and a non-410 failure left alone.

**Affects:** `src/lib/email/graph-source.ts`, `scripts/verify-email-delta-resync.mts`, `runbook.md`.

## ADR-236: files as a first-class citizen — any file in the editor, and a `file` type where the item IS the file

**Date:** 2026-08-29 · **Status:** accepted, not core (module + additive UI on existing machinery; heads-up in `COLLAB.md`) · **Builds on ADR-228/231, sits beside the "turn into markdown" idea (still queued)**

**The ask (Tyler, 2026-08-29).** Three upload modes, each answering a different "why am I uploading this": (1) convert a doc/PDF to markdown and keep the content — already queued separately; (2) attach a file mid-note and get a link where the cursor is; (3) an item that IS the file — Tyler makes standalone HTML pages with Claude constantly and wants to upload one, open it, and hand it to someone as a rendered page via the share function. The serving side needed nothing: uploads never had a MIME allowlist, `/files/<id>` 302s to a presigned GET that serves the stored content-type (so `text/html` renders as a live page, on R2's origin rather than Ledgr's), and ADR-231's `?s=<token>` already grants an anonymous read scoped to the attachment's parent item. What was missing was the front door — the in-app uploader was images-only, and nothing listed an item's attachments anywhere in the UI (the `GET /api/attachments?itemId=` endpoint shipped with zero callers).

**Mode 2 — any file in the editor.** The editor's `uploadImage` prop is now `uploadFile`; paste/drop intercepts any file (not just images), a paperclip **Attach** toolbar button (id `attach`, hideable like the rest) opens an any-file picker, and the slash menu gains **/file**. Images embed exactly as before; any other file inserts as a markdown link on its filename pointing at the stable `/files/<id>` address. The slash entry is registered per editor instance in a `WeakMap` (`setSlashFilePicker`) rather than the module-level flag the toggle command uses, because whether upload works depends on the host's prop (scratch/changelog pass none) and two editors with different hosts can be mounted at once — `enabled` therefore now receives the editor. The presign handshake moved out of `ItemEditor` into the shared `src/components/attachments/upload.ts`, which also finally surfaces ADR-231's `storageWarning` as a toast (the response carried it; the UI dropped it).

**Mode 3 — the `file` type.** A pre-built type (migration `0061` + `seed.mjs` mirror; `is_system=false`, out of quick capture since you can't upload mid-capture) declared by a new `files` module manifest routing to a `file` canvas. `FileCanvas` follows `LongformCanvas`'s shape: the file panel renders through `ItemEditor`'s `fields` slot where the longform byline sits, the body below is the owner's description of the file, and the arrange/custom-layout escape hatch still delegates to `MarkdownCanvas`. The panel (`FilePanel`, shared) lists the item's attachments — filename opens `/files/<id>` in a new tab (**Open in new tab is the v1 decision; inline preview is queued polish**), **Share** copies `origin + /files/<id>?s=<token>` after minting-or-reusing the item's share token, **Remove** hard-deletes via the existing endpoint behind a `ConfirmButton` (attachments were never soft-deleted; the confirm says so). Sharing one file deliberately rides the ITEM's token — for a file item they are the same act, and per-attachment tokens would be a real access-model change nobody has needed yet.

**The Files card.** `FilePanel` also mounts as a record tool: a `files` entry in `WIDGET_CATALOG` (kind `derived` — the one card backed by the attachments table rather than items), resolved in `record-widgets.ts` by `listAttachments`, rendered by the same component so card and canvas can't drift, offered on projects (`PROJECT_SECTIONS`) and every project-style page via Add a Tool. **Known limit, stated rather than hidden:** record cards exist only on widget-home pages, so "add files to this type" reaches projects/pursuits/any Project-style type — a longform note gets its files inline via /file instead. If a Files panel on longform canvases turns out to be wanted, that is its own slice.

**Not core, and why.** No schema change beyond an additive type row (the seeded-type recipe migrations 0031/0037/0044 already use), no body-dialect change (a file link is an ordinary markdown link), no provider or MCP contract change, and the module registers onto the existing boundary exactly as songs/papers/mindmap do. The one judgment call worth recording: shipping a pre-built type lands on Brandon's instance too, so this ADR + the `COLLAB.md` note are the heads-up; the type is `is_system=false` precisely so either owner can hide or retire it.

## ADR-237: deleting a reference is not deleting the file — purge deletes bytes, and Data Hygiene sweeps orphans

**Date:** 2026-08-29 · **Status:** accepted; **CORE TOUCH flagged: `StorageProvider` gains `listObjects(prefix)` — additive, but the provider interfaces are on the core list, so Brandon's ack is owed before this merges** (heads-up in `COLLAB.md`) · **Extends ADR-236; pays the debt noted in `item-mutations.ts` since before storage landed**

**What forced it (Tyler, 2026-08-29, first day of real file use):** "How do I delete a file? If I delete it from the note, does that delete it from my R2?" The honest answers were bad. Removing an inline link deletes only the reference; the bytes stay and keep counting against the quota — correct behavior, but nothing explained it and a NOTE has no surface listing its attachments. Worse, **purging an item cascaded its attachment rows and left the bytes in R2 forever**: the quota sum (which reads the rows) dropped while the bucket kept the bytes, so Ledgr's arithmetic and the real bucket drifted apart silently, invisibly, and unboundedly.

**Three moves:**
1. **The purge deletes bytes.** `purgeExpiredTrash` collects the doomed attachments' storage keys before the items delete and removes each object best-effort — a failed delete leaves an orphan for the sweep, never a blocked purge — and reports `purgedFiles`/`orphanedFiles`. Peers replicating a purge through sync deliberately do not repeat the byte deletes: two installs can share one bucket, and the origin deletes exactly once.
2. **`StorageProvider.listObjects(prefix)`** — the one new primitive, S3 ListObjectsV2 under the hood, paginated, regex-parsed (Principle 5; the only user-influenced text in the XML is the key, which is entity-decoded). This is the core touch: additive, no existing method changes shape, but the interface is on the core list so it is flagged rather than slipped through.
3. **Data Hygiene grows its first real tool.** `/build/hygiene` (a stub since ADR-063) now carries the **orphaned-files sweep**: Scan lists every object under the owner's prefix with no attachment row behind it, with filenames and sizes; Delete-all (ConfirmButton) reclaims them and toasts what it freed. Safe by construction: `reserveAttachment` inserts the row BEFORE any bytes exist, so "no row" can never describe an in-flight upload, and the DELETE endpoint re-scans server-side rather than trusting the list the owner was shown. The ADR-063 plan text stays on the page for the tools not yet built.

**Also in the same batch (small, Tyler's same-session feedback):** the share page footer names whose Ledgr it came from (Settings display name, escaped, possessive-aware; falls back to plain "Ledgr"); share-link rows carry an explicit "view" beside copy/revoke; `.ledgr-prose a` gets `cursor: pointer` (anchors inside contenteditable inherit the text cursor, which reads as not-clickable); FilePanel's actions are always visible instead of hover-revealed (hover hid Delete from the first real user, and touch never sees hover) and "Remove" is renamed "Delete"; the upload progress stack lingers 1.5s so a small file's bar registers instead of flickering.

**The precondition the sweep stands on: one bucket per database.** Checking the real deployments before shipping found two live violations. Tyler's dev and prod databases carry the SAME owner id and shared one bucket — a scan from the preview would have listed his production files as orphans and Delete-all would have destroyed them. Fixed structurally: a second bucket (`ledgr-dev`, same S3 credentials, `R2_BUCKET` differs per environment), so bucket↔database is 1:1 on both sides; proven live end-to-end (seeded orphan found and reclaimed, a real attachment spared, re-scan clean). Brandon's cloud+local pair is the second violation — one bucket, two databases, and `attachments` is NOT in `SYNCED_TABLES`, so each database only knows its own uploads (which also means a body synced to the peer can 404 its own attachments there — a pre-existing gap this surfaced). Until attachment rows join sync, `assertBucketIsOurs()` makes the sweep REFUSE on any syncing install, hub (live `sync_peers`) or spoke (`LEDGR_SYNC_HUBS` set), with a message that says why. **Proposed follow-up, core (both-agree): add `attachments` to `SYNCED_TABLES`** — it fixes the peer 404s and lifts the guard; flagged in `COLLAB.md`.

**Rejected: reference-counting deletes (removing the last body link deletes the file).** Bodies are markdown text; counting references means parsing every body on every save and being wrong about copies, revisions, and exports. The model stays: rows own bytes, deleting the row (file panel Delete, item purge) deletes the bytes, and the sweep reconciles what slips through.

**ADR-237 addendum (same day, Tyler's testing):** three additions from first real use. (1) **All files** joins Data Hygiene as tool #2: every attachment with size, parent-item link, and a "not linked" chip when nothing in the item's body or properties points at it anymore — because "I backspaced the link, did the file delete?" had no visible answer (it doesn't delete; the row stays, and now there is a place that shows it). (2) **A link can be one of your files** (Tyler: "we need both" — this AND the File type): the URL field in `FieldStrip` accepts a dropped file or the paperclip beside it, uploading and writing the stable `/files/<id>` address into `items.url`; everything downstream (Links card, byline chip, share rewrite) works untouched. `LongformCanvas` also stops hiding the URL field on a URL-less item — it had filtered it unconditionally, leaving a fresh link's page with no way to set a URL at all. (3) The upload progress stack moved from the bottom-right corner to bottom-center above the toast; the corner read as invisible.

**ADR-237 addendum 2 (same day, Tyler's second round):** the file surfaces settle into their homes. (1) **Build → Files** — the all-files browser moves out of Data Hygiene onto its own DATA page (`/build/files`, sidebar entry after Bespoke Tools): files are content the owner browses, not a mess to clean; hygiene keeps the orphan sweep. (2) **Every item shows its own files**: `ItemUtilitiesFooter` gains a Files section above Export & sharing, rendered ONLY when the item has files — each row with Open, **Copy link** (a markdown link to paste back into the body), Share, Delete, and the "not linked" chip. This is the direct answer to "I backspaced the link" — the file is right there on the item, restorable or deletable; the file canvas opts out (its panel already leads). (3) **Recover on the orphan sweep**: alongside Delete-all, Recover-all turns each orphan back into a reachable thing — one note per file, titled after it, body linking it, the attachment row recreated under the uuid embedded in the storage key so the object's original `/files/<id>` address is live again. Proven end-to-end on the rig (seeded orphan → recovered note → bytes served → no longer an orphan). (4) The upload progress stack lands top-center (third placement: corner was invisible, bottom collides with the mobile keyboard).

## ADR-238: the web clipper carries no credential — the relay popup is already signed in

**Date:** 2026-08-30 · **Status:** accepted · **Core:** yes (it changes how an existing endpoint authenticates)

Setting the clipper up meant getting a token: mint one signed with `LEDGR_CLIPPER_SECRET` (which needs that env var set on the host, and a redeploy to rotate), or paste an `api`-scoped token into a box. ADR-224 then replaced single-string tokens with two-part credentials (`lgrk_…:lgrs_…`), and the paste box takes one string — so the documented way to set up a clipper produced a bookmarklet that 401s. That is what prompted this, but the token was never carrying its weight: it made the bookmark a secret, made "drag this to your bookmarks bar" a three-step errand, and put the owner's on-switch in an env var, which CLAUDE.md's "the config file is never the end user's lever" already forbids.

**The token was redundant the moment the relay popup existed.** ADR-160's follow-up routed the save through `/capture/relay`, a page on Ledgr's own origin, to dodge CSP `connect-src` on sites like YouTube. That page carries the owner's session cookie. So the credential the clipper needed was already in the browser.

**What changes.** `/api/machine/capture` accepts a second door: no machine token, but a signed-in owner (`resolveOwner()`), and it saves as them. The bookmarklet drops the token from its payload; the relay drops the `Authorization` header. The bookmarklet is now one static URL, identical for every user of an instance — drag it, and if the first click finds you signed out, the popup lands on `/sign-in` (it is already Clerk-protected), you sign in once, and it saves from then on.

**Why the open CORS is still safe.** The route answers `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, which a cookie-authenticated route normally must not. Two things hold. The session cookie is `SameSite=Lax`, so it is never sent on a cross-site POST; and the route sets no `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`, so a browser refuses to attach credentials to a cross-origin fetch here regardless. The relay's own POST is same-origin, so it is unaffected by both. The verify script asserts the Allow-Credentials header stays absent, because adding it is the one edit that would turn this into a real CSRF hole.

**The handshake had to become repeatable.** The bookmarklet used to remove its `message` listener after the first reply. When the popup detours through sign-in, the relay that finally announces itself is a *second* page load, and a one-shot listener is gone by then. It now answers every `ledgr-relay-ready` ping for the life of the host page, which is what makes the sign-in-once flow work rather than silently doing nothing.

**Accepted, not mitigated: any site can spam your Inbox.** A page could `window.open('/capture/relay')` and postMessage a URL of its choosing. It needs a user gesture to beat the popup blocker, it can only create a link item, and soft-delete plus the undo toast reverse it. A confirm button in the popup would close it and was declined deliberately (Brandon, 2026-08-30): a click on every clip is a real cost paid every day against a hypothetical paid never.

**Back-compat.** `verifyApiToken` still accepts clipper tokens and every other machine credential, and the token path resolves its owner from env exactly as before, so a bookmarklet dragged before this change keeps working and `LEDGR_CLIPPER_SECRET` remains its kill switch. Only the minter is gone — a server action is a public entry point, and one that issues credentials nothing asks for is a door onto an empty room. A token that verifies but names no owner still returns 503, distinct from an anonymous 401.

**Rejected: a Launchpad-style authorize popup (ADR-224 / `/connect/launchpad`).** That shape is right for an app that must hold a durable credential of its own. A bookmarklet does not: it only ever runs in a browser that can just be signed in.

Check: `npx tsx scripts/verify-clipper-tokenless.mts` (new, 14 pure checks).

## ADR-239: a hub that keeps failing is retried more slowly, not every ten seconds

**Date:** 2026-08-30
**Status:** accepted — not core (the peer's own retry schedule; the machine sync contract, the stored hub shape and every response are unchanged)

**Context.** Brandon noticed the production Neon database was never idle and asked why, given his hub is set to check hourly. The hourly setting was being honored on the happy path. A FAILURE was not: `nextDueAfter` rescheduled a failed exchange at a flat `retryMs` (10 seconds), with no backoff and no ceiling, forever.

On 2026-08-30 between 08:20:54 and 08:44:51 UTC this rig failed 120 times in a row, once every twelve seconds, on one change the hub could never accept. A permanently broken hub costs about 8,600 requests a day at that rate. On a serverless hub each of those wakes a database that bills for the minutes it stays awake, so one stuck change is enough to hold the whole thing open around the clock.

**Decision.** Repeated failure doubles the wait, starting from the existing first-retry gap, capped at `MAX_RETRY_BACKOFF_MS` (15 minutes) and never longer than the hub's own cadence when that is longer. The FIRST retry keeps the old timing exactly, so an ordinary network blip still recovers at once; only a persistent failure slows down. A success clears the counter.

**The clamp had to learn about it.** `clampNextDue` exists so a cadence the owner changed takes effect within one interval, and it did that by capping the next-due time at `now + cadenceMs`. A continuous hub's cadence is ten seconds, so it would have dragged every backed-off retry straight back down and the backoff would never have happened at all. It now takes a `floorMs` the caller sets from the current backoff.

**Why not fix only the poison pill.** ADR-241 does that, and it is the better fix for the case we actually hit. This one is the guardrail underneath it: any persistent failure, including one nobody has thought of yet, must not become a hammer. Two independent causes had to line up to produce the outage, and removing either one alone is not enough.

**What this does not fix.** The failing exchange still happens; it just costs a handful of requests an hour instead of thousands a day. And it cannot help a peer that is not running this code, which is exactly the case the same investigation turned up: a second install (`bcdesktop`) on a build from before 2026-08-25 has been failing the schema version gate and re-asking every 12.06 seconds since, roughly 50,000 requests. It gets the backoff only by updating, which also removes the reason it was failing. The backoff is the guardrail for the next stuck peer, not the cure for that one.

**Verification.** Nine checks in `scripts/verify-sync-ui.mts`: the first retry is unchanged, the second doubles, the fourth is eight times, the cap holds, an hourly hub never backs off past its own cadence, a success clears it, and the clamp both honors a retry floor and still pulls back a stale cadence when nothing is failing.

**Affects:** `src/lib/sync/client.ts`, `scripts/verify-sync-ui.mts`.

## ADR-240: "only when there are changes" makes the cadence an idle heartbeat

**Date:** 2026-08-30
**Status:** accepted — not core (additive per-hub setting; the stored hub shape gains an optional boolean, every existing entry reads as off, and the machine sync contract is untouched)

**Context.** Brandon asked for a sync option where changes flow continuously but the copies do not talk at all when there is nothing to say. The reason is cost, not tidiness: an empty exchange on a serverless hub costs exactly what a useful one costs, because it wakes the database either way. The existing ladder could not express it. Continuous meant about 8,600 exchanges a day whether or not anything had changed; hourly meant an edit could sit for an hour.

**Decision.** A per-hub checkbox, **Only on changes**, off by default. When it is on the cadence stops being the schedule and becomes the **idle heartbeat**: this peer's own unsent changes bring the exchange forward immediately, and a quiet hub is contacted once per cadence and no more. The owner's existing ladder therefore sets the floor, which is why no new cadence value was added.

**Why a boolean and not a new cadence preset.** A preset would have needed its own interval, its own label, its own entry in the retention-gap refusal, and a second concept to explain. The boolean composes with every rung already on the ladder: "hourly, only on changes" and "daily, only on changes" both mean something obvious, and the retention guardrail keeps working unchanged because the worst case is still the cadence.

**The rule is pure and the signal is local.** `onChangeDue` decides it with no database and no network. The caller answers "do we have anything to send" by comparing the hub's stored push cursor to the local oplog head, which is one local read. Nothing goes over the wire to discover there was nothing to send, which would have defeated the point.

**A failing hub is never woken early.** This is the clause that keeps ADR-240 from re-creating the ADR-239 hammer. A change the hub cannot accept is pending forever, so "we have changes waiting" would otherwise fire on every tick. When a hub is failing the backoff wins and this rule stands down.

**What this does not do.** It cannot make INBOUND changes instant, because a peer cannot learn the hub has news without asking. The cadence is that floor. Making it truly zero-poll needs the hub to call the peer, which is a new direction in the machine API and therefore core: agreed with Brandon as the follow-up, to be opened as its own ADR with Tyler.

**Verification.** Ten checks in `scripts/verify-sync-ui.mts` covering the reader's tolerance, the four ways the rule says no, the debounce boundary, and the failing-hub clause.

**Affects:** `src/lib/sync/client.ts`, `src/app/api/sync/hubs/route.ts`, `src/components/network/HubActions.tsx`, `src/app/build/network/page.tsx`, `scripts/verify-sync-ui.mts`, `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`.

## ADR-241: a change the hub cannot apply is parked, not re-sent forever

**Date:** 2026-08-30
**Status:** accepted — not core (hub-side apply behavior plus one additive response field; no caller has to change and every existing one keeps working)

**Context.** The failure behind ADR-239 was a single change that could never succeed: "delete the `day_log` type", which rows on the hub still referenced. On the neon-http driver there is no session and therefore no transaction, so `applySyncOps` ran the batch action by action. The failing action threw, the whole exchange returned HTTP 500, the peer's push cursor never advanced, and the identical batch went back out on the next retry. Every retry also re-applied the actions that came before the failure.

**Decision.** On the non-transactional path each action runs in its own try/catch. A failure is **parked**: recorded with its kind, table, row id and reason, skipped, and the rest of the batch continues. The hub logs the parked set, captures it as an error so it reaches the errors surface and the weekly health check, and returns it in the response. The peer counts it, logs it, and carries it on the exchange result.

**Why parking beats retrying.** Retrying forever is not conservative, it is only louder: the change never lands, and the peer is also prevented from making progress on everything behind it. Parking makes exactly one thing true that was not true before, which is that somebody finds out. A parked change is a change that hub will never have, and that must be visible rather than inferred from a log full of 500s.

**The transactional path stays all-or-nothing.** A failed statement has already poisoned the surrounding transaction, so nothing after it can run, and per-action parking there needs a SAVEPOINT per action. Marked with a `ponytail:` comment naming the ceiling. The hub that hit this is the cloud one, which takes the branch that is fixed.

**What is still open.** The peer counts parked changes but the Network page does not yet show them; today they surface through the hub's own errors list and the weekly health check. That surface is queued in `next_steps.md` rather than bundled here.

**Affects:** `src/lib/sync/apply.ts`, `src/app/api/machine/sync/route.ts`, `src/lib/sync/client.ts`.

## ADR-242: saved YouTube videos transcribe themselves, as a scheduled job rather than a second service

**Date:** 2026-08-30
**Status:** accepted — not core (an additive machine endpoint, one owner setting, one job-table entry; every existing caller keeps working byte for byte, ADR-183 carve-out)

**Context.** `explorations/hub-runner-triggers.md` slice 1 wanted one button on a YouTube video to end with a `link` item holding the video and its full transcript, free and with no model in the loop. The doc's design was a separate long-lived runner service on the hub PC: its own repo, an HTTP queue behind a new Tailscale Funnel path, a shared bearer secret, a worker loop, and a heartbeat into Ledgr. That doc was written on 2026-08-29, against a Ledgr that did not yet have the supervisor.

**Decision.** Build it as an ordinary scheduled job inside Ledgr. The supervisor already fires `GET /api/machine/<job>` on a timer with its own minted cron token (ADR-214), job ownership already stops every other copy running the same job (ADR-225), and a failing run already lands in `error_log` and on `/health`. So the runner, the queue, the public path, the secret, and the heartbeat were all deleted from the design, and what remains is the part that actually pulls a transcript: `GET /api/machine/youtube-transcript` every ten minutes, `src/lib/youtube/{fetch,transcripts}.ts`, and `scripts/whisper-transcribe.py`.

**No new state, on purpose.** "Needs a transcript" is not a queue, a flag, or a column. It is a saved link whose address is YouTube's and whose body carries no `<!-- transcript:` marker. That is why a month of videos saved where the job cannot run costs nothing: the first run on a capable copy picks all of them up, oldest first, and there is nothing to drain or expire. The marker is an HTML comment, already legal in the body dialect, so it travels with the text to every copy. A video that cannot be transcribed gets its own marker plus one visible `> Transcript unavailable: reason` line, which is what stops a private video being retried every ten minutes forever; deleting that line asks again.

**Two switches, not one.** Whether the owner wants the feature is `settings.youtubeTranscripts.enabled`, which syncs with them and is off by default (ADR-222 posture: the job is scheduled unconditionally and the endpoint asks the setting, so turning it on is a checkbox with no restart). Which machine does the work is the existing per-job "Runs on" dropdown. Merging them would mean either every copy trying, or the feature being invisible on the machine where you would look for it.

**Instant, with one guard.** The kick lives in `createItem`, the one function every save path already goes through (phone share sheet, bookmarklet, quick capture, MCP), so no capture route carries a copy and a path added later inherits it. It is fire-and-forget, so the phone's reply never waits on Whisper. Because Whisper wants the whole graphics card, runs are single-flight per process: a second call leaves a note and returns, and the run in flight does another pass before releasing. Passes continue until the waiting list is empty or a twenty-minute budget is spent, inside the job's thirty-minute ceiling.

**Captions first, and both facts were measured rather than assumed.** yt-dlp is asked for the creator's English track and only then for the automatic one, as two calls: asked for both at once it downloads both and nothing in the filename says which is which. `--sub-langs` is exactly `en`, never `en.*`, because the wildcard matches YouTube's auto-translated tracks and fetching them one at a time earns an HTTP 429. Success is judged by whether a `.vtt` file exists, not by exit code or empty stderr, because yt-dlp currently warns on every call and still returns the file.

**Why this cannot live on Vercel, which is the whole reason it is local.** YouTube refuses data-center addresses, so the cheap captions path is blocked from the cloud too, not just Whisper, and a cloud function stops long before a Whisper run finishes. The endpoint therefore answers "yt-dlp is not installed on this copy" as a clean 200 skip rather than an error, because a cloud copy will say that on every single run forever and a red mark every ten minutes is the no-silent-failures rule inverted into noise.

**No new dependency, no schema change, no migration** (Principles 5 and the working conventions). yt-dlp and faster-whisper are Python programs shelled out to, because yt-dlp is what actually keeps up with YouTube's changes and wrapping it in an npm package would mean trusting a second maintainer to keep up with the first. **No ffmpeg either:** the audio is taken exactly as YouTube serves it and Whisper decodes it, which removes what would otherwise be a hard install requirement.

**Why / alternatives.** *The doc's separate runner service* — rejected, it rebuilds four things the supervisor already does, and adds a public path and a shared secret to the internet for no gain. *Poll only, no instant* — rejected by Brandon: instant is nearly free once the guard sits in `createItem`. *Whisper deferred to a later slice* — rejected by Brandon, so it ships here. *Reusing the personal `transcribe_media.py` from the skills folder* — rejected: Ledgr must not reach outside the repo, and Tyler's copy has no such file, so a trimmed copy lives in `scripts/`. *A transcript service called from the cloud* — declined, it costs money for what the machine on the desk does free. *Timestamps in the output* — dropped, plain paragraphs read and search better and nothing yet jumps to a moment in a video.

**Affects:** new `src/lib/youtube/fetch.ts`, `src/lib/youtube/transcripts.ts`, `src/app/api/machine/youtube-transcript/route.ts`, `scripts/whisper-transcribe.py`, `scripts/verify-youtube-transcripts.mts`, `src/components/updates/YoutubeTranscripts.tsx`; edited `src/lib/settings.ts`, `src/lib/item-mutations.ts`, `src/lib/job-owners.ts`, `supervisor/lib.mjs`, `src/app/build/updates/page.tsx`, `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`, `scripts/verify-job-owners.mts`, `scripts/verify-supervisor.mts`.

**Verification:** `verify-youtube-transcripts` 35/35 (pure: the real auto-caption format with its rolling duplicates and inline timing tags, the address matcher, and the marker round trip that stops infinite retries), `verify-job-owners` 27/27, `verify-supervisor` all pass, typecheck and lint clean. Live on the hub PC: captions off a real video in 2.6 seconds as clean prose, a dead video returning "the video is private or removed" in seconds without wasting a Whisper run, and the pending-videos query answering 87 against the real production database while correctly rejecting a saved page that merely mentions YouTube in its title. **Brandon-step to light it up:** `py -m pip install -U yt-dlp` on the machine that will do the work, then the checkbox at `/build/updates`.

## ADR-243: a status is whatever the type says it is, on write as well as on read

**Date:** 2026-08-31
**Status:** accepted. The loosening was solo under the ADR-183 carve-out; the one tightening half touches the machine/MCP API contract, so it went to Tyler, who **acked it 2026-08-31** (relayed via Brandon). See "The core question" below for exactly what he was agreeing to.

**Context.** ADR-082 made statuses user-defined per type: `items.status` is plain text holding a stage key, and `items.status_category` holds the fixed bucket the plumbing reasons about. `ITEM_STATUSES` (`open`/`done`/`archived`) survived as nothing more than the keys of the *inherited default* set, and `src/lib/item-enums.ts` says so in a comment. Three call sites never got the memo and kept treating that list as the closed set of legal statuses: `status` on `create_item`, `update_item` and `list_items` was declared `enum: [...ITEM_STATUSES]`, and the `status` list filter on both `/api/items` and `/api/machine/items` returned 400 for anything else.

The result was a capability that read as a missing feature. An assistant could not put a goal on Active or a project on Waiting for Others, so every goal it created landed on Someday and the owner had to finish the job by hand in the UI. Worse, it was invisible: the fix people reached for was to design *around* it, adding checkbox properties to stand in for stages that already existed. Brandon named the symptom directly, and it is the second time this shape of bug has cost real design decisions.

Underneath the enum sat a quieter hazard. Nothing below the API layer validated a status at all, so a caller that did send an unrecognised key got it stored: `categoryOfStatus` falls back to `not_started` for an unknown key, so the row came out with a status that renders as nothing on the canvas and silently buckets as not-started. The enum was the only thing standing between a typo and a corrupted row, and it was standing in the wrong place.

**Decision.** Statuses are resolved and validated once, in the write path every caller already goes through, and the enums come off.

1. `resolveStatusKey(schema, input)` in `src/lib/status.ts` is a new pure resolver: it matches a stage by key, or by **label**, in any case. A model reading `list_types` will send "Waiting for Others" as readily as `waiting`, and no caller should have to know which of the two Ledgr stores.
2. `requireStatusKey` in `src/lib/item-mutations.ts` wraps it for writes: resolve, or throw `bad_request` naming the type's real stages so the caller can retry without a second round trip. It sits in `createItem` and `updateItem`, which is the single chokepoint every writer routes through: canvas, board drag, REST, machine API, MCP. One guard, not five.
3. The three `enum: [...ITEM_STATUSES]` declarations on the MCP tools are gone, replaced by descriptions that say a stage key or label is accepted and point at `list_types`. The two REST list filters now shape-check a slug instead of gating on the default set.

**Forgiving on read, strict on write.** `categoryOfStatus`'s fallback to `not_started` is left exactly as it was, and its comment explains why: a stage dropped from the schema while rows still hold it should read as active rather than vanish. That is the right answer for a read. It is the wrong answer for a write, where the key was never real in the first place. Splitting the two is the whole point of putting the guard in the mutation rather than in the resolver.

**The core question, stated plainly.** ADR-183 makes a more capable API a solo change and keeps "tightening validation on an existing call" core. This change is mostly the former: accepting stage keys and labels is pure loosening, and every request that was valid before is still valid, byte for byte, on any type that inherits the default stages. There is one exception. On a type with *custom* stages, `status: "open"` used to be accepted by the enum and written as silent garbage; it is now refused by name. That is a behaviour change to an existing argument, so it belongs in front of Tyler even though what it removes is a data-corruption path rather than a capability. Flagging it rather than quietly shipping it is the point of the gate.

**What was deliberately not built.** *Validating custom property VALUES against their kind* (a `multi_select` given a bare string, a `select` given an undeclared option) is the same shape of bug one layer over, and it is real: property values are stored as untyped JSON and nothing checks them. It is not this change, and it is a genuine tightening with no loosening to justify it, so it stays a separate question. *Surgical per-field editing of `propertySchema`* was scoped and then dropped: `update_type` really does replace the property list wholesale and really does wipe it when the field is omitted, but that is a documented footgun rather than a missing capability, and it was not what the reported bug was about. Both are queued in `next_steps.md`. *Re-validating status when `move_item_type` changes an item's type* is a pre-existing gap this change neither causes nor fixes, and it is flagged separately.

**Why / alternatives.** *Widen `ITEM_STATUSES` to include every custom key* — impossible, the set is per type and the enum is static. *Validate in the MCP layer only* — rejected, it leaves the machine REST API and any future caller free to corrupt rows, and it is a bigger diff than the shared guard. *Loosen the enums and skip validation* — rejected, that trades a visible failure for a silent one, which is the worse of the two. *Accept keys only, not labels* — rejected, a model reads labels off `list_types` and will send them; refusing a name the owner would recognise is a round trip for nothing.

**Affects:** `src/lib/status.ts`, `src/lib/item-mutations.ts`, `src/lib/mcp/tools/items.ts`, `src/app/api/items/route.ts`, `src/app/api/machine/items/route.ts`, `src/lib/mcp/guide.ts`, `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`; new `scripts/verify-status-write.mts`.

**Verification:** new `verify-status-write` 25/25 against the dev branch, covering the pure resolver (key, case, label, no-match), a probe type with custom stages set by key and by label with the right category written, a stage the type lacks refused with its real stages named and the row left untouched, and the regression that matters most: types inheriting the default set still take `open`/`done`/`archived`, task checkbox completion still works, and a stage borrowed from another type is refused. Existing suites re-run green: `verify-statuses`, `verify-items`, `verify-mcp`, `verify-mcp-tasks`, `verify-recurrence`, `verify-project-done`, `verify-types`, `verify-today-inbox`, `verify-focus`, `verify-subtasks`, `verify-user-guide`. Typecheck and lint clean.

## ADR-244: the transcript job starts the work and answers, instead of holding the request open

**Date:** 2026-08-31
**Status:** accepted — not core (a correction inside ADR-242's own job; no contract, schema, or caller changes)

**Context.** ADR-242's endpoint awaited the whole drain and the supervisor's job entry carried a thirty-minute ceiling to allow for it. On the very first real run, on the hub PC, the scheduler recorded `fetch failed` after **306 seconds** and captured it as an error. The work had not failed: it had already transcribed one video from captions and went on to resolve seven more after the connection died. What ended the run was Node's own `server.requestTimeout`, **300 seconds by default**, which destroys a connection whose request has been open that long. The thirty-minute ceiling was therefore unreachable, and its only effect was to make the scheduler wait five minutes to be told a lie.

**And what made it slow enough to hit that, at all, was a second bug (fixed here too).** One of the saved links was a YouTube **channel page**, not a video. Handed a channel, yt-dlp does not decline: it begins enumerating everything the channel has ever posted. It burned the full caption timeout, then burned it again on the automatic-captions retry, ten minutes on one item, and wrote "took too long to fetch" into a link that was never transcribable in the first place. So a candidate now needs a real video id (`youtu.be/ID`, `/watch?v=ID`, `/shorts/`, `/live/`, `/embed/`); channel pages, playlists, search results and bare `youtube.com` are not videos and never enter the list. `isYoutubeUrl` is renamed `isYoutubeVideoUrl`, because a function that answers "is this YouTube" and returns false for a real channel URL is a name that will mislead somebody later. The caption timeout also drops from five minutes to ninety seconds: a caption track arrives in seconds, so five minutes never meant "nearly there".

**Decision.** The endpoint passes `detach`, so `runYoutubeTranscripts` returns as soon as its fast checks pass (switch on, not already running, yt-dlp present) and the passes continue behind it. The response becomes `{ok: true, started: true}`. The instant kick in `createItem` detaches for the same reason: the save that triggers it is an HTTP request too. The supervisor entry's custom `timeoutMs` is deleted; the default 120s is generous for a call that returns in under a second.

**Nothing is lost by not waiting.** The single-flight guard, not the request, is what prevents two runs overlapping. The loop logs its own totals. A failure still goes through `captureError` into `error_log`, where every other job's failures already surface, so Principle 9 holds. What the scheduler's cron state now records is "the run was started", which is the truth it is actually in a position to know.

**Why not the alternatives.** *Raise the server's request timeout* — rejected: it needs a custom server, it fights the platform instead of the design, and no ceiling is high enough for an arbitrary video. *Shrink each run to fit inside five minutes* — rejected: a single long video with no captions can exceed five minutes on its own, so the failure would come back on that one item no matter how small the batch. *Leave it and accept the noise* — rejected: a false failure every ten minutes is the no-silent-failures rule inverted into noise, exactly what ADR-242 avoided for the cloud copy's clean skip.

**The general lesson, worth remembering beyond this job:** a scheduled endpoint that does real work must not do it inside the request. Every other exclusive job in Ledgr finishes in seconds, which is why this ceiling had never been met before.

**Considered and rejected: expiring the single-flight claim.** Mid-diagnosis it looked as though the destroyed request had killed the run without releasing its flag, which would leave the feature dead until an app restart, so a liveness stamp was written. Then the evidence said otherwise: the run kept going for twenty more minutes and resolved seven more videos after its connection was gone. The guard was removed rather than kept. It defended against nothing observed, and it introduced a path where two runs could overlap. If a hang ever does strand the flag, the fix is a claim row in `job_state`, not a timer.

**Affects:** `src/lib/youtube/transcripts.ts` (the `detach` option, the passes split into `drain`, and `isYoutubeUrl` → `isYoutubeVideoUrl` now requiring a video id), `src/lib/youtube/fetch.ts` (caption timeout), `src/app/api/machine/youtube-transcript/route.ts`, `src/lib/item-mutations.ts`, `supervisor/lib.mjs`, `scripts/verify-youtube-transcripts.mts`.

**Verification:** typecheck and lint clean; `verify-youtube-transcripts` **47/47** (twelve new address checks, including every channel, playlist, and search-page form that must not be treated as a video) and `verify-supervisor` all pass. The production evidence for the diagnosis: `"job":"youtube-transcript","ms":306930,"detail":"fetch failed"` in the supervisor log, and in the database eight items resolved (six transcripts, one genuinely private video, one channel page reporting "took too long to fetch") with the waiting count down from 90 to 82. No unit test covers the held-open connection, deliberately: it is a platform timeout no pure check can reach.

**Still unproven in production:** the Whisper path. Every transcript so far came from captions, and the one video that reached the fallback was the channel page, which failed before Whisper was ever invoked.

## ADR-245: "flaky" was the network, not the app. Measure the hub from outside, and stop the laptop competing with itself

**Date:** 2026-09-02
**Status:** accepted (not core: a monitoring workflow, a supervisor process-priority nicety, and one `pg_dump` flag; no schema, contract, or provider-interface change)
**⚠️ Its cause ranking is SUPERSEDED BY ADR-246, written hours later the same day.** Everything measured below is accurate and the changes all stand, but the biggest cause was not in this list: the hourly snapshot ran `pg_dump` synchronously inside the single-process app, freezing the entire server for 132 to 160 seconds every hour. Read ADR-246 before chasing the Funnel or Wi-Fi on a report of Ledgr being unreachable. Left unedited otherwise, because what it got wrong is instructive: every measurement here was real, and a set of real measurements still added up to the wrong ranking.

**Context.** Two complaints had been running for weeks with no evidence behind either: Ledgr took a long time to load from other devices, and AI clients reaching the MCP endpoint would intermittently fail, which one of them described as "flaky." Neither had a timestamp, a duration, or a reproduction. The suspicion in the room was that the hub PC was falling asleep or needed waking.

**What the measurements actually said.** The app was never the problem. Probed from outside, `/health` on the hub answered 200 every time, and locally in about 30ms. Nothing in seven days of Windows power events supports a sleeping machine: sleep-on-AC is off, and the one recorded sleep was a single night. The three real causes, in order of size:

1. **The Funnel round trip, which is per-request and unavoidable.** A new connection costs ~0.5s (TLS through a Chicago DERP relay); each subsequent request on a warm connection ~0.15s; localhost is 4ms. The signed-out shell pulls 36 static assets, which is **6.2s through the Funnel against 0.15s locally** on one connection. Bandwidth is fine (a 300KB chunk moved at ~480KB/s), and only HTTP/1.1 is offered. So this is latency multiplied by request count, not a slow pipe.
2. **The hub is a laptop on Wi-Fi with its Ethernet port unplugged.** Windows logged **seven Wi-Fi disconnects in seven days**, four of them inside working hours on 2026-08-29, each taking about 45 seconds to reassociate. Tailscale is offline for that whole window, so the public address is simply dead, for phones and for every AI client, and then it recovers with nothing left to show it ever happened. Tailscale's own tracker carries matching reports of Funnel failing to recover after a node has been offline, so a drop is not always self-healing.
3. **The machine competes with itself.** `update.mode` is `auto` on a 15-minute poll, and each accepted commit spends **~4.5 minutes in `next build`** at normal priority on the same laptop that is serving pages (nine of them across 2026-08-29 to 08-31). The hourly snapshot added another 39 seconds of single-core compression.

**And the MCP 404s in that session were not Ledgr at all.** The Ledgr connector returned 404 three times, but so did the unrelated Todoist connector in the same session, while direct probes of the hub's own `/api/mcp` and OAuth discovery endpoints all answered correctly from outside. The failure was in the client-side connector bridge, not this codebase. Worth writing down, because the natural instinct was to go looking for a bug in the MCP route and there was none.

**Decision, three parts.**

**1. A reachability probe, with its blind spot stated in the file.** `.github/workflows/hub-reachable.yml` curls the hub's public `/health` every ~15 minutes and fails the run when three attempts over ~20 seconds all miss. The Actions tab becomes the uptime record, and a failure emails the owner. Three attempts rather than one, because a single miss could be the runner's own network or a relay hiccup, and a monitor that cries wolf gets ignored. It targets the `LEDGR_HUB_URL` repo variable and does **nothing** when unset, because Brandon and Tyler share one repo and one person's laptop being off must not redden the other's Actions tab.

**The honest limit, which is in the workflow's header comment too:** GitHub's minimum schedule is five minutes and its scheduled runs are delayed under load, so a ~15-minute sample has roughly a **1-in-20 chance of landing inside a 45-second Wi-Fi drop**. This instrument measures *sustained* outages (a reboot, a machine left asleep, a Funnel that did not come back) and will almost never see the blips that started this investigation. Those are already recorded for free on the machine, in `Microsoft-Windows-WLAN-AutoConfig/Operational`, which is where the seven drops above came from. Two instruments, each honest about its own resolution, beat one that looks complete and is not.

**2. Heavy build steps run at below-normal CPU priority.** `run()` in the supervisor takes `low: true`, used for `npm ci` and `next build`. The mechanism is deliberately boring: Windows children inherit the creating process's priority class and `spawnSync` blocks, so the supervisor lowers *itself* for exactly the duration of the call and restores in a `finally`. No argument quoting through `cmd /c start`, no new dependency, nothing to clean up. **`startApp` is pointedly not marked,** because the app must serve at normal priority and it is spawned outside that window. Migrations are not marked either, since DDL holding locks should finish fast rather than politely. Verified rather than assumed: a child spawned inside the window reports priority 10, a child spawned after it reports 0.

**3. Hourly snapshots compress with `zstd:1`.** Measured against the live database on the hub, which is the only fair place to measure it:

| method | time | size |
|---|---|---|
| default (`gzip:6`) | 39s | 304 MB |
| `gzip:1` | 19s | 361 MB |
| **`zstd:1`** | **10s** | **287 MB** |
| `lz4:1` | 10s | 472 MB |

Four times faster *and* smaller than the default, so there is no trade to weigh. **zstd needs `pg_dump` 16+, and that costs nothing here:** the client must already be at least the server's major (`findPgTool`'s own rule) and the embedded server is 18, so any `pg_dump` able to read this cluster can write this file. Proven end to end before shipping, because this is the restore path and a fast dump nobody can restore is worthless. The real code path produced a 287MB dump in 9.4s; it carries the `PGDMP` magic `local-restore.mjs` checks for; `pg_restore --list` reads its table of contents; and restoring it into a scratch database returned **23,847 items, identical to live**. The 29-check snapshot suite passes unchanged.

**Why not the alternatives.**
- *Cloudflare Tunnel plus a custom domain.* The real fix for cause 1 (HTTP/2, edge caching of static assets, no relay hop), and it would unblock the Clerk production upgrade that `next_steps.md` already has queued, since a `.ts.net` name cannot carry one. Not rejected, deferred: it is a bigger change than this session's brief, and it belongs with that open auth decision rather than smuggled in beside a monitoring workflow.
- *An external uptime monitor (UptimeRobot and friends).* Genuinely less work, and it can poll faster than GitHub will. Rejected for now because the repo already runs eight scheduled workflows through this exact door, so this adds one file and no new account, service, or dashboard to remember.
- *Probing every five minutes, GitHub's floor.* Rejected: it triples the runs to buy a 1-in-7 chance of catching a blip instead of 1-in-20, still misses most of them, and the blips already have a better instrument in the Windows event log.
- *Reporting probe failures into `error_log`.* Rejected as incoherent: when the hub is unreachable there is nothing to report to, and routing it to the Vercel copy instead means the two deploys' error logs no longer mean the same thing.
- *`lz4:1` for snapshots.* Same 10s, but 472MB against 287MB, so it pays 65% more disk every hour for nothing.
- *Lowering `pg_dump`'s priority too.* Rejected: it is `spawnSync` inside the app process, and the app must stay responsive, so the same self-demotion trick is unavailable. With the dump down to 10 seconds, the remaining contention is not worth a bigger change.
- *Setting `update.mode` to `manual`.* Would remove cause 3 outright, but auto-update is a posture Brandon chose deliberately, and a priority change is transparent where taking the automation away is not.

**The order that actually matters, so nobody mistakes this ADR for the fix:** plugging in the Ethernet cable outranks everything above it, and moving the phone back onto the tailnet skips the Funnel path entirely. Parts 2 and 3 here are second-order. Part 1 is the instrument that will tell us whether any of it worked.

**Affects:** `.github/workflows/hub-reachable.yml` (new), the `LEDGR_HUB_URL` repo variable (set for Brandon's hub), `supervisor/ledgr-supervisor.mjs` (`run()`'s `low` option and the two call sites), `src/lib/snapshots.ts` (`--compress=zstd:1`), `runbook.md` §6b.

## ADR-246: the hourly snapshot froze the whole server for two and a half minutes, and that was the "flaky" all along

**Date:** 2026-09-02
**Status:** accepted (not core: one library file made asynchronous, plus its callers). **Supersedes the cause ranking in ADR-245**, which is left standing as the record of what the measurements showed before this was found.

**Context, and why ADR-245 got the ranking wrong.** ADR-245, written hours earlier the same day, measured the Funnel round trip and seven Wi-Fi drops and ranked those as the causes of "Ledgr is slow from my phone" and "MCP is flaky." Then Brandon caught the failure live and produced the one observation that killed the Wi-Fi theory: **two machines could not reach Ledgr at the same moment, while he was driving this very machine over RustDesk with a perfectly smooth remote-desktop session.** The network was demonstrably fine. Something in the app was not.

**The cause, found in the log with a two-minute-wide fingerprint.** The hourly snapshot job ran from **15:45:38 to 15:48:18 UTC**, taking 160 seconds, and Brandon's outage was "the last two to five minutes" reported at 15:50. Every hourly run that day tells the same story: 132, 133, 135, 139, 140, 160 seconds. Never a fast one.

`takeSnapshot` shelled out to `pg_dump` with **`spawnSync`**, and it is called from the request handler of `GET /api/machine/snapshot`. Ledgr's app is **one Node process** (confirmed: pid 6980, no cluster workers). `spawnSync` blocks the event loop. So for the entire length of the dump, the server accepted TCP connections and answered none of them, from every device at once, once an hour, then recovered leaving nothing behind but a "snapshot taken" line that looked like success. Which it was. The dump was never the problem; doing it *inside the process that serves pages* was.

**That is 150 seconds in every 3600: Ledgr was completely unreachable about 4% of the time,** in blocks long enough for any phone or AI client to time out. "Flaky" was a precise description.

**Decision.** Every child process in `src/lib/snapshots.ts` is spawned asynchronously, through one `promisify(execFile)` helper. `takeSnapshot` and `findPgTool` become `async`; their four callers await them. `readTailscaleState` in `network-addresses.ts` gets the same treatment: it had a `spawnSync` with a five-second timeout, so the Network page could freeze every other request for up to five seconds, the same defect one order of magnitude smaller.

**Measured, both directions, with a real 287MB dump of the live database and an HTTP server polled every 200ms throughout:**

| dump path | requests served during the dump | longest window with nothing served |
|---|---|---|
| `spawnSync` (the old way) | **0** | **9.6s**, the whole dump |
| awaited `execFile` (now) | **48** | 0.23s, i.e. the poll interval |

The dump is 9 to 10 seconds in that test rather than 160 because ADR-245's `zstd:1` change had already landed. **Those two changes are independent and both were needed:** compression cut the dump's *length* fourfold, and this cuts the *blocking* to nothing. Either alone would have left a real defect, and the compression win is exactly why the freeze in the contrast test above is 10 seconds instead of the 160 the hub was actually suffering.

**A guard, not just a fix.** `verify-snapshots` grows a check that fails if `spawnSync`, `execSync`, or `execFileSync` ever reappears in `snapshots.ts`, with the incident named in the assertion message. A source-text check is crude, and it is the only kind that catches this: the bug typechecks, passes every behavioral test, and produces correct output. Nothing about it is visible except from outside, under load, on the clock.

**This is ADR-244's lesson with a second edge, and worth stating generally.** That ADR said a scheduled endpoint must not do real work *inside the request*, because the request times out. This is the sharper version: **a scheduled endpoint must not do real work synchronously, because the whole server stops.** The request timeout is a nuisance that reports itself in a log. The blocked event loop is an outage that reports nothing at all. Both jobs looked healthy in `error_log` the entire time they were misbehaving.

**Why not the alternatives.**
- *Detach the work like ADR-244 did.* Does not help on its own: a detached handler that still calls `spawnSync` blocks the same loop just as hard. Asynchrony is the fix; detaching is unnecessary once the dump is 10 seconds and non-blocking.
