- *Move snapshots into the supervisor process instead.* It would work, and it is the bigger redesign: the supervisor already owns the timer, and dumping from there would keep this class of work permanently out of the serving process. Rejected for now because the endpoint is also what the owner's "Snapshot now" button reaches, and ADR-217's one-runner property (both triggers take the same act) is worth more than the isolation. Revisit if a third heavy job wants the same treatment.
- *Run snapshots less often.* Treats the symptom, costs recovery granularity, and leaves the freeze in place for whenever it does run.
- *Only fix the snapshot and leave the Tailscale probe.* Rejected: same defect, same file class, five seconds of everyone's requests for one page's question, and the audit that found it took one grep.

**What ADR-245 still got right,** so this does not swing too far the other way: the Funnel genuinely does cost 6.2s for the signed-out shell's 36 assets against 0.15s locally, and Wi-Fi genuinely did drop seven times in a week. Those are real and unfixed. What changes is the ranking: they explain *slow*, and they explain *some* unreachability, but the hourly total blackout was this, and it was the biggest of the three by a wide margin.

**Affects:** `src/lib/snapshots.ts` (the async helper, `findPgTool`, `takeSnapshot`), `src/lib/snapshot-settings.ts`, `src/app/build/updates/page.tsx`, `src/lib/network-addresses.ts`, `scripts/local-snapshot.mts`, `scripts/verify-snapshots.mts` (30 checks, one new), `runbook.md` §7.

## ADR-247: the project review timeline becomes a rendering the view engine can use, not one page's private display

**Date:** 2026-09-03
**Status:** accepted (not core: no schema change, no migration, no `view_layout` enum value — the whole feature rides `views.display`, an already-tolerant jsonb, plus one extracted component).

**Context.** Tyler's everything-timeline (ADR-198) shipped as `/items/[id]/timeline`: a vertical center spine, meetings and milestones large, task completions and notes and links as small ticks, month markers, a Today line. Brandon wanted that display "as a lens or widget that can be used on any item/type," with filters by property, sort options, and a granularity control, the motivating case being reading his work log (`log_entry`) as a timeline of what he actually did.

Researching it first changed the shape of the work. Most of the ask already existed:

- **Filters by property** already exist twice over: `ViewFilter.propertyFilters` for select/multi-select, and the ADR-164 `where` rules group over any property, relation, priority, or status. The builder renders both.
- **Sort options** already cover every built-in field plus `{field:"property", propertyKey, numeric}`.
- **Granularity** already had a vocabulary: `TIMELINE_ZOOMS` (hour → halfDecade) in `display.zoom`, from ADR-166's horizontal Timeline.
- **Every mount point** already routes through one renderer: `ViewRenderer` serves the view page, list lens tabs, dashboard widgets, related-item groups, and the Desk.

So the missing pieces were three, and small: the spine was trapped in a page, the view engine had no spine rendering, and the builder would not let a view be placed by a custom date property.

**Decision 1: the spine is a CALENDAR MODE, not a sixth view layout.** `CALENDAR_MODES` gains `"spine"` (labelled **History (vertical)** in the UI), and `ViewRenderer`'s `case "calendar"` branches to it ahead of every planner check. A top-level `spine` layout would have meant a new `view_layout` Postgres enum value: a migration, and a plausible core change needing both-agree. A mode is a key in `views.display`, which is exactly where ADR-166 put the horizontal Timeline, so this is precedent-following rather than a dodge. Same reach, no schema touch, ships solo. The cost, accepted knowingly: the layout picker still says "Calendar" while offering a vertical narrative as one of its modes.

**Decision 2: `display.zoom` doubles as the grain.** Its values already are the granularity list Brandon described. It means px-per-day on the horizontal Timeline and "how much time one chip covers" on the spine. A second `display.grain` key would have left two knobs meaning the same thing on two renderings of one view, with no answer to which wins.

**Decision 3: `TimelineEntry` is promoted to the shared seam** (`src/lib/timeline-entry.ts`, dependency-free). Two gatherers now emit it: `gatherProjectTimeline` (one record, five collections, a different date rule per collection) and `viewEntries` (any view's rows, one date field). `TimelineSpine` is pure and hook-free — no fetching, no routing, no `Date.now()`, with "now" arriving as a caller-computed index — which is what lets a server page and a client dashboard widget both mount it. That purity is deliberate headroom: Brandon wants to build further on the mixed views/widgets/lenses idea, and a third gatherer (an activity-log spine, a cross-project roll-up, a composed record surface) should only have to emit the array.

**Decision 4: both gatherers stay.** Forcing the record spine into a view would mean five stitched views or a new multi-type filter, since a view has one type filter and one date field.

**Decision 5: one tier for a view spine.** A homogeneous row set has no natural hierarchy, and inventing one would guess at intent. Two tiers stay on the record spine, where meetings and milestones really are the headlines.

**Decision 6: hour grain is built for every type, not gated** (Brandon's call). A day-only date has no hour to sit in, so at hour grain it buckets by its day rather than inventing a midnight. Hiding the control per type would have been the wrong shape of honesty.

**Also fixed, found while testing.** `parseViewInput` back-filled `dateProperty` to `plan`/`meetingAt` for any calendar view without one. With `display.startField` now settable from the UI, that left a stored view claiming a date field it does not use, since every renderer prefers `startField`. The back-fill now skips when `startField` is set. And `viewView` (the MCP serializer) echoes `display`, because `update_view` replaces wholesale: without it in the read, an update would silently wipe a view's mode, grain, or custom-date placement.

**The unlocked case.** `log_entry` keeps its date in `properties.logdate`, and the builder's date-field picker offered custom types only "created" and "updated". `placement.ts` had read `DateRef = {prop}` since ADR-166; nothing could set it. Now the picker offers a type's own `date` properties and writes `display.startField`, which improves Month and the horizontal Timeline for every custom type, not just the spine.

**Verified on real data** (dev branch): the record spine renders unchanged at its defaults, then regroups by week and reverses and filters by collection; a `journal` view (112 rows, date only in `properties.date`, so unplaceable before this) renders as a spine with month markers, survives an edit-and-resave round trip, and renders again inside a faithful dashboard widget with no console errors. Grain bucketing is checked in `scripts/verify-timeline-geometry.mts`: zone handling both ways, week starting Monday to match the horizontal ruler, quarter/year/half-decade boundaries, and the hour-grain day fallback.

**Known rough edge, left alone on purpose.** In a narrow dashboard widget the two-column spine is cramped, because its breakpoint is the viewport rather than its container. Fixing it properly means container queries across the spine, which would change ADR-198's shipped markup; not worth doing blind. Every other faithful widget layout (mini table, mini board) shares the constraint.

## ADR-248: a sessionless driver has to carry the sync origin inside the statement

**Date:** 2026-09-03
**Status:** Accepted (bug fix; no change to the merge rules or the wire format)

**The report.** "Why are there dozens of revisions saying the same thing instead of only meaningful changes?" One note, `How We Use AI (Working Draft)`, had 37 revisions in an afternoon, 10 to 20 seconds apart, when an ordinary save snapshots at most one per 5 minutes (`REVISION_DEBOUNCE_MS`).

**The cause.** Those revisions never went through the debounce. They came from the body-conflict branch of the merge (ADR-206), which snapshots the losing body and flags the item `syncBodyMerged`. There was no real conflict. The oplog trigger stamps `origin_device_id` from the `ledgr.sync_origin` GUC, `SET LOCAL` needs a session, and the cloud runs neon-http, which has none: every write the cloud applied from a peer was logged as the cloud's OWN write. The merge reads those stamps back as "the last local writer of this body was the Cloud", compares that against an op from BrandonECC, sees two devices, and calls it a conflict. Once per synced save, forever. The old comment on `applySyncOps` accepted the null origin as harmless because echoes still terminated; the echo did, this did not.

**Measured before the fix:** 133 sub-debounce revision gaps in 10 days, every one of them on an item flagged `syncBodyMerged`; zero on unflagged items. 74 items carried the false flag.

**The decision.** Both drivers now reach the trigger with the origin set. The transactional path is unchanged (one transaction, `SET LOCAL` per action). The sessionless path carries the `set_config(…, is_local => true)` inside each statement, which works because a single statement is its own transaction, so a GUC that statement sets is still set when the AFTER trigger ends it. It has to sit where the planner cannot drop it: an unreferenced SELECT CTE is optimized away, but a `FROM` item, a `USING` item and a `RETURNING` expression are not. All three shapes were verified against Neon before the change landed, and `verify-sync.mts` now runs a whole exchange with `transactions: false` and asserts both halves: every op stamped, and three sequential edits on one device crossing that apply with no phantom revision and no flag.

**Rejected alternatives.** Batching each action with a preceding `set_config` in one neon transaction (`db.batch`) would give real GUC semantics, but it is all-or-nothing, which would undo ADR-241's per-action parking on exactly the hub that needed it. Post-stamping the ops after the batch, or parking the origin in a table the trigger reads, both open a window where a concurrent local write gets stamped with a peer's origin and is then never pushed to that peer: a lost change, which is worse than the noise being fixed.

**Backfill.** `scripts/backfill-sync-conflict-noise.mts` clears the 74 false flags and thins the phantom revisions back to the cadence a real save keeps (first snapshot per 5-minute window, plus the newest, per flagged item). Dry run by default, backs every deleted row up to `scripts/backups/` first, and only touches flagged items. Both tables are in the synced set, so the cleanup reaches the other peers on its own.

## ADR-249: the Inbox is a routing choice per arrival source, not a fact about capture

**Date:** 2026-09-06
**Status:** accepted (amends ADR-013, extends ADR-010). Not core, so it ships solo: no schema change, no change to the canonical body format, and the machine surface only grows an optional argument, which is exactly the ADR-183 carve-out.

**Context.** Brandon went looking for the switch that turns the Inbox off, and there wasn't one. Seven arrival paths each typed `inbox: true` into their own file, and ADR-013 stated the rule out loud: captures always arrive in the Inbox. That left three reasonable ways of working unsupported: never use the Inbox at all, use it only for what a machine brought in (email, the web clipper, Claude), or send only hand-typed captures there. The one lever that did exist was cosmetic. Dropping the Inbox slot in `/build/navigation` hides the doorway while items keep piling up behind it, flag still set.

**What the owner can now do.** Every arrival path gets its own setting on a new Build page, **Capture & Inbox** at `/build/capture`: queue it in the Inbox, file it straight away, or drop it into a named project. The seven paths are quick capture, the phone share sheet, the web clipper, email in, Todoist, create-from-an-@-mention, and Claude over the assistant connection. Defaults reproduce today's behavior exactly, so an owner who changes nothing sees nothing change. When no path routes to the Inbox and nothing is sitting in it, the Inbox drops out of the navigation on its own.

**Decision 1: an explicit `inbox` in the payload always beats the setting.** The setting supplies a default when the caller says nothing, and never an override. This is the whole reason the change is additive rather than core. Every request written before today carries an explicit flag and therefore behaves identically, byte for byte, which is what puts it inside the ADR-183 carve-out. Reversing this later would silently change what already-written callers do, and that is precisely the class of surprise ADR-010 refused.

**Decision 2: three states from the start, stored as one flat string.** A route is one value per source: `"inbox"`, `"filed"`, or a project's id. Not a nested object with a mode and a destination, which is the shape that invites a version field a year later. `SETTINGS_UUID_RE` already tells an id from a mode word, and flat string values are what the settings parser is already good at. Source keys stay free text, following `notifications.kind`, so a new arrival path never needs a migration. The whole thing rides the existing `users.settings` jsonb column.

**Decision 3: the destination edge is written inside `createItem`, not at the API route.** This is the trap worth remembering, because the obvious move is the wrong one. The existing `relateTo` argument is handled in `src/app/api/items/route.ts`, so it only covers callers arriving over HTTP. Four of the seven paths (email sync, Todoist sync, the clipper route, the share handler) call `createItem` directly and would have silently dropped their destination. `createItem` is the only seam all seven share. The relation is written best-effort after the insert, in the same spirit as the activity log, so a failed edge never undoes a capture.

**Decision 4: a Build page from the first cut, not a settings row.** The Web Clipper block moves to `/build/capture` from the bottom of User Settings, so the page begins life consolidating rather than adding. "How does anything get into Ledgr" now has one address instead of three.

**Decision 5: the Inbox hides itself when nothing feeds it.** Brandon's framing: if the owner isn't using it, the Inbox should just be off. `Nav.tsx` already awaits both the Inbox count and the settings in one `Promise.all`, so this is a filter over two values it already holds. **The nav slot hides, never the route.** `/inbox` keeps working and stays reachable from the Build page and the command palette. Hiding the route would strand anything already sitting in the Inbox and turn a preference into a trap.

**Decision 6: this cut does not stamp the source onto the item.** Worth knowing about because the moment a source lands on rows, back-compat starts: every item created before it has none, so any filter has to treat "unknown" as a real value rather than an error. When it earns its keep, `properties.capture.source` is additive and needs no migration, while a real column would (ADR-003 puts hot fields in columns, and a source chip on a list row is arguably hot). Deferring costs nothing except that items created between now and then are unattributed.

**Three smaller calls, for the record.** The page sits in the **DATA** group after Files, because capture routing shapes what data exists, while MAINTAIN is where cleanup tools live and this would get buried there. A destination may be **a project only**, matching the task-add card's picker, so the `"project"` relation role is always honest and there is no role-guessing branch. And **a trashed destination falls back to the Inbox** with the setting left alone: capture never vanishes into a place nobody can reach, the auto-hide rule un-hides the Inbox the moment something lands in it, and restoring the project from Trash restores the routing.

**What this amends.** ADR-013 said captures always arrive `inbox: true`. That sentence stops being true today: quick capture now names itself as a source and asks where it should land. Everything else in ADR-013 stands, including the `q` shortcut, the modal, and the rule that leaving the Inbox is a deliberate act rather than a side effect of filling in a due date. **ADR-010 is extended, not reopened.** It rejected a *derived* Inbox, one where membership is inferred from an item's own fields, because a dateless someday-task would squat there forever and setting a date would silently triage things behind Brandon's back. Nothing here infers anything from an item. `items.inbox` is still a real column, still set once on arrival, still cleared only by deliberate triage. What changed is who supplies the value when the caller doesn't: a setting the owner wrote down in advance, per source, rather than a constant compiled into seven files. An explicit value in the payload still wins over that setting every time, so the predictability ADR-010 was protecting is intact.

**Verification.** `scripts/verify-inbox-sources.mts` runs with no database and joins the CI suite automatically. It executes the route resolver against every source (the three routes, an unknown source key, nine shapes of unparseable value, and each source with nothing configured), checks that the settings parser drops junk before it is ever read, and then pins the four rules in the create gate that do need a database: the explicit flag short-circuits in both directions, the settings read happens only after that short-circuit, a destination is checked owner-scoped and excluding Trash, and a trashed or missing one falls back to the Inbox.

## ADR-250: the owner's accent becomes a tenth highlight, and it stores a reference instead of a color

**Date:** 2026-09-09
**Status:** accepted. Not core: no schema change, no new element in the canonical body dialect (`<mark class="hl-*">` is already in it), and no change to any existing value, so every body written before today parses and renders byte-identically.

**Context.** Tyler asked for his own highlight accent, the one he picks in Settings, to be available as a highlight in the editor, so the marker pen matches the app. Just one extra swatch, not an accent variant of every palette slot. The nine existing highlights are literal `rgba()` washes tuned for the dark canvas (the 2026-07-16 palette ADR), and the accent is already a per-owner CSS variable on `<body>` that drives every other accent surface.

**Decision 1: the value stored in the body is a live reference, not a resolved color.** An accent highlight serializes as `<mark class="hl-accent" style="background-color:color-mix(in srgb, var(--accent) 40%, transparent)">`. That makes it the only palette value in Ledgr that isn't self-contained, which is a real departure and the reason this has an ADR at all. The alternative, baking the accent's hex at the moment of typing, was rejected because it defeats the request: the point is that the highlight IS the owner's accent, so re-picking an accent in Settings has to restyle highlights already made. A frozen hex would leave a note full of last month's color, and there is no migration that fixes it afterwards, because nothing records which yellow-ish hexes were once "the accent". The cost is paid outside Ledgr: a plain Markdown reader that defines no `--accent` shows its own default highlight instead of the owner's color. Still visibly highlighted, which is the part that matters, and the `<mark>` and `hl-accent` class survive the trip, so the intent is never lost.

**Decision 2: the Sunday-proof copy resolves it server-side.** Principle 4 says nothing preached on Sunday may depend on the app being there, and the offline/share/PDF document (`print-html.ts`) deliberately carries no app context, so a `var(--accent)` in it would resolve to nothing and the highlight would silently disappear on paper. That document therefore gets a generated `mark.hl-accent{background-color:rgba(…);color:inherit}` rule, resolved from the owner's stored solid at render time, and both callers pass it. This is the one place the reference is flattened to a literal, and it is flattened per render rather than per save, so it still tracks the current accent. `color:inherit` for the same load-bearing reason the other nine rules carry it: a highlight owns the fill channel and must never repaint colored text.

**Decision 3: highlight-only, and deliberately NOT in `BLOCKNOTE_COLORS`.** Putting it in that table would have been two lines and would have added an accent *text* color for free, which nobody asked for and which cannot work: text colors round-trip by matching their value, so a `var()` reference would decode as "no color" and be dropped on every save. The accent lives beside the table as its own name with a widened `HighlightColor` type. A check in `verify-tiptap-markdown.mts` fails if it ever appears inside the nine, because the failure mode of that mistake is silent data loss rather than a broken build.

**Decision 4: a gradient accent reaches the mark through the image channel, veiled.** Gradient accents are a real Settings option (Tyler is using Sunset), and a CSS gradient is an image, not a color, so it cannot ride the `background-color` an ordinary highlight uses. `layout.tsx` sets `--accent-highlight-image` only when a gradient is actually chosen, and `globals.css` gives `mark.hl-accent` an image channel that falls back to `none`. The gradient is stacked under a page-colored veil, which supplies the alpha the nine literals get from their `rgba()`, so one layered value works for any gradient with no rewriting of its color stops. A solid accent sets the var to `none` and renders purely from the inline color.

**What this does not do.** It adds no element to the body dialect, so the dialect sentence in `CLAUDE.md` is unchanged. It does not touch the nine existing colors or their values, so `backfill-editor-colors.mts` stays a historical script. And the booth export needed no change at all: its highlight strip is `/<\/?mark\b[^>]*>/g`, attribute-agnostic, so an accent highlight already flattens in the presentation copy exactly like the other nine.

**Verification.** `verify-tiptap-markdown.mts` grows sixteen checks: the class and the round-trip in all three decode paths (class+style, class alone, style alone, the last being the paste path that drops the class), that the stored value still contains `var(--accent)` (the check that catches someone "simplifying" it to a hex), that the accent stays out of the nine-color table and is not a text color, that the offline literal resolves `#2563eb` to `rgba(37,99,235,0.4)` in either hex case and passes a non-hex through rather than emitting broken CSS, and that a veiled gradient keeps its own stops. `verify-print.mts` grows three: the shell emits the literal rule with no `var()` left in it, that rule keeps `color:inherit`, and no rule appears when the caller passes no accent. Both run with no database and join the CI suite automatically.

## ADR-251: a highlight may claim the foreground, but only where the text has no color of its own

**Date:** 2026-09-09
**Status:** accepted. Narrows the `mark { color: inherit }` rule that has stood since the slide-mark work; extends ADR-250. Not core (rendering, no stored value changes).

**Context.** Two things surfaced within minutes of ADR-250 reaching production, both reported by Tyler, and they are worth recording together because one of them is a bug I shipped.

**The bug: changing your accent appeared to do nothing.** `applyAccent` in `SettingsForm.tsx` pushes the new accent onto `<body>` live so the app re-skins without a reload. It wrote `--accent` and `--accent-gradient`, and ADR-250 had added a third var, `--accent-highlight-image`, that it knew nothing about. For a **gradient** accent that image is the only layer you can see: it paints over the `background-color` underneath. So the accent updated everywhere except the highlights that were supposed to be the point, and only a full reload corrected them, because the server writes the var correctly at render. Tyler is on a gradient accent, so he hit the one case where the symptom is total. Fixed by writing all three together, with a source-scanned check that fails if they ever diverge again: **these three vars are one setting.** The general shape is worth remembering — a server-rendered CSS var with a client-side live-apply twin is a two-site change, and the second site is easy to miss because nothing about the first one refers to it.

**The decision: highlighted text now takes a bright ink.** Highlighting text left it at whatever the surrounding prose was, a muted `--foreground` normally and `#a3a3a3` inside a blockquote, which is where Tyler first noticed it. A marker pen that makes text no easier to read than the line above it is not doing its job. `mark` now takes `--mark-ink` (white in dark, dark in the light palette that isn't built yet).

**Why this doesn't just delete the old rule.** `mark { color: inherit }` was there for a real reason: the UA stylesheet gives `<mark>` its own black `color`, and an element's own color beats an inherited one, so a highlight over colored text silently repainted it black. That matters most in the **booth export**, where a highlight means "put this on the screen" and the text color means "this is Scripture" — repainting Scripture destroys the distinction the preacher is reading from. So the claim is **narrowed, not dropped**: a bare highlight takes the bright ink, and `span[style*="color"] mark` sends anything inside a text-color span back to inheriting, so the color still wins. The other nesting order needs no rule, since the span's own inline style already beats the mark's. Both orders occur, because marks compose either way round.

**The print/share/offline document is deliberately excluded.** It prints black-on-white, so bright ink there comes out invisible on paper — a Principle 4 failure of exactly the kind ADR-250 was careful about. `print-html.ts` keeps `color:inherit`, and a check fails if `--mark-ink` ever appears in that file. The app and the paper copy differ here on purpose.

**Verification.** Five source-scanned checks in `verify-tiptap-markdown.mts`, chosen because all three of these bugs typecheck and pass every behavioral test: the three accent vars are written together, `mark` takes the bright ink, the text-color guard exists, and the print shell does not take the bright ink.
## ADR-252: the sync cadence is the fastest a copy is contacted, and "only on changes" decides whether to bother

**Date:** 2026-09-09
**Status:** accepted — supersedes ADR-240's reading of the same flag (not core: no schema change, no wire change, the stored shape is the same optional boolean, and a hub with the flag off behaves exactly as before)

**Context.** ADR-240 built the checkbox Brandon asked for and then read it the opposite way round from how he meant it. It made the cadence a **floor on silence**: changes went out immediately, and a quiet copy was still contacted once per cadence. What he wanted was the cadence as a **ceiling on speed**, with the flag deciding whether a due round happens at all. The difference is not cosmetic. Under ADR-240, "hourly, only on changes" still woke the cloud database every hour forever, and every burst of editing woke it again in between. Under this ADR the same words mean at most once an hour, and nothing whatsoever on a day nobody touched anything. The 2026-09-08 wake-up audit put a number on it: the cloud copy was being woken about 24 times a day by an idle heartbeat that had nothing to carry, and each wake holds a serverless database awake for a fixed idle tail whatever it did.

**Decision.** Same stored flag, inverted gate. The cadence is honored first and nothing overrides it but the owner's **Check in now** button. When the round is due and the flag is on, one local read asks "do we have anything to send"; if not, the round is skipped. `quietSkip` replaces `onChangeDue` and answers the question in the direction the loop now asks it.

**A liveness backstop, which is the piece the inversion needs.** An unbounded quiet spell is a new failure: a peer silent longer than the hub's retention window loses its place in the oplog and must be re-filled from scratch (ADR-208), and a fortnight away is an ordinary event, not an exotic one. So silence past the safe gap always breaks the quiet. That gap is not a new number: `maxSafeGapMinutes` is the same half-the-window arithmetic the cadence picker already refuses past (`cadenceRefusal`), now shared by both, so the dropdown and the gate cannot disagree about how long silence is safe. Fourteen days of retention gives seven.

**Two clauses kept from ADR-240, for the same reasons.** A **failing** hub is never skipped, because its retries are already spaced by the ADR-239 backoff and a hub nobody contacts can never come back while reporting itself fine. And the signal stays **local and free**: the hub's stored push cursor against the local oplog head, one read, nothing over the wire to discover there was nothing to send. The new shape is in fact cheaper on the peer, because that read now happens only when a round is due rather than on every two-second tick.

**What it costs, said plainly.** Inbound changes cannot arrive while a copy stays quiet, because a peer has no way to learn the hub has news without asking. That was already true of the cadence and it is now true for longer. It is right for a cloud archive that writes nothing worth having back, and wrong for a second machine of yours, which is why the flag is per-hub and off by default. **Check in now** remains the answer whenever the wait matters, and it is still the only thing that overrides a schedule.

**Why not a new preset instead of changing what the flag means.** A "when there are changes" rung on the cadence ladder would need its own interval, its own label, and its own retention arithmetic, and it would leave the misread checkbox sitting beside it. The flag composes with every rung already there, and only one person and one rig had it switched on, so the meaning could be corrected rather than duplicated.

**Verification.** `scripts/verify-sync-ui.mts`: three reader-tolerance checks, three on the shared safe-gap arithmetic, and seven on the gate itself, including both sides of the backstop boundary, the failing-hub clause, and a restarted process checking in once because it cannot measure a gap it never saw.

**Affects:** `src/lib/sync/client.ts` (`quietSkip`, `maxSafeGapMinutes`/`maxSafeGapMs`, `cadenceRefusal`, the loop's per-hub gate), `src/components/network/HubActions.tsx`, `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`, `scripts/verify-sync-ui.mts`. Companion to the same day's cron pruning (four GitHub Actions schedules stopped, runbook §5 and the Neon Free section rewritten).

## ADR-253: a date tracks its anchor unless it is pinned

**Date:** 2026-09-11
**Status:** accepted (Tyler; **Brandon agreed 2026-09-11**). **CORE.** It changes what `due_date` MEANS (a deadline now moves on its own) and adds a stored `properties.datePins`, so it lands under the both-agree rule even though there is no migration and no API break. Supersedes ADR-085's stored-offset model for live subtask trees and retires ADR-076's `maintainDueOffset` as the deadline lever. Flagged in `COLLAB.md`.

**Context.** Tyler opened 2026-09-11 with "Due date vs schedule is mucking up the UI and really confusing the system," and a screenshot of a recurring sermon-edit task whose six subtasks all read `Sep 11 · due Aug 28`. Three complaints, which turned out to have one cause and two missing write paths behind them:

1. **The deadline never moved.** ADR-076 shipped `maintainDueOffset` — "when the plan advances, shift due by the same delta" — honored in `advanceSeriesRow`, carried through rule edits, exposed as an MCP argument, and **with no GUI control anywhere**, defaulting OFF. So a recurring task could hold a deadline, but it froze at the first occurrence and read as a permanent stale overdue. A lever reachable only by asking Claude over MCP is the same failure ADR-222 named: the feature had a builder attached.
2. **Subtasks didn't follow their parent.** ADR-085 could move them, but only ones carrying a stored `relativeSchedule` offset, and **exactly one control in the codebase ever wrote one** (`SubtaskSchedule.tsx`, the little date chip on a subtask row, and only while the parent was already dated). Tyler's checklist came from MCP `add_subtasks`, so five of six had no offset and stood still forever. He bumped the parent to Sep 14 mid-conversation to prove it; one subtask moved.
3. **The rail read as two dates for everything.** `Schedule` and `Due` sat as equally-weighted peer rows on every task, when most tasks want one date.

**The decision — one rule, three surfaces.** A date tracks its anchor unless it is pinned.

1. **Children follow their parent by DELTA, not by stored offset.** When a task's scheduled date moves N days, every dated descendant moves N days (`shiftChildDates`). Nothing has to be stamped, so there is no backfill and Tyler's existing five stragglers started tracking the moment this landed. A child opts out by pinning, and a pinned child's subtree holds too, since it anchors to the child that stayed put.
2. **A deadline follows its own plan date by the same delta**, in `updateItem`, on recurrence advance, and on a recurrence-calendar log edit. Skipped when the caller sets both dates in one patch (they are being stated deliberately) and when the deadline is pinned.
3. **Pinning is the only opt-out**, stored as `properties.datePins: {scheduled?, due?}`, tolerant-parsed. "Pinned" means a hard external date: Apr 15, a grant submission, a hand-off.
4. ~~**The deadline stops being a rail row.**~~ **REVERSED same day (Tyler, 2026-09-11) — see the amendment below.** The deadline is a peer rail row again, directly under Schedule. The `DeadlineField` control built for the fold is unchanged; only its home moved back.
5. **Deadline-before-plan is flagged, never blocked**, with a one-click "move the plan to X too" — offered only when that deadline hasn't already passed, since "move the plan to Aug 28" in September helps nobody. `deadlineDisplay` is the single display rule every row shares: a deadline on the plan day is redundant and hides, before it or already past alerts, genuinely later shows quietly.

**Why not the alternatives.** *Removing `due_date`* — rejected on cost and on merit: 77 files touch it, it is a core column backing ICS, planner `placeBy`, milestones and the overdue predicate, and Tyler wants the real "work it Monday, due Friday" case. *One visible date with the deadline demoted to a flag* — simplest to use and it kills the bug class outright, but it loses that case. *Backfilling offsets onto existing children* — rejected; a migration that guesses intent on live production data, when inverting the default achieves the same thing and fixes items nobody migrates. *Authoring the gap as a number ("[3] days after")* — rejected on Tyler's read, and he was right: "you wouldn't want to be setting a new due date rule, just changing the due date for that specific task." The gap is never typed, it is simply what the two dates currently are, and editing either one re-states it. *Honoring a stored `maintainDueOffset: false` as a pin* — rejected, and this one is a trap worth recording: `parseRecurrence` collapses a stored `false` to `undefined`, making it indistinguishable from the unset default every task already carries, so honoring it would have preserved the exact bug this replaces. The flag is translated to a pin at the MCP **write** boundary instead, where an explicit `false` still carries intent. *A second mechanism for "this occurrence only"* — unnecessary; carving an occurrence into a detached one-off (ADR-083) already does it.

**What `relativeSchedule` still does.** It survives, deliberately narrowed to the **template apply** path (`deriveOffsetChildren`). A template prototype usually carries no concrete dates at all — its checklist says "day 0, +1, +5" as offsets — so there is no gap for anchoring to measure, and applying a template is not a move (undated → dated is not a delta). Live subtask trees no longer read it. This is the one place the offset is the only statement of intent, and the verify suite pins that behavior.

**The one write path deliberately left outside the rule: `rollOverdueScheduled`.** The "Roll N overdue → today" action is a single bulk UPDATE that sets `scheduled_date = today` and touches nothing else. It stays that way. Its deadline exception is the older and stronger rule (ADR-078: the roll is a recovery action for work you missed, not a replan, and advancing the deadline would erase the fact that you blew it), and the roll FLATTENS by design — every stale task lands on today, each row independently — so overdue children are already caught by the same predicate and a per-row delta on top would move them twice. The gap this leaves is narrow and named rather than papered over: a FUTURE-dated child of an overdue parent keeps its date while the parent jumps forward, closing the gap between them. It needs a subtask dated ahead of an already-late parent, so it is rare; logged in `next_steps.md` rather than silently resolved one way.

**Blast radius, honestly.** This changes behavior on live production data. The first time Tyler bumps a parent, children that have sat at fixed dates for weeks will move — which is the point, but it is a real write, so `updateItem` returns the prior child dates as an additive `datesShifted` field (allowed solo under the ADR-183 carve-out) for an undo toast, and `restoreChildDates` is the undo half. Clearing a parent's date is deliberately NOT a move: ADR-085 wiped its children's dates in that case, which lost work, and now they keep what they have.

**Also in this slice (non-core canvas cleanup, same session).** `+ Task` (`NewRelatedTask`) is gone from the task canvas — it created a *related* task, not a subtask, a distinction invisible next to "Add subtask". `+ Relate` moves into the rail as a `Linked` row beside Project / Tags / People, which are relation edges too; it had been a bare unlabelled button with no home whenever a task had no links. `Linked here` moves inside the two-pane main column, fixing the misalignment Tyler flagged: it had been re-centering its own `max-w-3xl` against the full width, rail included, so it sat visibly right of the title and didn't even line up with the footer under it. And Export & sharing / Version History no longer render on tasks — Save Offline, Share link and Download Markdown are body-shaped features, and a task's body is a line or two.

**Affects.** New: `src/lib/date-anchor.ts` (the pure pin + delta primitives), `src/components/canvas/rail/DeadlineField.tsx`, `src/components/canvas/rail/LinkedRow.tsx`. Rewritten: `src/lib/relative-subtask-service.ts` (`shiftChildDates` + `restoreChildDates` + the narrowed `deriveOffsetChildren`). Changed: `item-mutations.ts` (prior dates read into `existing`, the deadline shift, the child shift, the `datesShifted` return), `recurrence-service.ts` (advance + log-edit paths), `templates.ts` (both apply paths), `mcp/tools/tasks.ts` (the flag → pin translation + description), `format-date.ts` (`deadlineDisplay`), `TaskCanvas.tsx`, `SchedulePopover.tsx`, `RelatedPanel.tsx`, `AddRelation.tsx`, `Subtasks.tsx`, `SubtaskExpandableRow.tsx`, `row-ui.tsx`. Superseded but kept per defer-by-hiding: `rail/DueRow.tsx`. No migration, no dependency, no schema column.

**Amendment, 2026-09-11 (same day, Tyler): the deadline goes back to its own rail row, and the task footer was over-trimmed.** Two corrections after Tyler tested the preview:

1. **Folding the deadline into the Schedule popover was an overcorrection.** It answered "two dates for everything" by making the second date *invisible*: on a task with no deadline set, the rail showed no deadline affordance at all, the row summary mentioned `due` only when one already existed, and the only way in was to know the Schedule popover contained it. Tyler's report was simply "why did due disappear?", which is the right question to ask of a control with no label and no entry point. That violates the standing rule that a feature worth building is worth making legible. `DueRow` is restored as a peer row directly under Schedule, opening the same `DeadlineField` (date + pin + the before-the-plan flag), and the Schedule row no longer carries a `due` in its summary — one field, one home. **None of the anchoring behavior changed**; this is purely where the control lives.

2. **Hiding the whole `ItemUtilitiesFooter` on tasks hid two things it shouldn't have.** Export & sharing genuinely doesn't belong on a task (Save Offline, Share link and the presentation export are body-shaped, and a task's body is a line or two), but the same footer also carries **Files** and **Version History**. Dropping Files breaks the safety property ADR-237 exists for: a file whose inline body link is deleted is otherwise stranded with nowhere to find it. Dropping Version History removes a task's only undo for a clobbered description — and the code comment justifying the removal claimed revisions "stay reachable from the item actions menu," which is **false**; that menu has no history entry. Both are restored, below Linked in the main pane (Tyler's placement), via new `exportSharing` and `bare` props on the footer. The lesson worth keeping: "this section doesn't suit this type" was true of one of its three parts, and I removed the container instead of the part.

**Rail order (Tyler, 2026-09-11):** Schedule, Due, Priority, Tags, People, Project, Linked, custom fields, Focus today. Project had led the rail since the Todoist-order pass (2026-08-18); the dates now lead instead, on the reasoning that what you set most often should read first.

**Verification.** `verify-relative-subtasks.mts` is repointed at the new contract in place of the three assertions that encoded the old one (a child without an offset now shifts; a pinned child does not; clearing a parent's date no longer wipes its children), plus a new deadline block: the gap is preserved down the tree, a pinned deadline stands still, and an explicit deadline in the same patch wins. A third block round-trips the undo: the write reports the children as they were, `restoreChildDates` puts every one back, and a write that moves no dates reports nothing (so the toast stays silent). `verify-templates.mts` keeps its offset-derive check, which is now the regression guard on the one path that still uses offsets. Full `verify:ci` (80 pure scripts) plus the DB-backed recurrence/subtask/template suites pass; the 3 failures in `verify-mcp-tasks.mts` are **pre-existing on `main`** (hardcoded occurrence dates that have drifted into the past) and are logged in `next_steps.md`.

## ADR-254: a date property can carry a time of day (`withTime`), so one field is a timed range

**Date:** 2026-09-11 · **Status:** accepted (core: property-kind contract; Tyler agreed 2026-09-11) · **Requested by:** Brandon

**Context.** The work log (`log_entry`) kept its start and end as free text ("9:06 PM"), so the History spine and the Planner could only place an entry on its day. Brandon wants the log to be a real time-tracking history, viewable on the vertical spine by the hour. The `date` kind was day-only by design (ADR-166: "custom date props are ISO date scalars, day-only for v1"), with `withEnd` already letting one field carry a range end at `<key>__end`.

**Decision.** Add a second flag beside `withEnd` on a `date` PropertyDef: `withTime`. A timed field stores a full ISO instant in the same property (and, with `withEnd`, in `<key>__end`), exactly the shape `meeting_at` uses. No new kind, no sibling `__time` key, no schema migration.

**The one rule that makes it safe: readers detect the shape from the value, not the flag.** `propInstant` (placement.ts) treats anything longer than a day scalar that parses as an instant; a bare `YYYY-MM-DD` stays a UTC calendar day. So flipping the flag on a field with existing values changes nothing stored, the two shapes can coexist in one column, and turning the flag back off leaves the instants readable. Writers are value-driven the same way: a drag that produces minutes writes an instant, a drag that produces a day writes a day, so a plain date field never grows a clock by accident.

**What changed.** `types.ts` (flag + tolerant parse), `placement.ts` (`propInstant`; `readAnchor` splits an instant in the owner's zone like `meetingAt`; `writeRef` composes one with `zonedInstant`), `ViewRenderer.tsx` (`spineDate` honours the time so an hour grain works; a table cell formats an instant as day + clock instead of raw ISO), `CustomProperties.tsx` (a `datetime-local` picker for timed fields, and the first editor for a `withEnd` field's "to" value, which had no UI before), `TypeBuilder.tsx` (two checkboxes on a Date row: "Include a time of day", "Has an end (a range)", per ADR-222 the GUI is the lever, and this also closes the long-parked "expose `withEnd` in the builder" follow-up), MCP `list_types` echoes both flags and `create_type` documents them (additive, ADR-183). `scripts/verify-placement.mts` covers read + write of a timed range and the day-anchor guard.

**Alternatives declined.** A new `datetime` kind (a second kind for the same idea, and every kind switch in the app grows a case); a `<key>__time` sibling like `scheduledTime` (two keys to keep consistent, and sorts on the start key would ignore the time); leaving Start/End as text and parsing on read (a heuristic in a hot path, and the text stays the source of truth).

**Known corners.** The record picker converts through the browser's zone, not `users.settings.timezone` (marked `ponytail:` in the file); for a single-user app on one machine they agree. A day-only value shown in a timed field seeds the picker at 00:00 until the owner sets a time. The Planner's auto-pairing of a `withEnd` field's end still needs the view to name `endField: { prop: "<key>__end" }` explicitly; the builder's date picker writes only `startField`, unchanged here.

**The work-log migration** is `scripts/convert-log-times.mts`: over the machine API with a `/build/api` key, dry run by default, a JSON backup and `--rollback` when applied; "All day" entries keep a day-only date. The Start/End text fields stay on the type until the conversion is verified, then get hidden, not deleted.

## ADR-255: image is a property kind on any type

**Date:** 2026-09-11 · **Status:** accepted (core: property-kind contract; Tyler agreed 2026-09-11) · **Requested by:** Brandon

**Context.** Person's built-in Image (ADR-202 addendum 4) is the only picture box in Ledgr, hardcoded to the `person` type's `image` key. Brandon wants any type to be able to carry a picture field, named anything (Profile, Cover, Logo), without a bespoke build per type.

**Decision.** Add `image` to `PROPERTY_KINDS` as a sibling of `url`. It stores exactly what the person Image stores today: a plain string, either an http(s) URL or a stable `/files/<id>` attachment address (ADR-228). No object, no width/height, no alt text — the kind changes only how the value renders, never what it is. This is what makes it fully additive: no migration, and person's built-in Image keeps its `url` kind, its key, its box, and its avatars untouched.

**What changed.** `PersonImageBox` moved to `src/components/build/ImageBox.tsx` as `ImageBox`, generalized with a required `propKey` prop (`propertyPatch: { [propKey]: next }`, upload filename `${propKey}.jpg`); person's two mount points in `MarkdownCanvas.tsx` now pass `propKey="image"` and behave byte-for-byte the same. `person-image.ts` exports the validator as `imageUrl(v)`, with `personImage` kept as a one-line wrapper reading the person's `image` key. `CustomProperties.tsx` dispatches `kind === "image"` to `ImageBox`; the classic canvas renders one `ImageBox` beside the person box for every image-kind property on the type, and both canvases exclude image-kind keys from the plain properties list so the box isn't repeated as a raw row. `contact-links.ts` gives image the same "Open link" href as url; `view-where.ts` offers only is-set/is-empty (a picture isn't searchable text); `ViewRenderer.tsx` shows a 24px thumbnail in a table cell instead of the raw address. Over MCP: `create_type`/`update_type` accept the kind with no code change (they already validate against `PROPERTY_KINDS`); `update_item`'s `propertyPatch` fills, edits, or clears (`null`) an image property the same as any other; `attach_file` gained an optional `propertyKey` that, after the upload, writes the file's stable address into that property via the same `updateItem` call other tools use, and defaults `embedInBody` to false when a `propertyKey` is given (all additive, ADR-183 carve-out).

**What is deferred.** A per-field wide "cover" display style (v1 renders every image kind as the same 112px square box); a drag-to-reposition cropper (v1 stays a deterministic center crop, same as person's); avatars for non-person types on cards and chips.

**Why avatars stay keyed to person's `image`.** Card chips and task rows read `properties.image` directly, with no type-schema lookup, because the perf rule says list rendering can't afford one (Principle 8). Generalizing "the avatar is the first image-kind property" would push that lookup into every list row. So a second person picture, or another type's image, shows on the record and in list columns, but not on chips — deliberately, not an oversight.

## ADR-256: item grid cards always flow; the footer cards always sink to the bottom

**Date:** 2026-09-11 · **Status:** accepted (not core: the stored `canvas_layout` shape is unchanged, `mode` is still parsed) · **Requested by:** Brandon

**Context.** On grid-layout types (those with a saved layout, e.g. Hiring Candidate), Brandon saw scrollbars inside property cards, half-empty cards, and properties rendered below the Type/Created/Updated block and the Save Offline / Share rows, in both the side panel and the full page. He asked for a system fix, not a per-type one: tiles that fit their content and rearrange cleanly at any width.

**Root causes.** (1) System and custom property cards defaulted to ADR-069's `fixed` mode: a set 2-row box whose content scrolls. Short content left the box mostly empty; tall content (a textarea, an image box) scrolled inside it. (2) Even flow cards rounded their measured height UP to whole 40px rows (a 52px step with the margin), so a one-line field cost 92px. (3) `reconcile` appended a newly added property at the very bottom of the saved layout, beneath the footer cards.

**Decision.** Every card renders as flow: height follows content, nothing scrolls inside a cell. The row unit drops from 40px to 8px (a 20px step), so the dead space under any card is at most one step. `reconcile`, which already runs on every read, now sinks the four footer cards (`saveOffline`, `share`, `history`, `meta`) beneath all content cards on every breakpoint, preserving their arrangement relative to each other. So a property added later, or a footer card dragged upward while arranging, settles back beneath the content on the next load.

**What is hidden, not deleted.** The Flow/Fixed pin button is gone from the arrange header and `CardCell` ignores `mode`; the stored `mode` field is still parsed and preserved (`parseCards`, `reconcile`), so no saved layout is rewritten and the fixed rendering could be restored from the data. `scripts/verify-canvas-layout.mts` covers the footer sink.

**Alternatives declined.** Merging the four footer cards into one card (a vocabulary change that drops ids from saved layouts; the sink already gives the same reading order). Enforcing the footer rule inside the drag handler (the read-time rule is one function and also fixes already-saved layouts).
## ADR-257: the update policy is a file the service re-reads, and the install's own pages get a SYSTEM group

**Date:** 2026-09-12
**Status:** accepted — not core: no schema change, no wire change, no change to how any existing MCP or API call behaves. New surface is additive (a new local-only route, two new Build pages, a fourth sidebar group).

**Context.** Brandon asked how to turn off the 15-minute automatic update on his local install, and how to point it at another repository or branch. The answer was "edit `supervisor/config.json` and restart the service", which is exactly the shape ADR-222 rules out for anything an owner is expected to change. Three surfaces wanted the same knob: Build → Updates in the app, the tray icon for someone sitting at the machine signed into nothing, and the install wizard on day one. Two of those have no database and no login, so the `job_state` home that snapshots (ADR-222) and the sync mode use was not available to them.

The same sweep turned up three misreadings on the Updates page. The "Registered, with one catch" warning was a string recorded in `startup-state.json` on 2026-08-26 by an older build and never re-checked; Windows itself reported the task as S4U, Interactive/Background, which is correct. The page called the local install a "source" instance that "updates itself", because its deploy repo equals the shared repo, so it never listed pending commits or offered Update now while the supervisor quietly did the real work. And GitHub reads (the version compare, the Changelog) refused to run without `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which a public repository does not need.

**Decision.**

1. **`<dataDir>/update-policy.json` is the owner's lever for updates.** Shape: `{ mode: "auto" | "manual", everyMinutes, branch, repo, updatedAt }`. The supervisor seeds it from `config.json` on first boot when it is missing, then **re-reads it on a fixed one-minute tick** and asks `updateCheckDue` whether an automatic check is due. `config.update` and `config.branch` become the install-time seed and the testing escape hatch, never the owner's lever. Three writers: the app (`/api/local/update-policy`, owner-gated, refused off a local peer), the tray window's Settings tab, and the wizard by way of the seed. `mode: "prompted"` from old configs reads as `manual` and is never written back. `repo` is a git remote URL, applied with `git remote set-url origin` on the next due tick and logged; a wrong URL cannot break the running app (the fetch fails, keep-last-good holds, the page reports "unknown").
2. **The record re-asks Windows.** On every start the supervisor queries Task Scheduler and rewrites `scope` and `caveat` in `startup-state.json` from what Windows holds now, so a caveat recorded by an older build cannot outlive the truth. The app headline reads "On, with one catch: see below." whenever a caveat exists, so two lines on one card never contradict.
3. **A local peer compares against the branch it follows.** `InstanceIdentity.isLocalPeer` is a first-class fact; a local peer's repo and branch come from the policy file (env as fallback), and `getCodeStatus` runs for satellites *or* local peers. `resolveApplicability` checks the flag **and** the facts behind it (not on Vercel, supervisor dir present), so a fixture or bug that calls a Vercel deploy a local peer still cannot reach the supervisor path.
4. **GitHub reads need no token.** `getGithubConfig()` always returns a config; the one `gh()` chokepoint sends Authorization only when a token exists. Writes go through `requireToken()` and keep saying "not configured" without one. A private repository read anonymously fails as a 404 and surfaces as "unknown", never as "current".
5. **A fourth Build group, SYSTEM,** holds Updates, Network, and two new pages split out of Updates: **Scheduled Jobs** (`/build/jobs`: jobs on this machine, which install runs each shared job, video transcripts) and **Backups** (`/build/backups`: snapshots, and where the weekly backup and export are scheduled). MAINTAIN keeps the pages about caring for data; SYSTEM is the software and the machine it runs on. The word is the one general products use, and it reads correctly on a cloud copy too, which "install" and "machine" would not.
6. **The tray's status balloon becomes a window.** Windows 11 swallows balloon tips from PowerShell, so "Check status" appeared to do nothing. "Ledgr status…" opens a WinForms window: Status (state, version and when it landed, policy, disk use per folder measured after the window paints, jobs, sync role) and Settings (the same policy form as the app). Its only write is the policy file. Still PowerShell + WinForms, no new dependency.

**Why a file and not `job_state` for the policy.** The two readers that matter most, the supervisor and the tray, exist precisely for the moments the app is down or nobody is signed in. A row they cannot read is not a setting they can honor. The file is per-machine by nature, so not syncing it is correct, and it sits beside the signal files the same three parties already share (`update-requested`, `startup-requested`, `restart-requested`).

**Verification.** `scripts/verify-update-policy.mts` (9 checks): the `.mjs` and `.ts` parsers round-trip each other's output, both name the same file, `prompted` reads as manual and is never written, the due arithmetic fires on the first tick after boot and then only on the interval, the form validator refuses what the file must never hold, and the wizard's answers become the first-boot seed. `scripts/verify-updates.mts` gained the `isLocalPeer` field and still passes its fail-closed checks. The tray script passes the PowerShell parser with no errors.

**Affects:** `supervisor/lib.mjs`, `supervisor/ledgr-supervisor.mjs`, `supervisor/ledgr-ctl.mjs`, `supervisor/ledgr-tray.ps1`, `scripts/local-setup.mjs`, `scripts/local-setup-lib.mjs`, `src/lib/update-policy.ts` (new), `src/app/api/local/update-policy/route.ts` (new), `src/components/updates/UpdatePolicy.tsx` (new), `src/lib/updates.ts`, `src/lib/github/client.ts`, `src/components/updates/StartupToggle.tsx`, `src/lib/build-nav.ts`, `src/app/build/{updates,jobs,backups,network}/page.tsx`, `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`, `supervisor/README.md`, `.env.example`.
## ADR-258: type edits patch instead of replacing, and the owner's presentation choices survive a round-trip

**Date:** 2026-09-14
**Status:** accepted, shipped 2026-09-14 (PR #385). Mostly additive (a response field, a new tool, a catalog widget), but it **changes the behavior of two existing MCP tools**, which is the half of ADR-183's carve-out that stays core. Nothing about it changes the database, and no existing caller that sends a complete payload sees any difference.

**Context.** Tyler asked for a Scope field on his Project type and a tab on the project list page. Adding the field cost him the type's icon and every one of his custom status colors, and neither loss was recoverable.

The mechanism is one shape repeated twice. `update_type` and `set_type_statuses` replace wholesale, while `list_types` returned neither the icon nor the status colors. A caller that read the type, added a property, and wrote it back therefore could not preserve what it had never been shown: `parseCommon` maps an omitted `icon` to `null`, and the status mapper falls back to `CATEGORY_DEFAULT_COLOR` for any term resent without a color. Read-before-write, the documented discipline, was not sufficient to avoid the loss. There was also no recovery path: the live instance is hosted, the working copy's `.env.local` points at a stale database, and config writes have no revision history the way items do.

Two smaller findings came out of the same session. `WidgetCanvas` renders neither `CustomProperties` nor `RelationProperties`, so on a project-style record the type's own fields were invisible and uneditable, which is why the new Scope field could not be set from the record at all. And list tabs, stored in `users.settings.listTabs`, were reachable only from a Clerk session at `PATCH /api/types/[key]/list-tabs`, so "put this view on the Projects page as a tab" was the one part of workspace shaping an assistant could not do.

**Decision.**

1. **`update_type` patches.** The merge happens at the MCP boundary: the handler reads the stored type and fills in any field the caller omitted before calling `parseTypeInput`. `parseTypeInput`'s "patch" mode is unchanged, because the Build form legitimately posts every field and means it. `propertySchema` still replaces when sent (it is a list, and partial-list semantics would be worse), and `icon: ""` still clears deliberately. `label` is no longer required, so changing one field is one field.
2. **`set_type_statuses` preserves color per key.** A term resent without a color keeps the color stored against that key; only a genuinely new key falls back to its category color. Recategorizing a term keeps the owner's color, on the same reasoning: they picked it.
3. **`list_types` returns `icon` and each term's `color`.** Preservation on omission fixes the accident; returning the values is what makes a deliberate round-trip possible at all.
4. **A `properties` widget in the catalog.** Requires `custom_properties`, record scope, rendered by `WidgetCanvas` as a Properties card pairing `CustomProperties` with `RelationProperties`, exactly as `MarkdownCanvas` does. It follows the Overview self-healing rule already in that file: shown when the composition asks for it, **or** whenever the type defines fields and the owner has not hidden the section. `reconcileComposition` only drops vanished widgets and never back-fills new ones, so without the self-heal every existing record would have stayed blind to its own fields.
5. **`set_list_tabs` is an MCP tool.** Reads the effective strip when called with only `typeKey`, replaces it when given `tabs`, restores the virtual defaults on `reset`. It normalizes before handing to `parseLenses` (a view tab's label defaults to the view's name, an id is derived from the label) and refuses a `viewId` that is not one of the owner's saved views by name, because `parseLenses` silently drops a malformed entry, which is right for a stored blob and wrong for a tool call. `describe_workspace` gained a compact `listTabs` map.

**Why the merge sits at the MCP boundary and not in `parseTypeInput`.** The form and the model are different callers with different intents. A form that posts every field is stating the whole record; a model sending two fields is stating two fields. Changing the shared parser would have made the form's explicit clear unexpressible, so the seam is where the intent differs.

**Alternatives declined.** Making `list_types` return everything and leaving the writes destructive (documentation as a safety mechanism, which is what already failed here). Hardcoding a properties strip into the project canvas outside the widget catalog (faster, but unremovable, and wrong for every other widget-home type). A separate read tool for list tabs (a strip that must be resent whole is better read by the tool that writes it).

**Verification.** `npm run typecheck`, `npm run lint`, `npm run build`, `npm run verify:ci`. Not yet exercised against live data: the MCP tools are reached through the hosted instance, so the round-trip check (add a property, confirm the icon and colors survive) runs after deploy.

**Affects:** `src/lib/mcp/tools/types.ts`, `src/lib/mcp/tools/workspace.ts`, `src/lib/widgets.ts`, `src/lib/record-widgets.ts`, `src/components/canvas/WidgetCanvas.tsx`, `src/lib/mcp/guide.ts`, `src/lib/mcp/user-guide.ts`.

## ADR-259: a memory can be superseded, and `remember` warns about overlap and missing links

**Date:** 2026-09-14
**Status:** accepted (Brandon-directed, built on branch `feat/memory-supersedes`). **Not core** under the ADR-183 carve-out: one optional argument on an existing tool, new fields on its response, a new role value on the existing free-text `relations.role`, and one more marker string inside the `age` field search hits already carry. Every existing caller keeps working byte-for-byte on what it sends. Heads-up posted in `COLLAB.md`.

**Context.** A research review of how durable AI memory is structured (Anthropic's memory tool, Claude Code auto-memory, Letta, Mem0, Zep/Graphiti, LangGraph, LongMemEval; the report is a Ledgr note titled "Durable memory for an AI assistant: research review and Ledgr recommendations (2026-09-14)") scored the ADR-137/ADR-230 model as sound on shape and weak on two mechanisms. First, the protocol's "file a new dated memory when the world changes, never rewrite the old one" left contradicted pairs side by side with nothing but their ages to tell them apart: "the Mail MCP never sends" (08-29) beside "the connector CAN send" (08-30); "production is BC-EDGEWOOD over Tailscale" (09-01, filed evergreen) beside "the hub address is ledgr.brasco.fyi" (09-13). Zep's answer is an invalidation edge with a date, not deletion. Second, `remember` created unconditionally; nothing surfaced an existing near-duplicate or a person named in the title with no link, so the protocol's "check first" and "link, don't restate" rules had no help from the tool. A third finding was pure hygiene: STALE rendered in stumps but never in `search_items` hits, which is where Tier 2 memories actually appear, and a dozen facts carrying hostnames and URLs were filed evergreen, a horizon that is never flagged STALE.

**Decision.**

1. **A `supersedes` edge.** `relations.role = "supersedes"`, direction OLD -> NEW. `remember` takes an optional `supersedes: <old memory id>` and writes the edge after creating the new memory; `relate_items(old, new, role: "supersedes")` links a pair after the fact. The old memory is never edited, hidden, or deleted.
2. **One marker, rendered in both places.** `memoryMarker()` in `src/lib/memory.ts` returns `""`, `", STALE"`, or `", SUPERSEDED <date> -><new id>"` (SUPERSEDED wins). The stump index uses it, and `search_items` now appends it to the `age` field of memory hits, so `age` reads "13d ago, SUPERSEDED 2026-09-13 ->7965…" instead of a bare age. `MemoryStump` gains `supersededBy`.
3. **`remember` is advisory, never blocking.** Before the write it runs a pg_trgm title-similarity query over live memories (floor 0.2, top 3) and, when `about` is empty, a substring match of live person and project titles inside the candidate title. The response carries `possibleOverlap`, `aboutSuggestions`, and a one-line `hint` when either is non-empty. The agent decides; nothing is auto-merged or auto-linked (Principle 3).
4. **Horizon rule tightened in the protocol text and the tool description.** Evergreen is for identity, convictions, standing preferences, and how-to-work-with-the-owner rules. Anything carrying a hostname, URL, port, version, roster, price, or the current state of an install or project is seasonal.

**Declined, on purpose.** An access counter on memories (last-read, read-count) was proposed as the evidence for promote/demote and for access-based decay; Brandon declined it in favor of the stricter horizon rule plus STALE. Embeddings, an extraction cron, hard deletion or TTL, and a knowledge-graph engine were all judged wrong for a ~200-memory store; the reasoning is in the report note.

**Consequences.** No migration. The Build → AI Memory page shows a "superseded" badge on replaced stumps. A one-off consolidation pass on 2026-09-14 (logged in the Ledgr note "Memory consolidation log 2026-09-14") retagged misfiled evergreens, merged three overlapping pinned pointers into one, moved person facts onto person items, folded dated build-log memories into their project bodies, and linked the known contradicted pairs with `supersedes` edges.

## ADR-260: a type's content lives on named surfaces, and every reader resolves the same list

**Date:** 2026-09-16
**Status:** accepted (Tyler-directed; Brandon's agreement assumed at Tyler's direction, 2026-09-16, with Tyler to raise anything that should have waited). **Core**, on two counts: it adds a field to the module contract (`ModuleTypeDef.surfaces` / `ModuleCapability.surfaces`, and the module system boundary is core), and it changes what an existing write stores (the canonical-format stamp below). The MCP and REST read additions are separately covered by the ADR-183 carve-out. Heads-up posted in `COLLAB.md`.

**Context.** Songs and papers have had multi-surface canvases since their modules shipped, and the 2026-09-14 Notes tab added a fifth surface to papers and a second to songs. None of that was ever taught to the MCP layer or the REST API. Grepping `src/lib/mcp/` for "song", "paper" or "chordpro" returned two hits, both inside prose in `user-guide.ts`. Three concrete failures followed from that.

First, and worst, **every MCP write path stamped `{ format: "markdown" }`**, in `args.ts`, `context.ts`, `attachments.ts`, `items.ts`, `memory.ts` and `records.ts`. The `song` type declares `canonicalFormat: CHORDPRO_FORMAT`. So an agent creating or editing a song stored a ChordPro chart labelled markdown, and three things then misbehaved with no error anywhere: `print-html.ts` gates the chord-chart render on the format and silently printed prose, `body-text.ts` indexed chords and directives instead of routing through `chordProToText` for lyrics-only search, and `item-tokens-service.ts` began resolving `{{item.*}}` tokens inside a chart. `canonicalFormatForType()` already existed and answered this exactly; nothing called it.

Second, **`list_types` hid the type's bespoke nature.** Its own description tells every model to call it first, but the handler returned key, label, icon, statuses and properties while dropping `capability`, which `describe_workspace` and `typeView` both already returned. A song and a paper arrived looking like ordinary single-body types.

Third, **the surfaces were returned but never named.** `GET /api/items/[id]` hands back the item row including `properties`, and MCP's `rowView` passes `properties` through, so `notes`, `sections` and `quoteBank` were on the wire the whole time as an untyped blob. Nothing said which key was scratch and which was the deliverable, so an agent asked to "add my notes to this paper" appended to the draft, the one surface the .docx renders from.

**Decision.**

1. **A surface is a first-class part of the module contract.** `SurfaceDef` (id, label, storage, format, description, `primary`, `readOnly`) declared on `ModuleTypeDef.surfaces` and `ModuleCapability.surfaces` in `src/lib/modules.ts`. `storage` is one of `{kind:"body"}`, `{kind:"property", key}`, or `{kind:"derived", from:[...]}`. It sits in the registry because the registry already owns a type's code behavior (canvas, canonical format, exporters), so surfaces resolve through the same boundary rather than being special-cased in each reader.
2. **Papers declare five, songs declare two.** Paper: Notes (`properties.notes`), Shape (`properties.sections`), Quote Bank (`properties.quoteBank`), Outline (derived from Shape plus Quote Bank), Draft (body, `primary`). Song: Notes (`properties.notes`), Chart (body, chordpro, `primary`). Shape, Quote Bank and Outline are `readOnly`: the first two are structured JSON, the third stores nothing. Each carries a `description` written for a model deciding where to put something, which is the field that stops "add my notes" landing in the draft.
3. **One resolver, two readers.** `src/lib/item-surfaces.ts` pairs each declared surface with its stored content. MCP `get_item` and `GET /api/items/[id]` both call it, so the two cannot drift. The body-storage surface reports `isBody: true` and carries no `content`, because duplicating it would double a long paper's response and would bypass `get_item`'s large-body paging.
4. **Surface-targeted writes.** `update_item` takes `surface` plus `content` and routes to the body or the backing property, refusing an unknown id with the real list and a read-only one with the writable list. It rewrites its own arguments and then goes down the ordinary patch path, so validation, revision snapshots and `body_text` are untouched.
5. **The canonical format is stamped in the mutation layer, not per caller.** `createItem` and `updateItem` re-stamp a written body with `canonicalFormatForType`. Fixing it there rather than in the six MCP call sites makes it structural: the stored format no longer depends on which door a write came through, and the REST API is fixed by the same change. `assertTypeExists` now returns the type's capability, which it was already reading, so `createItem` pays nothing and `updateItem` pays one extra type lookup only when a body is actually written.

**Consequences.** No migration and no schema change. An ordinary note or task is byte-for-byte unchanged: it resolves to a single markdown body surface, and `get_item` omits `surfaces` entirely for it. A type that borrows `chord-chart` or `paper-workspace` inherits that tool's surfaces, so the contract is not pinned to the `song` and `paper` keys. Existing songs whose bodies were mis-stamped markdown heal on their next write rather than by a backfill, which keeps this additive and reversible. `scripts/verify-surfaces.mts` covers the contract in 30 pure checks.

**Not decided here.** `create_item` does not yet take a `surface` argument; creating a paper still writes its body and then patches its notes. The exporters (`song-chordpro-pco`, the .docx route) are still not reachable over MCP.

## ADR-261: the paper Draft is the shared editor, and footnote markers are protected from it

**Date:** 2026-09-16
**Status:** accepted (Tyler-directed). **Not core.** The Papers canvas is a module internal, and the shared body dialect is unchanged: footnotes are still not in it, still Papers-only, and still render as literal text on every other surface. The one shared-editor addition is an opt-in extension that is off by default.

**Context.** The Draft tab was a monospace `<textarea>` (`PaperMarkdownArea`), so writing a paper meant writing raw markdown with none of the slash menu, mentions, attachments or preview every other surface has. Tyler asked for it to become a proper canvas.

The textarea's own header gave two reasons for itself, and they turned out to be worth checking rather than trusting. The first, that the parent splices a citation at the caret through a forwarded ref, was **stale**: `draftRef` was declared and forwarded but never read by anything, so no live feature depended on it. The second was real. Driving the actual editor headlessly showed `@tiptap/markdown` backslash-escapes every footnote marker on serialize: `[^1]` becomes `\[^1\]`, and `[^1]: John Calvin…` becomes `\[^1\]: …`. `msm-docx.ts` matches definitions with `/^\[\^([^\]]+)\]:/` and skips any marker whose definition it cannot find, so a straight swap would have dropped every citation from the .docx, silently, on the first keystroke. That export is the module's whole deliverable.

**Decision.** `FootnoteMarkdownFix` in `src/components/markdown-editor/extensions.ts` patches the markdown manager's `serialize` to undo the escaping on footnote syntax, the same shape as `MarkdownEscapeFix` (ADR for the colored-span bug) and `EmptyListItemFix` before it. It patches `serialize` rather than `encodeTextForMarkdown` because a footnote marker carries no mark to key off; it is bare text, so the fix has to be a pass over the finished document.

It is **opt-in**, threaded as `preserveFootnotes` through `MarkdownEditor`, `BodyEditor` and `TabbedBody`, and set only by the Papers Draft. Un-escaping `\[^…\]` globally would rewrite text an owner typed literally in an ordinary note, and footnotes are deliberately not a shared-dialect element.

The Draft now mounts `BodyEditor` with `preserveFootnotes`. `PaperMarkdownArea` is left in the tree unused rather than deleted, per the defer-by-hiding rule, so the raw surface is one line away if the rich one proves wrong for academic prose.

**Also here.** The Notes surface on both papers and songs gets canvas tabs (`tabsEnabled` on its `BodyEditor`). Thinking space is exactly the content that wants splitting, and tabs are sections of the same markdown string, so `properties.notes` is still one string and `extractBodyText` still folds all of it into `body_text`. Tabs are deliberately **not** enabled on a paper's Draft: the Draft is the canonical artifact the .docx renders from, and a tab marker there would flatten into a stray `## Title` heading in the exported document.

**Consequences.** `scripts/verify-markdown-escape.mts` gains five checks covering the escaping, the round-trip, and that the exporter's own regex matches the result, including one asserting the fix stays opt-in. The .docx path itself is unchanged and `verify-papers.mts` still passes.

## ADR-262: the machine API can read a body, and refuses what it does not understand

**Date:** 2026-09-16
**Status:** accepted (Tyler-directed). **Not core**, under the ADR-183 carve-out: every change here is purely additive — a new route, two new query parameters, a new opt-in — and an existing caller's request comes back byte-for-byte what it did before. The one clause worth naming out loud is "list queries never select `body`" (CLAUDE.md rule 8), which this deliberately puts a door in; see below.

**Context.** `/api/machine/items` exists so that a bulk or byte-exact content move is not a retyping job. It could write a body and never read one, which broke the single workflow it was built for.

The case that surfaced it: copying two notes into a paper's `notes` property. The 94KB one worked only because an MCP `get_item` result that large spills to a file on disk, where `jq` could pick it up and push it back — an accident of tooling, not a supported path. The 10.7KB one fit in context, never touched disk, and had to be retyped into the payload character by character. It came out **10,736 characters against 10,737**. Every element anyone would think to check had been checked individually: emoji variation selectors, escaped tildes, `&amp;` entities, trailing newlines. The missing character was invisible and unlocatable without a reference copy, which is precisely the silent corruption this surface is supposed to make impossible.

Four smaller failures cost time on the way there, and they share a cause: the route ignored what it did not recognize. `?id=<uuid>` was dropped on the floor and answered with an unfiltered list, so a request for one item returned a different one under a 200. `?includeBody`, `?fields` likewise. And `GET /api/machine/items/<uuid>` matched no route, fell through to the Next.js page tree, and returned the app's **HTML shell** — which to a script that does not sniff content types is indistinguishable from a successful fetch.

**Decision.** Four parts.

1. **`?includeBody=true` on the list.** Off by default, so no existing payload changes size. On, each row carries its stored `{ format, text }` object — the same shape PATCH accepts, so a read feeds back into a write with nothing to reshape. Implemented as `listItemsWithBodies`, a separate function from `listItems` rather than a flag branching the `.select()`: a ternary there would have handed every existing caller a union row type, and keeping them separate means the body-free query stays the one everything in the app reaches for. Both share `listClauses`, so they cannot filter differently.

2. **`GET /api/machine/items/<uuid>`**, the token half of `GET /api/items/[id]`. Same `getItem`, same `resolveSurfaces` (ADR-260), so it returns the body, the custom `properties`, and the named surfaces.
